# Cabinet

> A productivity kit that makes one person a whole team: build anything with AI agents while the owner brings the vision, the judgment and the final say, for one person or every member of a team of any size. It amplifies people, never replaces them. It creates a "workspace" of plain Markdown and shell scripts: roles with clear authority, a handoff log between agents, a daily brief with the owner's sign-off queue, independent qa and security review, guardrails in each agent tool that keep push, merge, release and publish with the owner, schedules (launchd on macOS, systemd or cron on Linux) and encrypted backups. macOS and Linux. npm package `@tarekraafat/cabinet`, command `cabinet`.

Requirements: git, Node.js and npm, and at least one agent tool; openssl (and `secret-tool` on Linux) for backups only. `cabinet new`, `init` and `bootstrap` check them first and, in a terminal, offer to install the missing ones; `cabinet doctor --json` (check IDs `deps.required`, `deps.backups`) and `cabinet next --json` (step `deps`) give the exact install command. An agent tells the owner what is missing and that command, and does not install system packages itself.

**An agent asked to set Cabinet up for someone follows [docs/agent-setup.md](docs/agent-setup.md)**: the questions to ask, the commands to run (with `--yes` and `--dry-run` first), and what to show the person before `cabinet bootstrap` changes their machine. Agents inside a workspace follow its `CABINET.md` (from `core/CABINET.md`), then its `AGENTS.md`. Only agents changing the kit itself follow `AGENTS.md` at the root of this repository.

Every page below in one file, for reading in one go: [llms-full.txt](llms-full.txt).

This file is every page listed in llms.txt, in that order, generated by tools/build-llms-full.js. Links between pages are relative to the repository root.


========================================================================
File: docs/agent-setup.md
========================================================================

# Set up Cabinet for someone

For an AI agent that a person asked to set up Cabinet for them, from this repository or its link. Follow these steps in order. You are setting Cabinet up, not changing it: the `AGENTS.md` at the root of this repository is for people and agents who develop the kit, and does not apply to this job.

## Ground rules

- **The person decides; you prepare and explain.** Ask before anything that changes their machine outside the new workspace, and show what will change first.
- **Your shell is not a terminal,** so Cabinet's commands ask no questions there. Ask the person yourself, then pass every answer as an option with `--yes`. Run each command with `--dry-run` first and show the person what it would do.
- **Never install system packages yourself** (git, Node.js, a package manager's packages). Give the person the command; `cabinet doctor --json` names it (check `deps.required`).
- **Never run `cabinet new` or `cabinet init` inside this repository.** The workspace is a folder of its own, or a folder inside the person's project.
- **Never push, merge, release or publish.** The person does.

## 1. Check the machine

Cabinet runs on macOS and Linux (Windows only through WSL). It needs git, Node.js 18 or newer and npm, and at least one agent tool the person uses (Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, Qwen Code, Grok, opencode or the Cursor CLI; Gemini CLI for interactive sessions only, not scheduled runs).

```sh
git --version && node -v && npm -v
git config --global user.name; git config --global user.email   # empty: ask for them (step 3)
```

If a tool is missing, tell the person how to install it (the README's [Install](../README.md#install) has the commands) and wait.

## 2. Get the `cabinet` command

Install the package:

```sh
npm i -g @tarekraafat/cabinet
```

Only if the person wants the newest code from GitHub instead, from a clone they keep: it is what runs, so ask where it should live, and reuse the clone you already have if you cloned the repository to read it. Update it later with `git -C <clone> pull`. Linking the command changes the person's machine, so ask first:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/TarekRaafat/cabinet.git ~/cabinet-kit   # or reuse your clone
mkdir -p ~/.local/bin && ln -s ~/cabinet-kit/bin/cabinet ~/.local/bin/cabinet
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"   # for your own shell, which reads no rc file
command -v cabinet
```

If `~/.local/bin` is not on the person's own PATH, ask, then add that `export` line to their `~/.zshrc` or `~/.bashrc`.

## 3. Ask the person

Ask the first three, then propose the rest as defaults in one message and let the person change any of them.

| Ask, in plain words | Option | Default |
|---|---|---|
| What is the project called? | `--name "Name"` | the folder name |
| Is it a new project, or one that exists already (a folder or a code repository)? | `cabinet new` or `cabinet init` | |
| Which AI tool do you use? | `--runner claude\|codex\|antigravity\|qwen\|grok\|opencode\|cursor` | the first one installed |
| Where should its folder go? (new projects) | `[dir]` | `~/dev/<name>`; suggest a folder they know, such as `~/Documents/<name>`, to someone who is not a developer |
| What kind of work is it: code, or something else such as design, writing or music? | `--roles "..."` | the seven core roles: chief-of-staff, product-manager, architect, qa, security, design-lead, finance |
| Any code repositories to include? (new projects) | `--repo <url>`, repeatable | none |
| Your name and email, for the record of changes? | `--owner "Name" --email you@example.com` | git's global identity; when it is empty, pass both, or setup creates the workspace without saving it (no commit) |
| When should the daily brief with your decisions arrive? | `--brief-time "7 AM"`, or `off` | 7:00 AM every day |
| Which day does your week start? | `--week-start sunday` | `sunday` |
| Short or standard messages from the team? | `--writing short\|standard` | `standard` |
| A weekly spending limit for the agents' runs? Scheduled runs use the person's own agent tool account and its plan or usage costs. | `--budget <dollars>\|off` (and `--price "<in> <out>"` for codex, cursor, qwen or antigravity) | off |
| Encrypted daily backups, and to which folder (outside the project)? | `--backup-dir <folder>\|off` | off |

**Work that is not code** (design, writing, marketing, music, finance): pick roles that fit, for example `--roles "product-manager design-lead brand-designer qa"` for brand and design work (`chief-of-staff` is always on). Leave out `--repo`. Later the team works in folders of the workspace, each with one owning role in the team table of `AGENTS.md` (the template has `brand/` for brand-designer), and its standing documents (a brand guide, a style guide) go in `guides/`. Tell the person that Cabinet's defaults are still made for code first ([roadmap](../ROADMAP.md)), and that agents can only make what their tools can make: text, SVG and HTML well; files in a design or audio app only with a tool connected for it.

A website that is only designed (mockups) is design work: HTML and SVG pages in a workspace folder such as `website/`, with its own row in the team table. A website that is built and published is code: it needs a repository, which gets a builder (below).

**No repository yet:** leave out `--repo`. Builders, the roles that write code, come with repositories, so tell the person that coding starts once one exists: create it (an empty folder with `git init` is enough), then `cabinet repo add <url-or-path> --apply`.

**An existing folder of files that is not a repository** (design files, documents): `cabinet init` in that folder makes it the workspace and keeps every file in it.

## 4. Create the workspace

A new project:

```sh
cabinet new ~/dev/taskly --name "Taskly" --runner claude --yes --dry-run   # show the person
cabinet new ~/dev/taskly --name "Taskly" --runner claude --yes
```

An existing project, from its top folder. Choose the layout with the person ([layouts](layouts.md)):

| Layout | Options | When |
|---|---|---|
| Inside, private (the default) | `--inside --private` | One person's team. A `cabinet/` folder with its own git; no tracked file of the project changes. |
| Inside, shared | `--inside --shared` | The team is part of the project for everyone who clones it. Nothing is committed; the person reviews and commits. |
| Beside | `--beside [--workspace <folder>]` | A separate folder next to the project (default `<project>-hq`). |
| Around | (run in a folder that is not a repo) | A folder holding several repos becomes the workspace. |

```sh
cd ~/code/shopfront
cabinet init --inside --private --runner codex --yes --dry-run   # show the person
cabinet init --inside --private --runner codex --yes
```

When the project already has its own `AGENTS.md`, the private layout leaves it alone and says so. Codex, opencode, Gemini and Cursor read only that file, so without a pointer they never meet the team. Offer the person to add this section to the end of their `AGENTS.md` (it is the one the shared layout adds by itself):

```markdown
## Agent team

The agent team for this project works from `cabinet/`. Before any task that involves handoffs, specs, verdicts or the team's roles, read `cabinet/CABINET.md`, then `cabinet/AGENTS.md`. Their paths are relative to `cabinet/`.
```

Prefer it to starting those tools in `cabinet/`: Codex, for one, may write only inside the folder it starts in, so started in `cabinet/` it could not change the project's code. For the same reason Codex's default sandbox may not let a scheduled brief write its file; if `BRIEF.md` stays empty after the first scheduled run, tell the person ([agent tools](concepts.md#agent-tools-and-models)).

## 5. Set up the machine, only after a yes

`cabinet bootstrap` changes this machine for every project on it, so show the dry run and explain it first:

```sh
cabinet -C ~/dev/taskly bootstrap --dry-run
```

What to tell the person it does ([guardrails](guardrails.md)):

- **A push gate for every repository on this machine:** a global git pre-push hook (through `core.hooksPath`) that asks for `yes` at their terminal for every `git push`. Agents have no terminal, so their pushes are refused. A repository's own hooks still run.
- **Deny rules in each agent tool it finds** (for example `~/.claude/settings.json`, `~/.codex/rules/default.rules`): push, merge, release and publish commands are blocked. Rules are only added, and a backup copy of each file is made first.
- **Schedules:** the daily brief (and backups when they are on), through launchd on macOS or systemd or cron on Linux.
- **A secrets check** before each commit in the workspace.

Then, if the person says yes:

```sh
cabinet -C ~/dev/taskly bootstrap
```

For a machine that should not run the workspace's jobs (a teammate's), add `--no-schedules`. To undo: [Undoing the guardrails](guardrails.md#undoing-the-guardrails), or `cabinet remove` for the whole workspace.

Tell the person two more things before they answer:

- **It changes your own rules too.** The deny rules apply to you, the agent running the setup, from then on: you can no longer push, merge or publish, as intended.
- **It can wait.** Without `bootstrap` the workspace still works when they work with the team in person, but nothing runs on its own (no daily brief, no backups) and nothing guards a push. Work without code has nothing to push, so the brief schedule is the main thing it brings there. They can run it any time later.

## 6. Check the result

```sh
cabinet -C ~/dev/taskly doctor --json   # "problems": 0, or each problem with its fix
cabinet -C ~/dev/taskly next --json     # the steps left, in order
```

`-C` takes the workspace, or for an inside layout the project's top folder (commands find the workspace from there). Fix what you may (a step with a command that changes only the workspace); bring the rest to the person.

## 7. Tell the person

- Where the workspace is, and that it is saved (committed; or, without a name and email, how to commit it).
- **Fill the `TBD` lines in `AGENTS.md`:** what the project is, its rules, and how it is checked. Offer to draft them together.
- **How to work with the team:** open the agent tool in the workspace (for an inside layout, in the project, once the tool can find the team there: see step 4) and give it a task in plain words; each morning, read `BRIEF.md` and answer its sign-off queue in one message.
- They push and publish themselves; agents cannot.
- What `bootstrap` changed on the machine, and how to undo it.
- `cabinet next` always says what to do next.

More: [recipes](recipes.md) for everyday tasks, and [Use Cabinet from a script or an agent](recipes.md#use-cabinet-from-a-script-or-an-agent) for the JSON every command gives.


========================================================================
File: README.md
========================================================================

<img src="docs/logo.svg" width="96" height="96" alt="The Cabinet mark: seven seats around a table, one place left open for the owner">

# Cabinet

One person, a whole team. Build anything with AI agents, and stay in charge.

Cabinet is a productivity kit that makes one person a whole team. It does not replace you; it multiplies you. Agents fill every seat your work needs (architecture, design, writing, review, finance, and any specialty you lack), and you stay the one who decides. Alone, you work like a full company. In a team, every member does.

In practice, Cabinet gives a project a small company: roles with clear authority (chief of staff, product manager, architect, qa, security, design lead, finance, builders that write the code in each repo the way it is already built, optional specialists, and any role your project needs, drafted for it from a one-line brief), one place where agents hand work to each other, a daily brief that puts every decision you must make in one queue, independent review before anything ships, and guardrails that keep every push, merge and publish with you. It is plain Markdown and shell scripts, so any agent tool can run it.

Cabinet is for one person or a team of any size, and for anything agents can build: code, apps and websites, design, writing, marketing, music, finance. Beyond the core roles, every seat a project needs is drafted for it. Today its defaults are made for code (builders in repos, guardrails on push); other work runs through roles drafted for it and specs on workspace areas, and making that path as complete is on the [roadmap](ROADMAP.md).

- **Platform:** macOS and Linux ([what differs](docs/concepts.md#macos-and-linux)). Windows through WSL is on the [roadmap](ROADMAP.md).
- **Status:** on npm as `@tarekraafat/cabinet` ([Install](#install)); every version and what changed is in the [changelog](CHANGELOG.md).
- **Built with Cabinet:** Cabinet is built and maintained with Cabinet.
- **Works with:** Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Antigravity, Qwen Code, Grok, opencode, the Cursor CLI, and any other tool that reads `AGENTS.md`.
- **Set up by your AI agent:** give your agent tool this link with "Set up Cabinet for me, following docs/agent-setup.md". [The guide](docs/agent-setup.md) tells it what to ask you, what to run, and what to show you before anything changes on your machine.

## Contents

- [Why Cabinet](#why-cabinet)
- [Quick start](#quick-start)
- [A day with Cabinet](#a-day-with-cabinet)
- [Words you will see](#words-you-will-see)
- [Install](#install)
- [Start a new project](#start-a-new-project)
- [Add Cabinet to an existing project](#add-cabinet-to-an-existing-project)
- [Change settings later](#change-settings-later)
- [Update the kit](#update-the-kit)
- [Remove Cabinet](#remove-cabinet)
- [Develop the kit](#develop-the-kit)
- Learn: [tutorial](docs/tutorial.md) (your first day, about 15 minutes), [recipes](docs/recipes.md) (common tasks)
- Reference: [commands](docs/commands.md), [layouts](docs/layouts.md), [concepts](docs/concepts.md), [guardrails](docs/guardrails.md), [backups](docs/backups.md), [troubleshooting](docs/troubleshooting.md)

## Why Cabinet

Cabinet started as one person's own setup: a product manager, UX/UI designer and developer, with more than ten years in each. For a year and a half, on small, medium and large products in production, it has been how he works. Working alone, he has the agents do most of the work across product, design, development and writing, while he brings the vision and signs off; his output grew about tenfold. With a team of five on a project that needed three times as many people, it gave each person two more teammates, all following the same guidelines, design system, workflow and process toward one goal. A few colleagues who saw the results tried it and found the same. It became this kit so anyone can start with it instead of rebuilding it. It is open source.

What it believes:

- **People amplified, not replaced.** Every person becomes a whole team, or a whole company. Agents bring the skills and the hours; the person brings vision, judgment, and the final say.
- **More output per person, not more headcount.**
- **A small company, not a corporate org chart.** Every repo and area has exactly one owner, and nothing is done twice.
- **People decide, agents do the work.** Agents recommend; you sign off on anything irreversible, public or costly, and you always know what is happening.
- **For anyone.** One person or a team of any size, building anything, working their own way.

## Quick start

```sh
npm i -g @tarekraafat/cabinet     # the cabinet command, everywhere
cabinet new                       # answers a few questions, creates and commits the workspace
cd <your new workspace>
cabinet next                      # what to do next, in order
cabinet bootstrap --dry-run       # see what it would change on this machine
cabinet bootstrap                 # guardrails for your agent tools, and the daily brief schedule
cabinet doctor                    # everything that needs attention; --fix runs the fixes it knows
```

New to Cabinet? The [tutorial](docs/tutorial.md) walks through the first day. Then fill the `TBD` lines in `AGENTS.md`: what the product is, its rules, and how to test it. Every command works from any folder inside the workspace or its project, and all of them follow one pattern: one word for the workspace as a whole (`cabinet doctor`), a noun then a verb for what it holds (`cabinet role add`, `cabinet repo list`); `cabinet help` lists them ([how commands are named](docs/commands.md#how-commands-are-named)). Several projects? One workspace each; `cabinet list` shows them all, and `cabinet digest` gathers every sign-off queue into one morning read.

## A day with Cabinet

1. **Morning.** At the time you chose, the chief-of-staff agent writes `BRIEF.md`. It starts with the sign-off queue: every decision only you can make, each as a plain question with lettered options, the experts' recommendations and whether it can be undone.
2. **You answer in one message**, for example "approve 1 and 3; 2: no; 4: wait until Friday". The agents write your answers into the right specs and handoffs.
3. **The agents work.** Each owns its repos and passes work to the others through `HANDOFFS.md`. The agent that built something never verifies it: qa and security do, and either can block it. Screenshots and recordings of the work are links in the brief, one click to open. `cabinet spec run <spec>` runs those steps for a whole feature, start to ready, so you start no agent by hand.
4. **You push** what has passed review, from your own terminal. No agent can push, merge, release or publish.

## Words you will see

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Workspace | The folder that holds the team's files (`CABINET.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `HANDOFFS.md`, roles, specs, notes) and usually the product repos. It is its own private git repo. |
| Layout | Where the workspace sits: a new folder, around an existing folder of repos, inside a project as `cabinet/`, or beside a project. See [layouts](docs/layouts.md). |
| Slug | The workspace's short name (`acme`). It names its schedules, logs, backups and backup key, so projects on one machine never collide. |
| Guide | A standing document the agents follow, such as a brand guide, style guide, policy or business document. It lives in `guides/`, with a row in `AGENTS.md`. |
| Role | An agent's job description: what it owns, decides, escalates and may write. Kit roles live in `.cabinet/roles/`; a project adds notes in `roles/`. |
| Spec | One file per feature in `specs/`: the problem, the rules, testable acceptance criteria, your decisions, and the builders' plan. Work bigger than a small task is built only from a spec that is ready. |
| Handoff | One entry in `HANDOFFS.md`: who it is for, what changed, what they need to do. The only channel between agents. |
| Sign-off queue | The top of `BRIEF.md`: every decision waiting on you. |
| Tiers | Who decides what: the agent (reversible, in its own files), its lead (reversible, across repos), or you (irreversible, public, or costs money). |
| Guardrails | Rules installed in each agent tool, plus a git hook, that keep push, merge, release and publish with you. See [guardrails](docs/guardrails.md). |

More in [concepts](docs/concepts.md).

## Install

You need macOS or Linux, and:

| Required | For |
|---|---|
| git | Every command, handoffs and the guardrails |
| Node.js 18 or newer, and npm | Installing Cabinet and pinning its version in each workspace; the scripts' shared logic runs with Node |
| At least one agent tool | Running the team and its scheduled jobs: Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, Qwen Code, Grok, opencode, the Cursor CLI, or your own command (Gemini CLI for interactive sessions only) |
| A scheduler | launchd on macOS (built in); systemd user timers on Linux, or cron where the machine did not boot with systemd |

| Optional | For | Without it |
|---|---|---|
| openssl | Encrypted backups (built into macOS) | No backups; everything else works |
| `secret-tool` (Linux) | Keeping the backup passphrase in the secret store, as the keychain does on macOS | Not needed with cron, which reads a passphrase file; or set `CABINET_BACKUP_PASSPHRASE` ([macOS and Linux](docs/concepts.md#macos-and-linux)) |
| `notify-send` (Linux) | `cabinet digest --notify` | The digest is still written, with no notification |
| lsof | `cabinet move` checking that no agent session still has the folder open | The move skips that check |

`cabinet new`, `init` and `bootstrap` check for the required tools first and, in a terminal, offer to install the missing ones with your package manager; `cabinet doctor --fix` does the same later, and asks first for openssl or `secret-tool` when backups are on. Node.js and npm come first by hand, since npm installs cabinet:

- macOS: `brew install node` (git and openssl come with macOS and its command line tools).
- Debian or Ubuntu: `sudo apt install git nodejs npm`, and for the optional ones `openssl libsecret-tools libnotify-bin lsof`. Ubuntu 22.04 and Debian 11 install a Node.js older than 18; there, install a current one from [nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org).

```sh
npm i -g @tarekraafat/cabinet     # the short `cabinet` command everywhere
npx @tarekraafat/cabinet new      # or no install: run it through npx when you need it
```

To run the newest code from GitHub instead of the released package, clone the repository somewhere you keep (the clone is what runs) and link the command into a folder on your PATH:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/TarekRaafat/cabinet.git ~/cabinet-kit
mkdir -p ~/.local/bin && ln -s ~/cabinet-kit/bin/cabinet ~/.local/bin/cabinet
command -v cabinet   # nothing printed? add  export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"  to ~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc
```

Update it with `git -C ~/cabinet-kit pull`. Create workspaces elsewhere, never inside the clone. Moving from a clone to the npm package: remove the link first (`rm ~/.local/bin/cabinet`), or the clone keeps running instead (`command -v cabinet` shows which one runs), then install from npm and run `npm install` in each workspace.

With a Node.js version manager (nvm, fnm, asdf, volta), a global install belongs to one Node version: after switching versions, `cabinet` is not found until you run `npm i -g @tarekraafat/cabinet` again under the new one. Workspaces and their schedules are not affected: they run their own copy.

Tab completion: add `eval "$(cabinet completion zsh)"` to `~/.zshrc` (or `bash` to `~/.bashrc`).

Every workspace also pins its own copy as a dev dependency. Inside a workspace, the global `cabinet` hands off to that pinned copy, so it always acts with the project's version.

### What setup changes on your machine

Creating a workspace changes only its folder (and, inside a project, the few lines [layouts](docs/layouts.md) lists). `cabinet bootstrap`, which `new` and `init` offer at the end and always show as a dry run first, also sets up this machine for every project on it ([guardrails](docs/guardrails.md)):

- **A push gate for every repository:** a global git pre-push hook (`core.hooksPath`) asks for `yes` at your terminal for every `git push`, so agents, which have no terminal, cannot push. Each repository's own hooks still run.
- **Deny rules in each agent tool it finds,** such as `~/.claude/settings.json` or `~/.codex/rules/default.rules`, blocking push, merge, release and publish. Rules are only added, and each file is backed up first.
- **Schedules** for the daily brief and backups: launchd on macOS, systemd or cron on Linux.
- **A secrets check** before each commit in the workspace.

[Undoing the guardrails](docs/guardrails.md#undoing-the-guardrails) says how to take them out; `cabinet remove` removes a workspace with its schedules.

## Start a new project

```sh
cabinet new
```

It asks, each with a default you keep by pressing Enter:

- the project name, folder, and owner name and email (defaults from your git config);
- which roles to enable (chief-of-staff is always on: it writes the brief and routes work);
- the agent tool that runs scheduled jobs, the brief time (`7 AM`, days and a time like `fri 4 PM`, or `off`), and the first day of the week;
- a folder for the encrypted daily backup, outside the workspace (or `off`);
- the product repos, as git URLs.

It shows a summary, creates and commits the workspace, then offers to pin the kit (`npm install`) and to set up the machine (`bin/bootstrap.sh`, shown as a dry run first).

Every answer is also an option, and `--yes` skips the questions:

```sh
cabinet new ~/dev/acme --name "Acme" --roles "qa security" --runner claude \
  --brief-time "7 AM" --week-start sunday --writing standard --backup-dir off --repo git@github.com:acme/api.git --yes
```

All options: [commands](docs/commands.md#cabinet-new).

## Add Cabinet to an existing project

```sh
cd ~/dev/acme-app
npm i -D @tarekraafat/cabinet
npx cabinet init
```

In a project repo, `cabinet init` asks where the team's files go:

| Choice | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Inside, private** (default) | `cabinet/` inside the project, with its own git. The project's git ignores it, and no tracked file of the project changes. |
| **Inside, shared** | `cabinet/` inside the project, committed with it, for teammates who clone it. |
| **Beside** | A workspace folder next to the project, pointing at it. The project does not change. |

In a folder that is not a repo (one already holding your repos, for example), `init` makes that folder the workspace. In every layout, files that already exist are kept, never replaced.

Setup also reads what the project says about itself: its name, description, scripts and repository from `package.json`, and its own git identity. It copies them as facts, each marked with its source, and leaves `TBD` what no file can tell.

Details: [layouts](docs/layouts.md).

## Change settings later

```sh
cabinet config        # in the workspace, or the project's top folder when cabinet/ is inside it
```

It asks the setup questions again with your current answers as defaults, lists the changes, writes them (settings, team tables, roles), and offers to update schedules and clone new repos. Options, `--dry-run` and `--yes` work as in `new`; `cabinet config --budget 20` sets a weekly budget for the agent runs Cabinet starts ([what they cost](docs/concepts.md#what-agent-runs-cost)). `cabinet config --writing short` makes every brief, question and answer as short as it can be, for when you have little time to read ([writing to the owner](docs/concepts.md#writing-to-the-owner)). `cabinet config --hard-to-undo "api/migrations/"` names what a small task must never touch ([ready to build](docs/concepts.md#ready-to-build)). Details: [commands](docs/commands.md#cabinet-config).

## Update the kit

Each workspace pins its kit version, so projects update independently.

```sh
cabinet status        # this workspace's version, and any kit file edited here
cabinet outdated      # is a newer version published?
npm update            # take a newer version
cabinet update        # apply it: replace kit files, rebuild roles, print the changelog since your version
git diff              # review, then commit
```

An update never overwrites a kit file you edited in the workspace: it stops and names it. Without a global install, use `npx cabinet` in place of `cabinet`.

## Remove Cabinet

- **A workspace:** `cabinet remove` (`--dry-run` shows the plan first). It stops the workspace's schedules, deletes its folder, and inside a project removes what setup added there. It refuses work that exists nowhere else unless `--force`. Details: [commands](docs/commands.md#cabinet-remove).
- **The guardrails:** they stay in your agent tools' settings, since other workspaces may rely on them. Bootstrap saved a `.bak` copy of every file it changed; see [guardrails](docs/guardrails.md#undoing-the-guardrails).
- **The command:** `npm rm -g @tarekraafat/cabinet`.

## Develop the kit

```sh
npm test                                        # the whole kit in a scratch home folder, about a minute
npm test -- init                                # only the sections about init, and what they need
CABINET_PRIVATE_WORDS="word1 word2" npm test    # also checks that none of your private words is in the kit
```

Agents working on the kit: read [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) first. To contribute, see [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md); to report a security problem privately, [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md). Everyone taking part follows the [code of conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

A release, by the maintainer: date the `## X.Y.Z - Unreleased` section at the top of `CHANGELOG.md` (`## X.Y.Z - D Mon YYYY`, with anything a workspace must do by hand), set the same `version` in `package.json`, commit and push, then publish a GitHub release tagged `vX.Y.Z`. That runs `.github/workflows/release.yml`: it checks the tag against `package.json`, runs `npm test`, and publishes to npm with provenance, signing in as the package's trusted publisher (set once on npmjs.com, so no token is stored). The package is scoped, which npm would publish as private; `publishConfig` in `package.json` makes it public.

The code is licensed under the [Apache License 2.0](LICENSE), copyright 2026 Tarek Raafat. Anyone who redistributes it or builds on it keeps the [NOTICE](NOTICE). The Cabinet name, logo and the other brand assets are not part of that license: see [brand/LICENSE.md](brand/LICENSE.md).

# Tutorial: your first day with Cabinet

About 15 minutes. You create a workspace for a made-up product, Acme, set up your machine, give the team its first task, and read the first brief. The output shown is what Cabinet prints, shortened where it says `...`.

You need macOS or Linux, git, Node.js and at least one agent tool (Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, Qwen Code, Grok, opencode or the Cursor CLI). See [Install](../README.md#install).

## 1. Create the workspace

```sh
cd ~/dev
cabinet new acme --name "Acme"
```

In a terminal, `cabinet new` asks a few questions, each with a default you keep by pressing Enter: the owner, which roles to enable, the agent tool that runs scheduled jobs, a weekly budget (and a price, for a runner that reports only tokens), the brief time, how agents write to you (standard, or short for little time to read), backups and the product repos. Here we keep every default (`--yes` does the same without asking):

```
== Project files
  placed: 14 files
== Kit files
roles: chief-of-staff product-manager architect qa security design-lead finance
== Committed the new workspace as Ann Owner

Created Acme at ~/dev/acme (slug acme, cabinet 0.1.1).
Next:
  - Fill the TBDs in AGENTS.md: what Acme is, its product rules, how to test, the repo rows.
  ...
```

The workspace is a git repo of plain files: `AGENTS.md` (the project's rules), `HANDOFFS.md` (how agents pass work), `roles/`, `specs/`, `notes/`, `jobs/` and the kit's own `CABINET.md` and `bin/`. [Concepts](concepts.md) explains each.

## 2. Ask what is next

From anywhere inside the workspace:

```sh
cd acme
cabinet next
```

```
Next in Acme (~/dev/acme):
  1. Fill the TBDs in AGENTS.md: What Acme is, Contracts that cross repo lines, House rules, Product rules, How to test.
  2. Download the pinned kit (in ~/dev/acme). Run: npm install
  3. Set up this machine: guardrails and schedules (add --dry-run to see the changes first). Run: cabinet bootstrap
  4. The first brief comes at 7:00 AM (or write it now). Run: cabinet brief
  5. The doctor found 9 thing(s) to fix (cabinet doctor --fix runs the ones it can). Run: cabinet doctor
  Optional: Daily encrypted backups. Run: cabinet config --backup-dir <a folder outside the workspace>
```

`cabinet next` changes nothing. Come back to it whenever you are unsure what to do.

## 3. Tell the team about the product

Open `AGENTS.md` and replace each `TBD` with a few plain sentences: what Acme is, the rules every agent follows (for example "prices are the owner's decision"), and how to test. The agents read this file at the start of every session, so short and exact beats long. Longer documents the team must follow, such as a brand guide or a support policy, go in `guides/` with a row in the "Guides" table ([recipes](recipes.md#add-your-own-rules-guidelines-and-business-documents)).

Then download the pinned kit, so the workspace keeps its own version, and commit:

```sh
npm install
git add -A && git commit -m "Describe Acme"
```

## 4. Set up this machine

See first, then apply:

```sh
cabinet bootstrap --dry-run
cabinet bootstrap
```

```
== Git push gate
  placed ~/.config/git/hooks/pre-push
  ...
== Claude Code
  added 61 permission rule(s) to ~/.claude/settings.json
== Codex
  placed ~/.codex/rules/default.rules
...
== Schedules (launchd)
  installed ai.cabinet.acme.brief (7:00 AM)
```

Bootstrap installs the guardrails: every push now asks you at your own terminal, and each agent tool on this machine denies push, merge, release and publish ([guardrails](guardrails.md)). It also schedules the daily brief. It saves a `.bak` copy of every settings file it changes, and running it again is safe.

## 5. Check everything

```sh
cabinet doctor
```

```
All good. 3 note(s) below.

== Product repos
  ok    product repos checked
== Kit and roles
  ok    cabinet 0.1.1
...
```

When something needs you, the doctor starts with the list, and `cabinet doctor --fix` runs the fixes it knows. Every message is in [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md).

## 6. Give the team its first task

Open your agent tool in the workspace and describe a feature, for example:

> We want a public pricing page. Spec it.

The product-manager agent writes the spec in `specs/`, with any decision only you can make framed as a question. When work moves from one agent to another, it goes through `HANDOFFS.md`:

```sh
cabinet handoff list          # every open handoff, oldest first
cabinet handoff list owner    # everything waiting on you, in full
```

## 7. Read the brief

Each morning at the time you chose, the chief-of-staff agent writes `BRIEF.md`. To get one now:

```sh
cabinet brief
```

The brief starts with the sign-off queue: each decision only you can make, as a plain question with lettered options, the experts' recommendations, and whether it can be undone. Answer them all in one message to your agent, for example "approve 1 and 3; 2: no; 4: wait until Friday". The agents apply your answers.

## 8. Ship

When qa and security have recorded PASS on a piece of work, you push it from your own terminal. The push gate asks you to confirm. No agent can push, merge, release or publish.

## Where next

- [Recipes](recipes.md): add a role or a job, switch agent tools, move to a new machine, add a teammate.
- [Commands](commands.md): every command and option. `cabinet <command> --help` shows them too.
- [Layouts](layouts.md): add Cabinet to an existing project instead.


========================================================================
File: docs/recipes.md
========================================================================

# Recipes

Short answers to common tasks. Every command runs from anywhere inside the workspace, or the project around a `cabinet/` workspace. Commit the workspace after each change.

## Contents

- [Add your own rules, guidelines and business documents](#add-your-own-rules-guidelines-and-business-documents)
- [Add a role](#add-a-role)
- [Turn a role off, or back on](#turn-a-role-off-or-back-on)
- [Give a kit role project notes](#give-a-kit-role-project-notes)
- [Add a scheduled job](#add-a-scheduled-job)
- [Change the brief time, or turn it off](#change-the-brief-time-or-turn-it-off)
- [Switch the agent tool for scheduled jobs](#switch-the-agent-tool-for-scheduled-jobs)
- [Add a product repo](#add-a-product-repo)
- [Turn on backups](#turn-on-backups)
- [Move to a new machine](#move-to-a-new-machine)
- [Add a teammate to a shared workspace](#add-a-teammate-to-a-shared-workspace)
- [Run several projects](#run-several-projects)
- [Update the kit](#update-the-kit)
- [Use Cabinet from a script or an agent](#use-cabinet-from-a-script-or-an-agent)

## Add your own rules, guidelines and business documents

Pick the place by what it is:

| You have | Put it in | Followed by |
|---|---|---|
| A rule that fits in a line or two ("prices are the owner's decision", "every page works on a phone") | `AGENTS.md`: "House rules" for how the team works, "Product rules" for what the product must and must not do | every agent, every session |
| A whole document: brand guide, writing or code style guide, security or privacy policy, pricing rules, support promises, any business document | `guides/<file>`, plus a row in the "Guides" table of `AGENTS.md` | every agent, or the roles its row names, before any work it covers |
| Duties, paths or limits for one role ("qa tests on the staging account") | `roles/<role>.md`, plain Markdown, then `cabinet role build` | that role |
| Rules for one repo | that repo's own `AGENTS.md` | agents working in that repo |
| How to test, and what must never be touched | "How to test" in `AGENTS.md` | qa, and every agent that runs the product |
| Thinking, research or a decision with its reasons | `notes/`, with `status: draft` or `decided` | agents whose task touches its topic |

**Add a guide in three steps:**

1. Put the file in `guides/`: `guides/brand.md`. Markdown or plain text works with every agent tool; a PDF works with the tools that read PDFs.
2. Add its row to the "Guides" table in `AGENTS.md`:

   ```markdown
   | Guide | What it covers | Who follows it |
   |---|---|---|
   | `guides/brand.md` | Voice, names, colors and logo use in anything people see | every agent |
   | `guides/refunds.md` | What support may promise a customer | product-manager, qa |
   ```

3. Commit the workspace. `cabinet doctor` reports a guide with no row (agents would never read it) and a row whose file is missing.

**Or ask an agent:** "Add this as a guide every agent follows: <paste or file>". It saves the file, adds the row and commits, as `guides/README.md` says.

**What wins:** a repo's `AGENTS.md` over the workspace's `AGENTS.md` and its guides, over the kit's `CABINET.md`. No rule or guide can loosen "Never push, merge, publish or release" or "The builder never verifies"; the guardrails enforce the first anyway. Never edit `CABINET.md`: it is the kit's, and `cabinet update` stops on an edited kit file.

**Folders:** the workspace's git tracks only the folders its `.gitignore` lists (`guides/`, `notes/`, `specs/`, `roles/` and the rest). A new top-level folder of your own is not committed until you add a `!/<folder>/` line to `.gitignore`; prefer `guides/` for documents agents follow.

## Add a role

First, check whether a kit role fits. Besides the seven on by default and the four builders, the kit has four optional roles, off until you turn them on:

| Role | For |
|---|---|
| brand-designer | logos, graphics and templates inside the brand, and a draft brand guide for you to decide |
| dba | reviewing every migration, database performance, backups and access plans |
| code-reviewer | reviewing each change's code before a push (PASS or CHANGES) |
| auditor | audits of dependencies, access, personal data and configuration |

Turn one on with the other roles you keep: `cabinet config --roles "qa security dba"`.

For anything else, make a role of the project's own. You need only its name:

```sh
cabinet role add brand-strategist
```

In a terminal it asks four questions: what it should do, what it owns, what it may decide on its own, and what it must bring to you. Answer what you know and press Enter for the rest; `--does`, `--owns`, `--decides` and `--escalates` give the answers as options, and `--yes` asks nothing. It writes `roles/<role>.md` with your words under "The owner's brief", turns the role on, adds its rows to the team tables, and builds it.

Then have it drafted, in one of two ways:

- **In your agent session:** "draft the brand-strategist role". Any agent tool follows `.cabinet/rules/seats.md`, "Drafting a role".
- **From the terminal:** `cabinet role draft brand-strategist` (or `--draft` on `role add`) runs your configured agent tool as chief-of-staff. It may cost money.

The draft starts from your brief, which wins, and learns the rest from the project: `AGENTS.md`, the specs and roadmap, the notes, the repos and the roles already on the team. It writes the role a strong specialist would hold on this product: what it owns, decides, brings to you, how its work is checked, and where it stops and its neighbours start. Every choice your brief did not make is listed under "Assumed, for the owner to confirm", and chief-of-staff puts those in your sign-off queue until you answer.

Know more later? Add it to "The owner's brief" in `roles/<role>.md` and run `cabinet role draft <role>` again. Until a role is drafted, the doctor reminds you, and the role does only what your brief asks.

A role of yours is never mixed with a kit role: if a later kit adds a role with the same name, yours is still used, and the doctor says so (`roles.shadows`). Each repo or area has one owner in the team table (the doctor checks), and when you turn a role off, the doctor notes any open handoff still addressed to it.

By hand instead: write `roles/<role>.md` with frontmatter (`name`, `description`, `tools`) like the kit's roles in `.cabinet/roles/`, then `cabinet config --roles "<the roles you keep> <role>"`.

A new role is your decision (`.cabinet/rules/seats.md`).

## Turn a role off, or back on

`cabinet config --roles "<every role you want>"`. The list replaces the old one; chief-of-staff is always on. A role you turn off leaves the team tables, and a kit role you turn back on returns with its row.

## Give a kit role project notes

Write `roles/<role>.md` (for example `roles/qa.md`) as plain Markdown, no frontmatter: the paths, duties and limits this project adds. Then `cabinet role build`. The notes are added to the kit's definition under "Project notes".

## Add a scheduled job

1. Write `jobs/<job>.job`:

   ```sh
   AGENT=growth
   WHEN="sun 9:00 AM"        # a time every day ("9 AM"), days and a time ("fri,sat 10 AM"), or "" for by hand only
   MINUTES="5"
   TIMEOUT="30"              # stop it after 30 minutes; "" uses CABINET_JOB_TIMEOUT (60), "0" for no limit
   RESULT="specs/weekly.md"
   PROMPT="Write this week's numbers."
   AFTER=""
   QUIET_DAYS="0"            # skip scheduled runs while nothing changed, for up to this many days; "0" runs every time
   ```

2. Name the job in `OPERATIONS.md` (the doctor checks that the manual names every job).
3. `cabinet bootstrap` schedules it. `cabinet job run <job>` runs it now.

Remove a job by deleting its file and running `cabinet bootstrap`.

## Change the brief time, or turn it off

`cabinet config --brief-time "8:30 AM" --apply` (or `--brief-time off`, `--brief-time "fri 4 PM"` for Fridays only, or `--brief-time "sun,mon,tue,wed,thu 8 AM"` for chosen days; full day names work too). `--apply` updates the schedule right away.

## Switch the agent tool for scheduled jobs

`cabinet config --runner codex --apply`. Install that tool first: the doctor checks that scheduled jobs can find it. For any other tool, `--runner custom --runner-cmd '<command using "$CABINET_PROMPT">'`.

## Add a product repo

`cabinet repo add git@example.com:acme/web.git --apply`: it adds the repo, then runs bootstrap, which clones it and gives it a builder. `cabinet repo list` shows them all; `cabinet repo remove <name>` takes one out of the workspace and leaves its folder as it is.

## Turn on backups

1. `cabinet config --backup-dir ~/Backups/cabinet --apply`. The folder must be outside the workspace and its repos.
2. Choose a passphrase, keep it in your password manager, and put it in the keychain: `security add-generic-password -a "$USER" -s cabinet.<slug>.backup -w`. On Linux, in the secret store: `secret-tool store --label=cabinet.<slug>.backup service cabinet.<slug>.backup account "$USER"`.
3. `cabinet backup create` makes one now; the schedule makes one daily. Once a quarter, `cabinet backup verify`. See [backups](backups.md).

## Move to a new machine

1. Install Cabinet and its needs ([Install](../README.md#install)).
2. Put the backup passphrase in the keychain or secret store, as in step 2 of [Turn on backups](#turn-on-backups).
3. `cabinet backup restore <newest archive> ~/dev/acme`. It works before the workspace exists, and never loses a file ([backups](backups.md#restoring)).
4. `cd ~/dev/acme`, then `cabinet bootstrap` and `cabinet doctor`.

Without a backup, clone the workspace's own repo instead, then `cabinet bootstrap`.

To move a workspace to another folder on the same machine: `cabinet move <new-path>`.

## Add a teammate to a shared workspace

A shared workspace (`cabinet init --inside --shared`) is committed with the project, so a teammate gets it by cloning:

1. The teammate clones the project and runs `npm install`, which installs the pinned kit.
2. They run `cabinet bootstrap --no-schedules` on their machine, then `cabinet doctor`. This installs the push gate and their agent tools' guardrails, but no schedules: one machine, usually the owner's, runs the brief and the other jobs, so it is written once. The choice is saved for that machine only (`cabinet.local.env`, which git does not track).

3. Backups follow the workspace's `CABINET_BACKUP_DIR`, which is shared. Each teammate sets their own folder for their machine, or none: `cabinet config --this-machine --backup-dir ~/Backups/cabinet --apply` (or `--backup-dir off`). That also lives in `cabinet.local.env`.

Any teammate can still run a job by hand (`cabinet job run <job>`). To make another machine the one that runs the jobs: `cabinet bootstrap --no-schedules` on the old one, `cabinet bootstrap --schedules` on the new one.

## Run several projects

One workspace per project: `cabinet new` (or `cabinet init`) for each. Each has its own slug, so its own schedules, logs, backups and brief; the guardrails are shared by the whole machine. One project with several repos or products is one workspace, with every repo in `repos.tsv`.

`cabinet list` shows them all in one table: what waits on you, what the doctor finds, the latest brief. Each morning, `cabinet digest` gathers every project's sign-off queue and your actions into one read (`cabinet digest --schedule --notify` writes it to `~/Library/Logs/cabinet/digest.md` every day at 10:00 AM and tells you; `--schedule "8 AM"` for another time, `--schedule "sun,mon,tue,wed,thu 8 AM"` for chosen days); answer each queue in its own workspace (`cd` there and tell its agent). Then `cabinet next` inside any of them.

## Update the kit

```sh
cabinet outdated      # is a newer version published?
npm update            # take it
cabinet update        # apply it, and read the changelog since your version
git diff              # review, then commit
```

An update never overwrites a kit file you edited: it stops and names it.

## Use Cabinet from a script or an agent

Read JSON, never the text output, which may be reworded:

```sh
cabinet help --json              # every command and option
cabinet next --json              # the next steps, each with a stable id and its command
cabinet doctor --json            # every check, each with a stable id
cabinet handoff list owner --json    # what waits on the owner, in full
```

A missing tool shows as the doctor check `deps.required` (or `deps.backups`) and the `next` step `deps`, each with the install command for that machine. An agent passes it to the owner; installing is the owner's (`cabinet doctor --fix` asks first).

The fields are in [commands](commands.md#output-for-agents-and-scripts). For the whole manual in one file, read `llms-full.txt` in the kit.


========================================================================
File: docs/commands.md
========================================================================

# Commands

Every command Cabinet has, its options and defaults, what it changes, and its exit codes. `cabinet help` (or `cabinet` alone) lists them; `cabinet <command> --help` (or `cabinet help <command>`) shows one command's usage and options, and a noun alone (`cabinet role`) shows its verbs. Agents and scripts: `cabinet help --json` gives every command and option, and every command that reports prints JSON (see [Output for agents and scripts](#output-for-agents-and-scripts)).

## Contents

- [How commands are named](#how-commands-are-named)
- Start: [cabinet new](#cabinet-new), [cabinet init](#cabinet-init)
- Daily: [cabinet next](#cabinet-next), [cabinet brief](#cabinet-brief), [cabinet digest](#cabinet-digest), [cabinet list](#cabinet-list), [cabinet doctor](#cabinet-doctor)
- Team: [cabinet role](#cabinet-role), [cabinet handoff](#cabinet-handoff)
- Work: [cabinet repo](#cabinet-repo), [cabinet job](#cabinet-job)
- Safety: [cabinet secret](#cabinet-secret), [cabinet backup](#cabinet-backup)
- Setup: [cabinet bootstrap](#cabinet-bootstrap), [cabinet config](#cabinet-config), [cabinet move](#cabinet-move), [cabinet remove](#cabinet-remove)
- Kit: [cabinet update](#cabinet-update), [cabinet status](#cabinet-status), [cabinet outdated](#cabinet-outdated), [cabinet changelog](#cabinet-changelog), [cabinet completion](#cabinet-completion), [cabinet version](#cabinet-version)
- [Which copy of Cabinet runs](#which-copy-of-cabinet-runs)
- [Workspace scripts](#workspace-scripts): the same commands without the `cabinet` command
- [Output for agents and scripts](#output-for-agents-and-scripts): `--json`
- [Files you can edit](#files-you-can-edit): `cabinet.env`, `jobs/<job>.job`, `cabinet.local.env`, `repos.tsv`
- [Environment variables](#environment-variables)
- [Removing a workspace](#removing-a-workspace)

## How commands are named

Once you know one command, you can guess the next:

- **One word** acts on the workspace as a whole, or on this machine: `cabinet doctor`, `cabinet update`.
- **A noun, then a verb** acts on something the workspace holds: `cabinet role add`, `cabinet repo list`, `cabinet handoff archive`. The nouns are `role`, `handoff`, `spec`, `manual`, `repo`, `job`, `secret` and `backup`, always singular.
- **The verbs** mean the same on every noun: `add` (put one in, or turn on one the kit has), `remove` (take one out), `list` (show them), `check` (look for problems), and a few a noun needs: `role draft`, `role build`, `handoff attach`, `handoff record`, `spec record`, `handoff archive`, `repo snapshot`, `job run`, `backup create`, `backup verify`, `backup restore`.
- **The same options everywhere:** `--json` on every command that reports, `--dry-run` on every command that changes the setup or deletes anything, `--yes` (`-y`) on every command that asks.
- **Any workspace, from anywhere:** every command finds the workspace from the folder you are in, upward, so it works anywhere inside the workspace or the project around a `cabinet/` workspace. `cabinet -C <dir> <command>` runs it as if started in `<dir>`, as git does.
- **Exit codes:** 0 done (or nothing found), 1 failed or found a problem, 2 wrong usage (an unknown command or option, a missing value). An unknown command gets one short answer, with the closest command when one is near, never the whole help.
- **The same words without the `cabinet` command:** every workspace has its scripts in `bin/`, named the same way (`bin/role.sh build`, `bin/handoff.sh list qa`), for agents, schedules and machines without the command ([Workspace scripts](#workspace-scripts)).

## cabinet new

```sh
cabinet new [dir] [options]
```

Creates a workspace in an empty or missing folder. In a terminal it asks a question for each setting; options set the defaults, and `--yes` skips the questions.

**Tools first.** `new`, `init` and `bootstrap` first check for the tools Cabinet needs (git, node, npm). When one is missing, they name it and the command that installs it here (`brew install`, or `sudo apt-get`, `dnf` or `pacman` on Linux). In a terminal they offer to run it and go on once it worked; with `--yes` or `--dry-run` they never install, and stop with that command (exit 1).

| Option | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `[dir]` | asked (`~/dev/<name>`) | Must not exist, or be empty. |
| `--name "Name"` | the folder name | The project's display name. |
| `--slug <slug>` | the folder name, made lowercase with dashes | Lowercase letters, digits and dashes. Refused when another workspace on this machine holds it. |
| `--owner "Name"`, `--email you@example.com` | `git config --global user.name` / `user.email` | The commit author written into `AGENTS.md`. With no identity, setup does not commit. |
| `--roles "qa security ..."` | the seven core roles, and `code-reviewer` when the workspace starts with repos | `chief-of-staff` is always added. `code-reviewer` is on by default when setup starts with product repos (`--repo`, `init` in a project, or a folder of repos), since nothing else reviews the code itself; the chief-of-staff proposes it later for a workspace that gains repos without it. The other optional kit roles, `brand-designer`, `dba` and `auditor`, are off unless named. Builders are never listed here: they come with the repos they own. |
| `--runner <tool>` | the first installed of `claude`, `codex`, `antigravity` (`agy`), `qwen`, `grok`, `opencode`, `cursor`, else `claude` | The agent tool for scheduled jobs. `cursor` means the Cursor CLI, never the editor's `cursor` command. `custom` needs `--runner-cmd`. |
| `--runner-cmd '<command>'` | none | With `--runner custom`: the command to run, using `"$CABINET_PROMPT"` (and `$CABINET_AGENT`). No single quotes. |
| `--brief-time <when>` | `7:00 AM` | When the brief is written: a time every day (`"7 AM"`), or days and a time, one day (`"fri 4 PM"`) or several (`"sun,mon,tue,wed,thu 8 AM"`), or `off`. See [Schedule times](#schedule-times). |
| `--week-start <day>` | `sunday` | Written into `AGENTS.md` house rules. |
| `--budget <dollars>\|off` | off | A weekly budget in US dollars for the agent runs Cabinet starts, in `cabinet.env`. Asked for every built-in runner ([what agent runs cost](concepts.md#what-agent-runs-cost)). |
| `--price "<input> <output> [<cached>]"\|off` | off | Dollars per million tokens, for a runner that reports only tokens (`codex`, `cursor`, `qwen`, `antigravity`), in `cabinet.env`. Asked after the budget for those runners. |
| `--writing short\|standard` | `standard` | How agents write to you, written into `AGENTS.md` house rules. `short` gives the shortest briefs, questions and answers: answer first, one point per line, three points at most, a decision in three lines. See [writing to the owner](concepts.md#writing-to-the-owner). |
| `--backup-dir <folder>` | `off` | Made absolute. Refused when it is inside the workspace or any repo it lists. |
| `--repo <git url>` | none | Repeatable. `https://`, `http://`, `ssh://`, `git://`, `file://`, `git@host:path`, an absolute path, or `./` / `../` (relative to the workspace). Two repos with the same name are refused. |
| `--dry-run` | | Prints everything setup would write and change, then stops: `Nothing was written.` |
| `--yes`, `-y` | | No questions: defaults and options only. |

Values written into `cabinet.env` (name, owner, email, backup folder) cannot contain `$`, a backtick, a backslash, a double quote or a line break.

**What it writes:** the project files from the kit's templates (`AGENTS.md`, `cabinet.env`, `HANDOFFS.md`, `OPERATIONS.md`, `README.md`, `repos.tsv`, `jobs/brief.job`, `roles/`, `guides/`, `specs/`, `notes/`, `package.json`, `.gitignore`), the kit files (`CABINET.md`, `bin/`, `.cabinet/`), the built roles (`agents/`, `.claude/agents/`), and `CLAUDE.md` as a link to `AGENTS.md`. Then `git init` and one commit of those files. It records the slug in `~/Library/Logs/cabinet/<slug>/workspace`.

**In a terminal, afterwards:** it offers `npm install` (to download the pinned kit) and `bin/bootstrap.sh` (shown as a dry run first, and applied only when you say yes).

**If it fails part way:** it removes the folder it created, or empties the empty folder it was given, and nothing else.

## cabinet init

```sh
cabinet init [dir] [options]
```

Adds Cabinet to an existing folder (default: the current one). It takes every option of `cabinet new`, and these:

| Option | Notes |
|---|---|
| `--inside` | In a project repo: the workspace is `cabinet/` inside it (the default there). |
| `--private` | With `--inside` (the default): `cabinet/` has its own git; the project's git ignores it and no tracked project file changes. |
| `--shared` | With `--inside`: `cabinet/` is part of the project's repo. Nothing is committed in the project; you review and commit. |
| `--beside` | In a project repo: the workspace is a folder next to it (default `<project>-hq`). |
| `--workspace <folder>` | With `--beside`: where that folder goes. |

What it does depends on where it runs (see [layouts](layouts.md)):

| Run in | Result |
|---|---|
| The top folder of a project repo | Inside (private or shared) or beside, asked or from the options. |
| A subfolder of a repo | Refused: run it at the repo's top folder. |
| A folder that is not a repo | The folder becomes the workspace, "around" what is there. The repos it finds in subfolders are listed in `repos.tsv`. |
| A folder that already has a workspace | Refused: use `cabinet update`. |

In every case, existing files are kept and reported, never replaced. Around a folder, a file of its own at a path the kit uses (such as `bin/doctor.sh`) stops setup before anything is written.

**What it reads from a project** (as defaults you can change):

- From `package.json`: the name (scope dropped: `@acme/shop` becomes `shop`), the description (quoted as the project's own words), the repository URL (when the repo has no `origin`), and the `test`, `dev`, `start`, `build`, `lint` and `typecheck` scripts (run with bun, pnpm or yarn when their lockfile is there). A value with shell characters, or a URL that is not a plain git URL, is not used.
- The project's own `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `README.md`, named as where its rules live.
- The repo's own git `user.name` and `user.email` as the owner.

## cabinet next

```sh
cabinet next [--json]
```

Says what to do next in the workspace you are in, as a numbered list, and changes nothing: missing tools Cabinet needs (step `deps`, with the install command), the `TBD` headings left in `AGENTS.md`, a workspace with no commits, a pinned kit not yet downloaded, a machine without the push gate or schedules (`cabinet bootstrap`), handoffs waiting on the owner, today's brief (with when it was written) or when the first one comes, and how many problems the doctor finds. Outside a workspace it says how to start one. When nothing waits: `Nothing waits on you.` Each step ends with the command that does it, when there is one.

## cabinet brief

```sh
cabinet brief
```

Writes the brief now: the same as `cabinet job run brief`, which runs `jobs/brief.job` as chief-of-staff and writes `BRIEF.md`, the sign-off queue first. It prints nothing until the agent tool finishes.

## cabinet digest

```sh
cabinet digest [--json]
cabinet digest --write <file> [--notify]
cabinet digest --schedule [<when>|off] [--file <file>] [--notify]
```

One morning read for every workspace on this machine: from each one's latest `BRIEF.md`, the "Sign-off queue" and "Actions for the owner" parts, by their `## ` headings (the chief-of-staff role writes them with these names), and how many handoffs wait on you. It flags a brief older than a day and a half (is the brief job running?), a workspace with no brief yet, and a brief without the "## Sign-off queue" heading. It also shows what each workspace's agent runs cost this week against its budget ([what agent runs cost](concepts.md#what-agent-runs-cost)), each by its own week start, with no line for a workspace whose runner does not report cost. It reads only: you still answer each queue in its own workspace, to that workspace's agent. It starts with one line of counts (decisions, actions and handoffs waiting, briefs late, missing or unreadable, and projects at 80% of their budget or more) and the week's total cost across them, and ends by saying whether it is scheduled.

| Option | Notes |
|---|---|
| `--write <file>` | Write the digest to that file (replaced each time) instead of the screen. |
| `--notify` | Also show a desktop notification with the counts line (`notify-send` on Linux). |
| `--schedule [<when>]` | Write it on a schedule. With no time: every day at 10:00 AM. Or any [schedule time](#schedule-times): `"8 AM"`, `"fri 10 AM"`, `"sun,mon,tue,wed,thu 8 AM"`. Run again to change it. `--schedule off` stops it and keeps the last file. |
| `--file <file>` | With `--schedule`: where it is written. Default `digest.md` in the log folder (`~/Library/Logs/cabinet/` on macOS, `~/.local/state/cabinet/` on Linux), which a scheduled job can always write. macOS may block a scheduled job from writing to Documents, Desktop, Downloads or iCloud Drive until you allow it (System Settings > Privacy & Security > Files and Folders); Cabinet says so when you choose one. |
| `--json` | The digest as JSON (below). |

The schedule is one job for the whole machine, `ai.cabinet-digest` ([launchd, systemd or cron](concepts.md#macos-and-linux)), apart from every workspace's `ai.cabinet.<slug>.*` jobs; it runs this `cabinet` (so install it globally, not only through npx, whose cache can be cleared) and logs to `digest.log` in the log folder. On macOS the first notification may need you to allow notifications for Script Editor, which macOS uses to show them. Exit 0, or 1 for a bad time, no scheduler, or a schedule the scheduler would not load.

## cabinet list

```sh
cabinet list [--json]
```

Every workspace on this machine, from anywhere: its slug, project name, kit version (marked `*` when it is not the installed kit), how many handoffs wait on you, what the doctor finds, when the latest brief was written, and its folder. The doctors run side by side, each with its workspace's own scripts, so it takes about as long as one doctor run. A workspace is listed once setup or bootstrap has claimed its slug on this machine; `cabinet remove` takes it off the list. A workspace whose folder is gone shows as `folder gone`, with how to free its slug. Changes nothing. Exit 0.

## cabinet doctor

```sh
cabinet doctor [--fix [--yes]] [--json]
```

Checks everything: repos, kit files, roles, guardrails for every installed tool, the manual, handoff IDs, secrets in the workspace's files, uncommitted work, schedules, backups. It starts with a summary (`N thing(s) need attention:` and the list, or `All good.`), then the full report. In a terminal the report colors each result's label: `ok` green, `note` blue, `FIX` red. Output to a script or a file has no colors, and none are printed when `NO_COLOR` is set. Changes nothing in the workspace or your settings (it runs `opencode debug` and `grok inspect`, which may write their own caches). `--fix` then runs the fixes it knows (`bin/bootstrap.sh`, `bin/role.sh build`, `bin/repo.sh snapshot`, and installing missing tools), asking before each unless `--yes`, and checks again. Installing tools always asks in a terminal, even with `--yes`: it changes the machine and can need your password. `--json` prints the results for scripts (see [Output for agents and scripts](#output-for-agents-and-scripts)). Every message is explained in [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md). Exit 0, or 1 when anything says FIX.

## cabinet role

```sh
cabinet role add <name> [--does "..."] [--owns "..."] [--decides "..."] [--escalates "..."] [--reports-to <role> [--covers "<builders or repos>"]] [--title "..."] [--name "..."] [--function "..."] [--draft] [--dry-run] [--yes]
cabinet role remove <name> [--dry-run]
cabinet role list [--json]
cabinet role draft <name>
cabinet role build [--check]
```

**`add`** turns on a kit role (`cabinet role add dba`), or adds a role of the project's own from as little as its name (lowercase letters, digits and dashes, not a builder's name). For a role of its own, in a terminal with no option given, it asks what the role should do, what it owns, what it may decide on its own and what it must bring to you; Enter skips any of them, and `--does`, `--owns`, `--decides` and `--escalates` give those answers instead. It writes `roles/<name>.md` with your answers word for word under "The owner's brief" (`not said yet` for the rest) and a `TBD` description. Either way the role is turned on through `cabinet config --roles`, which adds its rows to the team tables and builds it. `--owns` (or the answer to "What does it own") is checked against the team table: a repo or path that is already another role's row is refused (exit 1), naming who owns it; a path inside another role's area (`specs/seo/` inside `specs/`) is accepted with a note, since drafting gives the new role its own row there and the most specific row wins. A new role does only what the brief asks until it is drafted. `--draft`, or yes to the question that follows in a terminal, drafts it at once; `--yes` asks nothing; `--dry-run` says what it would do.

**`remove`** turns a role off: its built files and its rows in the team tables go. A role of the project's own keeps `roles/<name>.md`; delete it to drop the role for good. chief-of-staff is always on. Builders come and go with the repos they own in the team table, not through `role add` or `remove`.

**Committing a role change.** In a workspace with its own git, `add` and `remove` commit what they changed (`roles: <name> on`, `off`, or `added from the owner's brief`), unless the files they touch (`AGENTS.md`, `OPERATIONS.md`, `ORG.md`, `cabinet.env`, `roles/`, `agents/`, `.claude/agents/`) held uncommitted edits of yours: then, and in a shared `cabinet/`, they leave the change for you to review and commit, and say so.

**Sub-teams.** `--reports-to <lead>` adds a role to a lead's sub-team ([concepts](concepts.md#sub-teams)): its lead, on the team, owns its onboarding and settles its disagreements. `--covers "<builders or repos>"` names whose work it reviews for its lead: on a handoff from one of them, its verdict counts for its lead's, and `cabinet handoff run` runs it instead of the lead. It starts with a 30-day trial, during which the lead's PASS is needed too. Both go into a "## Team" section of `roles/<name>.md` (`- Reports to:`, `- Covers:`, `- Trial until:`), kept when the role is drafted; edit it there later. Refused (exit 1): a lead not on the team, the role itself as its lead, `--covers` without `--reports-to`, or a name in `--covers` that is no builder or repo.

**Titles.** `--title "Head of Product"` and `--name "Product Agent"` give a role the title and display name decisions name it by (the sign-off format names each expert by its title where it has one) and the org page shows; `--function "Growth"` places a role in a function of its own on the org page (by default, its lead's, or a kit role's own, or Other). They go into the role's "## Team" section, and they work when turning on a kit role too, written to its notes in `roles/<name>.md`. Plain words only. Edit them there later, then `cabinet role build`.

**`list`** shows every role on the team (kit, optional, builder or project; a project role not yet drafted is marked; its title and display name; for a sub-team role, its lead, what it covers and its trial) and the optional kit roles that are off.

**`draft`** has an agent write the whole role for this project, as `.cabinet/rules/seats.md`, "Drafting a role", says: it keeps your brief, learns the rest from the project, writes the role, lists what it assumed for you to confirm, fills the team table rows and commits. It runs the configured agent tool as chief-of-staff (a few minutes; it may cost money), logging to `~/Library/Logs/cabinet/<slug>/role-<name>.log`. In an agent session, asking the agent to draft the role does the same. Add to the brief at any time and draft again.

**`build`** writes `ORG.md`, the org page (each function with its lead and members; each role's title, what it does, what it owns in the team table, who it reports to, what it covers and its trial), and builds `agents/<role>.md` and `.claude/agents/<role>.md` for every role (and, inside a project, the project's `.claude/agents/` and pointer files); `--check` only reports. Setup, config, update and bootstrap run it for you.

Exit 0; 1 when the role could not be added, removed or drafted, or `build --check` finds a role missing or out of date; 2 for a name that is not valid.

## cabinet handoff

```sh
cabinet handoff add --from <name> --to <name> --changed "..." --needed "..." [--depends-on "..."] [--spec <file> | --small] [--evidence <file or URL>]... "<title>"
cabinet handoff attach <ID> <file or URL>... --from <name>
cabinet handoff record <ID> --role <role> <PASS|BLOCK|CHANGES> --commits <hash,...>|none --note <file>
cabinet handoff list [name] [--ready] [--json]
cabinet handoff run <ID> [--retries <n>] [--dry-run]
cabinet handoff run --scheduled
cabinet handoff archive
```

**`add`** files one handoff: appends the entry at the bottom of "Open" in `HANDOFFS.md` with the next free ID for today (`H-20261019-01`, unique across `HANDOFFS.md` and the archives), today's date, status `open` and the template's lines, then commits it on its own (`handoffs: <ID> <title>`). `--depends-on` defaults to `none`. Each value is kept on one line. It prints the new ID first. When `HANDOFFS.md` already has someone else's uncommitted lines, it writes the entry but does not commit, so their lines never go into its commit. Two agents filing at once get different IDs: each write takes a lock (`.cabinet/handoff.lock`), and a lock left for more than a minute by a writer that was stopped is taken over. Entries are filed only this way, never by hand, so no two take the same ID. Two copies of a workspace (a teammate's clone) do not share the lock; `cabinet doctor` flags an ID used twice after they are merged (`handoffs.unique-ids`).

`--spec specs/<feature>.md` names the spec the handoff builds, on a `Spec:` line, and refuses (exit 1) unless the spec is committed, `ready` or `building`, and passes `cabinet spec check`: work bigger than a small task is routed only from a spec that is ready to build ([concepts](concepts.md#ready-to-build)). `--small` instead marks a small task (one repo, no contract change, no decision for you, easy to undo) with a `Size: small` line. A handoff to a repo, a kit builder, or a role that owns a repo in the team table needs one of the two (exit 2 with neither, or both).

`--evidence`, once for each, attaches what shows the work, so you can check it without reading code: a file (a screenshot, a short recording, saved command output) is copied to `specs/evidence/<ID>/` with a name safe in a link and committed with the entry; an `http` or `https` link is kept as it is. The entry gets an `Evidence:` line of links from the workspace root, which open with a click from `HANDOFFS.md` and `BRIEF.md` in an editor or on GitHub. `archive` rewrites them to open from `handoffs/`, and `cabinet digest` to full paths. A file path is read from the folder you run it in, else from the workspace.

**`attach`** adds evidence to an open handoff after it was filed (after a BLOCK, a fix, a missed screen), the same way `--evidence` does: files copied to `specs/evidence/<ID>/`, every link added to the entry's `Evidence:` line, committed. Only the entry's sender may: `--from` must match its `From:`.

**`record`** writes a reviewer's verdict on an open handoff as one line, `- Verdict: <role> <PASS|BLOCK|CHANGES> <YYYY-MM-DD> <commits> <note>`, with today's date, replacing that role's earlier verdict, and commits it (`handoffs: <ID> <role> <verdict>`). The verdict may be in any case; commits may be joined by commas or spaces. `--commits none` is for work that changes no repo (copy, research, a campaign), and is refused when the handoff is addressed to a repo or a role that builds one. For a reviewer a [critical area](concepts.md#critical-areas) the work touches names, a PASS first runs that area's check, a command in `tools/`, in the workspace with `CABINET_AREA`, `CABINET_HANDOFF` and `CABINET_COMMITS` set and the run's time limit, never through a shell; a failing check refuses the PASS (exit 1, with its last lines), and a passing one's output is saved as `specs/evidence/<ID>/check-<area>.txt`, linked on the entry and committed with the verdict. It refuses when the note is not a committed `.md` file under `specs/` (read from the folder you run it in, else from the workspace), when the role is the entry's sender (the builder never verifies its own work), and a qa PASS on an entry with no evidence: qa records BLOCK instead, and the sender runs `attach`. On a small task, it refuses a PASS whose commits are in more than one repo (or in none on this machine), or change a path `AGENTS.md` guards: a contract's files, written as `` `<repo>/<path>` `` under "Source of truth" in the contracts table, or a path under "Hard to undo". The work goes back to be routed from a spec.

**`list`**, without a name: every open handoff with its age in days, oldest first (`?` when it has no date). With a repo or role name (`qa`, `owner`): every entry addressed to it, in full; this is the start-of-session read. `--ready`: only the work ready for you to push (`No handoffs ready to push.` when there is none; with a name, only with `--json`).

**Readiness** is computed from the verdicts. An entry needs a verdict from each reviewer it is addressed to, from every reviewer of a critical area it touches, and, for code (sent by a builder, or with a verdict that names commits in a product repo), from qa, security and code-reviewer, and design-lead when a web or mobile builder sent it, each only when on the team; a builder addresses dba (or any other reviewer) when the change touches its subject. The work's commits are every commit any verdict on the entry names (short and full hashes match), and a PASS counts only when it covers them all: after a fix, a reviewer whose PASS names only the earlier commits is `stale` until it records again. An entry is ready when every reviewer it needs has a PASS that counts and none has BLOCK or CHANGES. An entry that needs no review (a decision for you, say) is neither ready nor waiting. PASS, BLOCK or CHANGES written outside a `- Verdict:` line is reported as unread and never counted.

**`run`** moves one piece of work through the steps the team already has, each an agent run with the configured agent tool, so you start no agent by hand. It takes a handoff to one builder (a repo, or the role that owns it), filed with `--small` or with `--spec` for a spec that still passes `cabinet spec check`. It reads the state (`handoff list --json`) and runs whoever is next:

1. No review handoff for the work yet: the builder builds it and hands it on for review with `--depends-on <ID>`, then closes the work entry.
2. Reviewers missing, or stale after a fix: each verifies and records its verdict.
3. A BLOCK or CHANGES: the builder fixes it, then the blocking reviewers check again. After `--retries` fix rounds (default 2) it stops and leaves it to you.
4. Ready (as `handoff list --ready` says): it stops and tells you to push, with what the runs cost.

It decides nothing itself: it also stops when an agent fails or hits its time limit (`CABINET_JOB_TIMEOUT`), when a builder files no review handoff or sends the work back, or when a reviewer records no verdict. Each run is logged in `run-<ID>.log` in the workspace's log folder and recorded in the spend file under the work's ID, so `handoff list --json` gives its `cost_usd`. One run at a time per piece of work. `--dry-run` prints the next step and runs nothing. It may cost money, like any agent run.

**`run --scheduled`** is what the pipeline job runs (see `cabinet config --pipeline`). It takes the work `CABINET_PIPELINE` allows, oldest first: with `all`, each spec ready to build (as `spec run`), then each handoff filed `--small` that is open or waiting on its review (as `handoff run`). It writes what happened to `PIPELINE.md` in the workspace (untracked, like `BRIEF.md`; the brief reports it): each piece of work and how it ended, then what the run spent of its limit. Before each agent it checks the limit, `CABINET_PIPELINE_LIMIT` dollars: once reached, the work is paused, not stopped, and the next run goes on from there. Work whose last run stopped for you (still blocked after its fix rounds, sent back, an agent that left no trace) is skipped, so a run never pays for the same stop twice, until you run it by hand (`cabinet handoff run <ID>`, or `spec run`), which clears it. It runs nothing when the runner is off, when it has no limit, when this week's budget (`CABINET_BUDGET`) is spent, or when the agent tool's cost cannot be counted.

**`archive`** moves every committed `done` or `rejected` handoff to `handoffs/archive-YYYY-MM.md` and commits the move; chief-of-staff runs it daily. It refuses while `HANDOFFS.md` has uncommitted lines.

`add`, `attach` and `record` write one at a time, and with someone else's uncommitted lines in `HANDOFFS.md` they write but do not commit.
