Exit 0 (for `run`: the work is ready to push); 3 when `run` pauses at a scheduled run's cost limit; 1 when `run` stops before that, `add` could not commit (the entry is written), `attach` or `record` refuses (no such open entry, not its sender, a note not committed, the builder's own verdict, a qa PASS with no evidence, a PASS on a small task that was not), or `archive` meets uncommitted lines; 2 for a missing value, an unknown option, a value in the wrong form, or evidence that is neither a file nor an `http(s)` link.

## cabinet manual

```sh
cabinet manual build [--check]
```

**`build`** writes `OPERATIONS.html`, the owner's manual (`OPERATIONS.md`) as one page you open in a browser: a table of contents, a search box that narrows the page to the sections that match, light and dark themes, and each `- [ ]` line as a tick box, remembered in that browser for the day, so a daily list starts fresh. The page holds everything it needs (no fonts, scripts or styles fetched) and works offline. Nothing in the Markdown runs: it is all escaped, and only `http(s)`, `mailto`, relative and `#` links become links. Like `BRIEF.md` it is untracked: setup, `cabinet update` and the brief job (its `AFTER`) rebuild it, and the doctor notes when it is older than `OPERATIONS.md` (`manual.page`). `--check` only reports (exit 1 when it is behind).

## cabinet spec

```sh
cabinet spec check [spec] [--json]
cabinet spec record <spec> --role <qa|architect|design-lead> <PASS|BLOCK> --note <file>
cabinet spec run <spec> [--retries <n>] [--dry-run]
```

**`check`** holds every spec in `specs/` (or the one named) to what its status needs (`--json` adds `repos`, `missing_plans` and `plan_review`, the architect's review of the plan as it is now: `PASS`, `BLOCK`, `changed` or `none`) ([concepts](concepts.md#ready-to-build)). `draft`, `shipped` and `dropped` need nothing. `ready` needs acceptance criteria, no `TBD` in "Rules", every row of the Decisions table answered, at least one repo in `repos` (or a workspace area, for work with no code), only declared critical areas in `areas`, and a qa PASS on the acceptance criteria as they are now. A spec built in a repo whose owner in the team table is the web or mobile builder also needs, while design-lead is on the team, a "Design" section and a design-lead PASS on it as it is now. `building` also needs a plan for each repo (a `### <repo>` part under "## Plan" with something in it) and, for more than one repo, an architect PASS on the plan as it is now. It prints each spec, its status and its problems (or `ok`). `--json`: `[{spec, status, problems}]`. The doctor runs it (`specs.ready`).

**`record`** records a review of a spec under its "## Reviews" heading: qa's of the acceptance criteria (can each be tested as written?), design-lead's of the design, or architect's of the plan. It writes `- Verdict: <role> <PASS|BLOCK> <YYYY-MM-DD> <fingerprint> <note>`, replacing that role's earlier review, and commits the spec (`specs: <feature>.md <role> <verdict>`). The fingerprint is of the part reviewed, so a later change to it shows as unreviewed in `check`. The spec and the note must be committed, the note a `.md` file under `specs/`; both are read from the folder you run it in, else from the workspace.

**`run`** moves a spec that passes `check` (`ready` or `building`) until all its work is ready to push, an agent run per step, so you start no agent by hand: chief-of-staff routes it (one handoff per owning builder, filed `--spec`), each builder writes its plan for its repo, and, for more than one repo, architect reviews the plan; then each of its handoffs runs in the order routing set, as `cabinet handoff run` runs one (`--retries` is passed on). It stops at the first step that does not finish: an agent that fails or leaves no trace, a plan the architect blocks, or a handoff that does not reach ready. Run again after you settle it: work already done is not redone. It ends with what all its runs cost. Logged in `run-<feature>.log` in the log folder; one run at a time per spec; `--dry-run` prints the next step. It may cost money.

Exit 0; 1 when `check` finds a spec not ready for its status, `run` stops before all its work is ready, or `record` refuses (a file not committed, not a spec, or the spec given as its own note); 2 for a missing value, an unknown option, a role other than qa, architect or design-lead, or a verdict other than PASS or BLOCK.

## cabinet repo

```sh
cabinet repo add <git url> [--apply] [--dry-run]
cabinet repo remove <name> [--dry-run]
cabinet repo list [--json]
cabinet repo snapshot
```

**`add`** adds a product repo: a row in `repos.tsv` and in the team table of `AGENTS.md`, through `cabinet config --repo`, with the same checks as setup. Like `config`, it commits the change (`cabinet config: add repo`) in a workspace with its own git that had no uncommitted changes. `cabinet bootstrap` then clones it and gives it a builder; `--apply` runs bootstrap right away.

**`remove`** takes a repo out of the workspace: its row in `repos.tsv` and in the team table. Its folder, its history and `local/<name>/` are left as they are. `bin/doctor.sh` then notes any open handoff still addressed to it.

**`list`** shows every repo: its owner in the team table, whether it is on this machine, and where it lives.

**`snapshot`** copies each repo's local-only files and `.git/info/exclude` entries into `local/<repo>/`, so they can be reviewed and committed in the workspace. The backup runs it first.

Exit 0; 1 for a repo that is not in `repos.tsv`, or a URL setup refuses; 2 for wrong usage.

## cabinet job

```sh
cabinet job run <job>
cabinet job list [--json]
```

**`run`** runs `jobs/<job>.job` now with the configured agent tool, logging to `<job>.log` in the workspace's log folder (`~/Library/Logs/cabinet/<slug>/` on macOS, `~/.local/state/cabinet/<slug>/` on Linux), and stops it after its time limit (`TIMEOUT`, or `CABINET_JOB_TIMEOUT`). The limit counts only time the machine is awake: a run the machine slept through is not stopped for it, and a run that ends on its own is never reported as stopped. By hand it shows the result too; the scheduler runs the same on the job's schedule, except that a scheduled run of a job with `QUIET_DAYS` is skipped when nothing changed since its last full run (see below). **`list`** shows each job's role, schedule, time limit and [what it cost this week](concepts.md#what-agent-runs-cost), then the week's total and the budget.

Exit 0; 1 when the run failed; 124 when it was stopped by its time limit; 2 for an unknown or incomplete job.

## cabinet secret

```sh
cabinet secret check [--staged] [--json]
```

Looks for keys, tokens and passwords in the workspace's own files (tracked, and new files git does not ignore; not the product repos, which have their own git): private key blocks; AWS, GitHub, Slack, Stripe live, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google API and npm keys; and lines that set a password, secret, token or API key to a value that is not a placeholder (`<...>`) or a variable (`$X`). It prints each file and line with the kind of secret, never the value. A false alarm: add `not-a-secret` anywhere on its line. `--staged` checks only the lines staged for the next commit; the workspace's pre-commit hook runs it ([guardrails](guardrails.md#what-bootstrap-installs)). Exit 0, or 1 when something is found (with `--staged`, the commit is refused).

## cabinet backup

```sh
cabinet backup create [folder]
cabinet backup verify [folder] [--json]
cabinet backup restore <archive> [dir]
```

**`create`** writes one encrypted archive now ([backups](backups.md)); the default folder is `CABINET_BACKUP_DIR`, and the schedule runs the same. **`verify`** writes nothing there: it restores the newest archive into a temporary folder, checks each repo against the workspace, and deletes the copy ([backups](backups.md#checking-it)). **`restore`** rebuilds the workspace and its repos from an archive, never losing a file; outside any workspace it runs the installed kit's copy, since a new machine has no workspace yet. It starts by naming the backup's date.

Exit 0; 1 with no passphrase, no archive, or (for `verify`) a problem found; 2 for a missing, relative or inside folder, or a keep count under 1.

## cabinet bootstrap

```sh
cabinet bootstrap [--dry-run] [--no-schedules | --schedules]
```

Sets up this machine for the workspace: clones missing repos, restores local-only files, links `CLAUDE.md`, gives each repo whose owner is `TBD` a builder ([concepts](concepts.md#the-team)), builds the roles, installs the guardrails ([guardrails](guardrails.md)) and the workspace's secrets check before each commit, and adds, updates or removes the schedules to match `jobs/` and the backup setting. `--dry-run` only prints. `--no-schedules` stops and from then on skips the jobs' schedules on this machine, for a workspace whose jobs another machine runs (a teammate's, in a shared workspace); `--schedules` undoes it. Both are saved in `cabinet.local.env`. The backup schedule is not affected. Safe to rerun. Exit 0, or 1 when any step did not complete (each one says why).

## cabinet config

```sh
cabinet config [options]
```

Changes a workspace's settings after setup: the whole setup at once. To change one thing, the noun commands are shorter (`cabinet role add`, `cabinet repo add`). Run it in the workspace, or in the project's top folder when the workspace is `cabinet/` inside it (or name it: `cabinet -C <dir> config`). In a terminal it asks the setup questions again with the current answers as defaults, lists the changes, and asks before writing.

Options: `--name`, `--slug`, `--owner`, `--email`, `--roles`, `--runner`, `--runner-cmd`, `--brief-time`, `--week-start`, `--writing`, `--hard-to-undo "<repo>/<path> ..."|off` (paths a small task never touches, see below), `--pipeline off|small|all`, `--pipeline-limit <dollars>` and `--pipeline-time <when>|off` (the scheduled runner, see below), `--backup-dir`, `--backup-time <time>` (like `"1 PM"`), `--budget <dollars>|off` (a weekly budget for the agent runs Cabinet starts, like `20` or `12.50`), `--price "<input> <output> [<cached>]"|off` (dollars per million tokens, for a runner that reports only tokens), `--repo` (adds a repo, as `cabinet repo add` does), `--apply` (run `bin/bootstrap.sh` without asking), `--dry-run` (list the changes and write nothing), `--yes`.

**Committing the change.** In a workspace with its own git that had no uncommitted changes before, `config` commits what it changed (`cabinet config: <the settings changed>`), only the files it writes, so a file someone else writes while it runs stays theirs to commit. When the workspace already held uncommitted changes, or the workspace is committed with a project (a shared `cabinet/`), it leaves the change for you: review with `git diff`, then commit.

**For this machine only:** `cabinet config --this-machine --backup-dir <folder>|off [--backup-time <time>]` writes the backup settings into `cabinet.local.env` instead of `cabinet.env`, so they apply on this machine and are never committed. In a shared workspace, each teammate picks their own backup folder, or none. `cabinet config --this-machine --clear` makes this machine follow `cabinet.env` again. With `--this-machine`, no other setting can be changed (they are shared by every machine), and nothing is asked.

**What it changes:**

| Setting | Where |
|---|---|
| Name | `CABINET_PROJECT`, and the titles setup wrote in `AGENTS.md`, `HANDOFFS.md`, `OPERATIONS.md`, `README.md`, `specs/ROADMAP.md`, plus the workspace's own `package.json` |
| Slug | `CABINET_SLUG`; stops the old schedules, renames them in `OPERATIONS.md`, `README.md` and `jobs/*.job`, claims the new slug and releases the old one, and says how to move the backup passphrase in the keychain |
| Owner and email | the "Commits" line in `AGENTS.md` |
| Roles | `CABINET_ROLES`, the team tables in `AGENTS.md` and `OPERATIONS.md` (a dropped role's row leaves; a returning kit role's row comes back; a project role gets a `TBD` row), and the built roles |
| Runner | `CABINET_RUNNER`, `CABINET_RUNNER_CMD` |
| Brief | `WHEN` in `jobs/brief.job` |
| Week start | the house rule in `AGENTS.md` |
| Writing | the "Writing to the owner" house rule in `AGENTS.md` (added after the week start when an older `AGENTS.md` lacks it) |
| Hard to undo | the list under "Hard to undo" in `AGENTS.md`, keeping the section's other text (the section is added before "House rules" when an older `AGENTS.md` lacks it); `off` writes `- none` |
| Backups | `CABINET_BACKUP_DIR`, `CABINET_BACKUP_TIME` |
| Budget and price | `CABINET_BUDGET`, `CABINET_PRICE` |
| Scheduled runner | `CABINET_PIPELINE`, `CABINET_PIPELINE_LIMIT`, and `WHEN` in `jobs/pipeline.job` (made the first time it is turned on; turning it off leaves it, doing nothing) |
| Repos | new rows in `repos.tsv` and the team table in `AGENTS.md` |

**The scheduled runner** moves ready work through build and review while no one watches: each run is `bin/handoff.sh run --scheduled`, from `jobs/pipeline.job`. It is off until you turn it on. `small` lets it move handoffs filed `--small`; `all` adds every spec that `cabinet spec check` finds ready or building. Turning it on needs `--pipeline-limit`, what one run may spend, and a runner whose cost Cabinet counts (claude, grok or opencode, or a token runner with `--price`), or the limit could not hold. `--pipeline-time` sets when it runs (default `10:00 PM`; `off` runs it only by hand: `cabinet job run pipeline`). In a terminal, `config` asks for all three.

**Hard to undo** is the list of paths where a change is hard to undo, such as migrations and public API files: a handoff marked small never touches them ([ready to build](concepts.md#ready-to-build)). Each is `<repo>/<path>`, for a repo in `repos.tsv`; a path ending in `/` covers its folder. It is refused when the repo is unknown, the path has characters other than letters, digits, `.`, `_`, `-` and `/`, or the repo is on this machine and the path is not in it. In a terminal, the question shows what the repos on this machine hold that looks hard to undo (`migrations/`, `db/migrate/`, `prisma/migrations/`, `supabase/migrations/`, `alembic/versions/`, an `openapi` file), as the default when nothing is set yet; nothing is written until you answer, and `--yes` keeps the current list. Editing the section by hand works too.

Roles the project defines itself (`roles/<role>.md` with frontmatter) are accepted and asked about. Layout and visibility (inside, beside, private, shared) are not changed by `config`. When nothing changes, it prints `Nothing to change.` and writes nothing.

## cabinet move

```sh
cabinet move <new-path> [--dry-run]
```

Moves a workspace folder and updates what remembers its path: Claude Code's memory and trusted folders, Codex's trusted folders, the schedules. Refused for the inside and beside layouts. Exit 0, or 1 when refused.

## cabinet remove

```sh
cabinet remove [--dry-run] [--yes] [--force] [--delete-key]
```

Removes the workspace you are in from this machine (another one: `cabinet -C <dir> remove`). It first prints the plan:

- stop and delete the workspace's own schedules (a schedule is its own when it runs this workspace's `bin/`; another workspace's are never touched);
- delete its log folder (`~/Library/Logs/cabinet/<slug>/` on macOS, `~/.local/state/cabinet/<slug>/` on Linux), which frees the slug;
- the backup passphrase and archives stay, unless `--delete-key` (archives always stay);
- inside a project, private: remove the pointers in `CLAUDE.local.md`, `QWEN.local.md` and an untracked `AGENTS.md` (a file left empty is deleted), the role files setup built in `.claude/agents/`, and their `.git/info/exclude` lines, so the project is as it was before `init`;
- inside a project, shared: remove the "Agent team" section from `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` and the `@tarekraafat/cabinet` devDependency; you commit that change;
- delete the workspace folder.

| Option | Notes |
|---|---|
| `--dry-run` | Print the plan only. |
| `--yes`, `-y` | Do not ask. Without it you type the slug to confirm. |
| `--force` | Go ahead even when the workspace has uncommitted changes or commits on no remote. Without it, those stop the removal (`Not safe to delete`). |
| `--delete-key` | Also delete the backup passphrase `cabinet.<slug>.backup` from the keychain or secret store, and its passphrase file if there is one. |

The guardrails in your agent tools stay, since other workspaces use them. Exit codes: 0, or 1 when refused or not confirmed.

## cabinet update

```sh
cabinet update
```

Copies the installed kit's files into the workspace, rebuilds the roles, and prints every changelog section between the workspace's old version and the new one. It never replaces a kit file that was edited in the workspace: it stops, names the file, and keeps the old version (exit 1). In a workspace with its own git it then commits the update (`cabinet: update to <version>`, with the pin in `package.json` and its lockfile; when `package.json` holds other edits of yours, it leaves both files out and prints the commit for them), unless the files it rewrites (`.cabinet/`, `CABINET.md`, `bin/`, `agents/`, `.claude/agents/`, `ORG.md`) held uncommitted edits of yours: then, and in a shared `cabinet/`, it ends with the exact `git add` and `git commit` to run. With nothing to commit (no git of its own, or a private `cabinet/` the project ignores) it ends with `Updated to <version>.`

## cabinet status

```sh
cabinet status [--json]
```

Prints the workspace's kit version, the installed kit's version, and every kit file edited in the workspace. `--json` prints `{workspace, version, kit_version, kit, edited}`.

## cabinet outdated

```sh
cabinet outdated [--json]
```

Compares the workspace's kit version, the installed kit and the newest version on the npm registry, and says what to run. Without the registry it says the newest is unknown. Exit 0.

## cabinet changelog

```sh
cabinet changelog [from-version] [--json]
```

Prints the changelog sections newer than `from-version` (all of them when it is left out).

## cabinet completion

```sh
eval "$(cabinet completion zsh)"     # in ~/.zshrc
eval "$(cabinet completion bash)"    # in ~/.bashrc
```

Tab completion for commands, their verbs and options, and the job names of the nearest workspace after `cabinet job run`.

## cabinet version

```sh
cabinet version [--json]
```

Prints the installed kit's version. In a terminal it prints the Cabinet mark beside it: seven seats around a table, with the eighth left open for the owner. It draws the seats as dots when the terminal's locale is UTF-8, and as the letter `o` otherwise. When the output goes to a script or a file, it prints only `cabinet <version>`.

## Which copy of Cabinet runs

`cabinet update`, `status` and `config` hand off to the workspace's own pinned copy when it exists (`<workspace>/node_modules/@tarekraafat/cabinet`, or the project's `node_modules` above a shared `cabinet/`), so they always act with the project's version. They do this only in a Cabinet workspace: the nearest from the current folder upward (after `-C`). `new`, `init`, `changelog` and `version` always run the copy you called.

## Workspace scripts

Every workspace has its own scripts in `bin/` (`cabinet/bin/` inside a project), named like the commands: one script per noun, taking the verb, and one per one-word command that has a script. Agents, the schedules and a machine without the `cabinet` command use them; all of them read `cabinet.env`, and their options and exit codes are the commands'.

| Command | Script |
|---|---|
| `cabinet doctor` | `bin/doctor.sh` |
| `cabinet bootstrap` | `bin/bootstrap.sh` |
| `cabinet move` | `bin/move.sh` |
| `cabinet brief` | `bin/job.sh run brief` |
| `cabinet job run`, `job list` | `bin/job.sh run <job>`, `bin/job.sh list` |
| `cabinet handoff add`, `attach`, `record`, `list`, `run`, `archive` | `bin/handoff.sh add`, `attach`, `record`, `list`, `run`, `archive` |
| `cabinet spec check`, `record`, `run` | `bin/spec.sh check`, `record`, `run` |
| `cabinet manual build` | `bin/manual.sh build` |
| `cabinet role list`, `draft`, `build` | `bin/role.sh list`, `draft <role>`, `build` (`role add` and `remove` need the `cabinet` command: they change settings) |
| `cabinet repo list`, `remove`, `snapshot` | `bin/repo.sh list`, `remove <name>`, `snapshot` (`repo add` needs the `cabinet` command) |
| `cabinet secret check` | `bin/secret.sh check` |
| `cabinet backup create`, `verify`, `restore` | `bin/backup.sh create`, `verify`, `restore` |

## Output for agents and scripts

Text output is for people and may be reworded at any time. For a script or an agent, use JSON: a field or ID is never renamed or removed without a changelog entry that says so.

| Command | Prints |
|---|---|
| `cabinet help --json`, `cabinet help <command> --json` | `{name, version, docs, commands: [{name, group, usage, summary, options: [{name, value, text}]}]}` |
| `cabinet next --json` | `{workspace, project, steps: [{id, text, command}], optional: [...]}`. Step IDs: `deps`, `tbd`, `commit`, `install`, `bootstrap`, `handoffs`, `brief`, `doctor`; `command` is empty when the step is not a command. Outside a workspace, `workspace` is `null` and the one step is `start`. |
| `cabinet doctor --json` | `{workspace, problems, notes, can_fix, results: [{level, section, id, message}]}`. `level` is `ok`, `fix` or `note`; `id` names the check (every ID is in [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md)) and does not change when its message is reworded. Exit 1 when `problems` is above 0. |
| `cabinet handoff list --json` | The open and acknowledged entries, oldest first: `[{id, status, status_line, date, age_days, from, to, title, verdicts, needs, missing, blocking, stale, ready, unread_verdicts}]`. `date` and `age_days` are `null` when the status line has no date. `verdicts` is `[{role, verdict, date, commits, note}]` (`commits` empty for `none`); `needs`, `missing`, `blocking` and `stale` are role names (where a sub-team role covers the sender's work, it is named in place of its lead, and both during its trial); `ready` is `true`, `false`, or `null` when the entry needs no review; `unread_verdicts` lists lines with PASS, BLOCK or CHANGES outside a Verdict line. `areas` are the critical areas it touches, by its commits or its spec; `depends_on` is the entry's "Depends on" line, `small` and `spec` say how it was filed, and `cost_usd` is what the agent runs recorded under its ID cost (`handoff run`), or `null`. `--ready` keeps only the entries with `ready` true. |
| `cabinet handoff list <name> --json` | Every entry addressed to that repo or role and not closed, with its full `text`. `owner` and `founder` are the same person. |
| `cabinet status --json` | `{workspace, version, kit_version, kit, edited}` |
| `cabinet digest --json` | `[{slug, project, path, exists, brief_written, brief_stale, sign_off_queue, queue_heading_found, actions_for_owner, waiting_on_owner, spend_this_week_usd, budget_usd}]`. The two parts are the Markdown under their headings, or `null`; `queue_heading_found` is `null` with no brief; `spend_this_week_usd` is `null` when the runner does not report cost, `budget_usd` when no budget is set. |
| `cabinet list --json` | `[{slug, project, path, exists, version, update_available, waiting_on_owner, doctor_problems, brief_written}]`. `brief_written` is ISO 8601 UTC, or `null`; the counts are `null` for a workspace whose folder is gone. |
| `cabinet role list --json` | `[{name, kind, on, drafted, reports_to, covers, trial_until, title, display_name, function}]`; `title` and `display_name` are `null` when not set; `reports_to` and `trial_until` are `null`, and `covers` empty, for a role in no sub-team. `kind` is `kit`, `optional`, `builder` or `project`; an optional kit role that is off is listed with `on: false`. |
| `cabinet repo list --json` | `[{name, path, present, owner, url}]`. `owner` is `null` while the team table says `TBD`; `url` is `null` for a repo with no clone URL. |
| `cabinet job list --json` | `[{name, role, when, timeout_minutes, cost_this_week_usd}]`. `when` is the schedule as people read it, or `by hand only`. `cost_this_week_usd` is `null` when the runner's runs are not counted in dollars (a token-only runner with no price, or `custom`). |
| `cabinet secret check --json` | `[{file, line, kind}]`, never the value. Exit 1 when the list is not empty. |
| `cabinet backup verify --json` | `{archive, backed_up, ok, problems, results: [{repo, result, text}]}`. `result` is `ok`, `skipped` or `problem`; `repo` is `null` for the archive as a whole. Exit 1 when `ok` is false. |
| `cabinet outdated --json` | `{workspace_version, kit_version, latest, update_available}`. `latest` and `update_available` are `null` when the registry cannot be reached. |
| `cabinet changelog --json` | `[{version, date, text}]`, newest first. `date` is as written (`Unreleased` until a release). |
| `cabinet version --json` | `{name, version}` |

## Files you can edit

### cabinet.env

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `CABINET_PROJECT` | Display name. |
| `CABINET_SLUG` | Short name for everything machine-wide. Change it with `cabinet config --slug`. |
| `CABINET_ROLES` | Roles to build, space separated. |
| `CABINET_RUNNER` | `claude`, `codex`, `antigravity`, `qwen`, `grok`, `opencode`, `cursor` or `custom`. |
| `CABINET_RUNNER_CMD` | With `custom`: the command, single-quoted. |
| `CABINET_LAYOUT` | `new`, `around`, `inside` or `beside`. Set by setup; not changed by `config`. |
| `CABINET_VISIBILITY` | Inside only: `private` or `shared`. |
| `CABINET_BACKUP_DIR` | Absolute folder for archives, outside the workspace and its repos; empty turns backups off. |
| `CABINET_BACKUP_TIME` | Time of the daily backup, like `1:00 PM` (default). |
| `CABINET_BACKUP_KEEP` | How many of this workspace's archives to keep (default 14, at least 1). |
| `CABINET_JOB_TIMEOUT` | Minutes a job may run before it is stopped, for jobs without their own `TIMEOUT` (default 60; `0` for no limit). |
| `CABINET_BUDGET` | A weekly budget in US dollars for the agent runs Cabinet starts; empty for none. The doctor warns from 80% (`spend.budget`). See [what agent runs cost](concepts.md#what-agent-runs-cost). |
| `CABINET_PRICE` | Dollars per million tokens, `"<input> <output> [<cached input>]"`, to count runs of a runner that reports only tokens; empty for none. |
| `CABINET_SKILLS`, `CABINET_PLUGINS` | Claude Code skills and plugins the doctor expects (a missing one is a note). |

### jobs/&lt;job&gt;.job

One scheduled agent run each. Keys: `AGENT` (the role), `PROMPT` (or, instead of both, `COMMAND`: a command run in the workspace that starts and limits its own agent runs, as `jobs/pipeline.job` runs `bin/handoff.sh run --scheduled`), `WHEN` (a [schedule time](#schedule-times), or empty for by hand only), `MINUTES` and `RESULT` (shown when run by hand), `TIMEOUT` (whole minutes before the run is stopped, with everything it started, and the reason written to its log; empty uses `CABINET_JOB_TIMEOUT`, `0` means no limit), `AFTER` (an optional shell command run in the workspace after a successful run), `QUIET_DAYS` (whole days; empty or `0` runs every time). After a change, run `bin/bootstrap.sh`.

**Quiet days.** With `QUIET_DAYS`, a scheduled run starts no agent when nothing changed since the job's last full run: no commit, branch or fetch in the workspace, the project around it or any repo, no new doctor problem (by check ID), and the `RESULT` file as that run left it (an answer written into `BRIEF.md` counts as a change). It logs `<job> skipped: nothing changed since the full run of <time>` and touches the `RESULT` file, so `cabinet digest` and `cabinet next` see the brief as current. It never skips when any of those folders has uncommitted changes (the brief asks about work pending for more than a day), when the sign-off queue in the `RESULT` file holds a `default` item (it goes ahead after 72 hours of silence, and only a run says so), after a failed run, or once `QUIET_DAYS` days have passed since the last full run. A run by hand always runs. The brief has `QUIET_DAYS="6"`: on a quiet week, one full run a week. The state is `<job>.quiet` in the log folder, on this machine only.

### cabinet.local.env

Settings for this machine only. Git never tracks it (the workspace's `.gitignore` tracks only its own files), so in a shared workspace each teammate's machine keeps its own. It is read, never run as shell. Its keys:

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `CABINET_SCHEDULES` | `off`: this machine schedules none of the jobs in `jobs/` (another machine runs them). Set and cleared with `cabinet bootstrap --no-schedules` and `--schedules`. Jobs still run by hand with `cabinet job run <job>`. |
| `CABINET_BACKUP_DIR`, `CABINET_BACKUP_TIME` | When present, they replace `cabinet.env`'s on this machine; an empty `CABINET_BACKUP_DIR` turns backups off here. Set with `cabinet config --this-machine`, removed with `cabinet config --this-machine --clear`. |

### Schedule times

Every schedule takes the same forms: the brief (`--brief-time`), any job (`WHEN` in `jobs/<job>.job`) and the digest (`cabinet digest --schedule`).

| Form | Means |
|---|---|
| `7 AM`, `7:00 AM`, `7am`, `daily 7 AM` | Every day at 7:00 AM. |
| `fri 4 PM`, `Friday 4:00 PM` | Every Friday at 4:00 PM. |
| `fri,sat 10:30 AM` | Every Friday and Saturday at 10:30 AM. |
| `sun,mon,tue,wed,thu 8 AM` | Sunday to Thursday at 8:00 AM. |
| `12 PM`, `12 AM` | Noon, midnight. |

Times are 12-hour, with `AM` or `PM` in any case (`pm`, `p.m.` too); the minutes can be left out (`4 PM`). A time without AM or PM is read as 24-hour (`16:00` is 4:00 PM, `7:00` is 7:00 AM), so files and scripts written that way keep working; a bare hour (`10`) is refused, since it could be either. Put a time with a space in quotes on the command line: `--brief-time "fri 4 PM"`.

Days are `sun`, `mon`, `tue`, `wed`, `thu`, `fri`, `sat`, or their full names, in any case, separated by commas. All the days named share one time. Naming all seven is the same as every day. Setup and config store one form, `fri,sat 10:30 AM`, and every message shows times as `4:00 PM`.

### repos.tsv

Tab separated, one row per repo: name, clone URL (`-` for none), local-only files (space separated, `-` for none), `CLAUDE.md` link (`yes` or `no`), and an optional path where the repo lives (absolute, `~/...`, or relative to the workspace; default `<workspace>/<name>`). Windows line endings are fine. A row whose name is not a plain folder name is skipped with a message.

## Environment variables

| Variable | Used by | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `CABINET_BACKUP_PASSPHRASE` | backup, restore, doctor | The archive passphrase, instead of the item `cabinet.<slug>.backup` in the keychain, the secret store or the passphrase file. Never put it in `cabinet.env`, which git tracks. |
| `CABINET_SCHEDULER` | bootstrap, doctor, digest, config, remove, move | `launchd`, `systemd`, `cron` or `none`: the scheduler to use instead of the one Cabinet finds ([macOS and Linux](concepts.md#macos-and-linux)). |
| `CABINET_PROMPT`, `CABINET_AGENT` | the `custom` runner | The prompt and role, for `CABINET_RUNNER_CMD`. |
| `CABINET_TTY` | setup, config, remove | Read answers from this file instead of the terminal (the tests use it). |
| `CABINET_PRIVATE_WORDS` | `npm test` | Words that must not appear in the kit. |

## Removing a workspace

`cabinet remove` does all of this (see [cabinet remove](#cabinet-remove)). By hand:

1. Stop its schedules. On macOS: `launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/ai.cabinet.<slug>.<job>` for each, then delete `~/Library/LaunchAgents/ai.cabinet.<slug>.*.plist`. With systemd: `systemctl --user disable --now ai.cabinet.<slug>.<job>.timer` for each, then delete `~/.config/systemd/user/ai.cabinet.<slug>.*.service` and `.timer`. With cron: delete `~/.config/cabinet/cron/ai.cabinet.<slug>.*.cron`, then run `cabinet bootstrap` in any other workspace, which rewrites Cabinet's block of the crontab (or delete its lines from `crontab -e` by hand).
2. Delete its log folder (`~/Library/Logs/cabinet/<slug>/` on macOS, `~/.local/state/cabinet/<slug>/` on Linux), which also frees the slug.
3. If it had backups: `security delete-generic-password -a "$USER" -s cabinet.<slug>.backup` (on Linux: `secret-tool clear service cabinet.<slug>.backup account "$USER"`, or delete `~/.config/cabinet/passphrases/cabinet.<slug>.backup`), and delete its archives if you no longer want them.
4. Delete the workspace folder.
5. Inside a project: for private, remove the `/cabinet/`, `/CLAUDE.local.md`, `/QWEN.local.md`, `/AGENTS.md` (if setup created it) and `/.claude/agents/<role>.md` lines from the project's `.git/info/exclude`, and the files they name if setup made them; for shared, remove the "Agent team" section and the `@tarekraafat/cabinet` devDependency from the project.

The guardrails stay; see [guardrails](guardrails.md#undoing-the-guardrails).


========================================================================
File: docs/layouts.md
========================================================================

# Layouts

Where a workspace sits, and what that means for your project. `cabinet new` makes the first; `cabinet init` picks one of the other three from where you run it. The layout is recorded as `CABINET_LAYOUT` in `cabinet.env` and does not change later.

| Layout | Made by | The workspace is | Your project |
|---|---|---|---|
| `new` | `cabinet new <dir>` | a new folder; product repos are cloned into it | (cloned into the workspace) |
| `around` | `cabinet init` in a folder that is not a repo | that folder, around what is already in it | the repos in its subfolders, listed in `repos.tsv` |
| `inside` | `cabinet init --inside` in a project repo | `cabinet/` inside the project | unchanged files, plus what is listed below |
| `beside` | `cabinet init --beside` in a project repo | a folder next to the project (default `<project>-hq`) | not changed at all |

## new

The simplest: one folder holding the team's files and, under it, every product repo (cloned by `bin/bootstrap.sh` from `repos.tsv`). The workspace's `.gitignore` tracks only its own files, so the product repos stay out of its git.

## around

For a folder that already holds your repos side by side. `cabinet init` keeps everything there: existing files are never replaced, the folder's own `.gitignore` is kept, and only the files setup placed are committed (never a `.env` or other files that were already there). The repos it finds are listed in `repos.tsv`. If the folder already has a file at a path the kit uses, such as `bin/doctor.sh`, setup stops before writing anything: rename or move that file, then run `cabinet init` again.

## inside

For one project repo that should carry its team with it. The workspace is `<project>/cabinet/`. Agents usually start in the project's top folder, so setup points them at `cabinet/` with an "Agent team" section, and also writes the role definitions into the project's `.claude/agents/` (a file of the project's own with the same name is kept). Paths in `CABINET.md` and the roles are relative to `cabinet/`: run its scripts as `cabinet/bin/<script>`. `cabinet status`, `update` and `config` work from the project's top folder.

There are two kinds, set once as `CABINET_VISIBILITY`:

### Private (the default)

`cabinet/` has its own git, and the project's git never sees it. No tracked file of the project changes:

- the pointer goes only into files the project does not track: `CLAUDE.local.md` (read by Claude Code and Grok), `QWEN.local.md` (Qwen), and `AGENTS.md` only when the project has none;
- `cabinet/`, those pointer files and the role files are added to the project's `.git/info/exclude`;
- the version pin goes in `cabinet/package.json`;
- `bin/role.sh build` rebuilds the pointers on every update and after a restore.

When the project has its own `AGENTS.md`, it is left alone. Codex, opencode, Gemini and Cursor read only that file, so start them in `cabinet/`, or add the "Agent team" section to `AGENTS.md` yourself. If you later write a real `AGENTS.md` for a project that had none, remove `/AGENTS.md` from `.git/info/exclude` first, or git will ignore it.

Fits: solo work, open source projects, client repos.

### Shared

`cabinet/` is part of the project's repo, for everyone who clones it. Setup adds the "Agent team" section to the project's `AGENTS.md` (or `CLAUDE.md`, or a new `AGENTS.md`) and pins the kit in the project's `package.json` as a devDependency (with npm's own `npm pkg set`: formatting kept, no network, an existing entry left alone). Setup commits nothing in the project: review the new files and commit them yourself. Without a `package.json` in the project, the pin goes in `cabinet/package.json`.

Fits: a private repo whose teammates should see the team's handoffs and specs.

## beside

The project is not changed at all. The workspace is a folder next to it and points at it with a relative path (`../<project>`) in `repos.tsv`, so the project stays where it is and nothing is cloned again. Fits a product with several repos, or a project you would rather not touch.

## What lives where

| | What | Who changes it |
|---|---|---|
| **Kit files** | `CABINET.md`, `bin/*.sh`, `.cabinet/` (roles, rules read when a task needs them, guardrails, schedule template, version, manifest) | Only `cabinet update`. Never edit them in a workspace: an update stops at an edited one. |
| **Project files** | `AGENTS.md`, `cabinet.env`, `roles/`, `jobs/`, `HANDOFFS.md`, `OPERATIONS.md`, `repos.tsv`, `specs/`, `notes/`, `tools/` (the project's own scripts) | You and the agents. Placed once by `new` or `init`; afterwards `cabinet config` changes only the settings it manages in them. |
| **Built** | `agents/<role>.md`, `.claude/agents/<role>.md`: the kit's role plus your `roles/<role>.md`; `ORG.md`, the org page | `bin/role.sh build` |

Instructions layer from general to specific: `CABINET.md`, then the workspace's `AGENTS.md`, then each repo's own `AGENTS.md`.

## Switching layouts

Not supported: moving between layouts, or between private and shared, means moving files and changing git by hand. `bin/move.sh` moves a `new` or `around` workspace to another folder; it refuses the inside and beside layouts, whose relative paths would break.


========================================================================
File: docs/concepts.md
========================================================================

# Concepts

The ideas Cabinet is built on. The rules themselves are in `CABINET.md`, which every workspace gets and every agent reads first; this page explains them for people.

Cabinet is a productivity kit that makes one person a whole team. It amplifies people and never replaces them: agents bring the skills and the hours, and the owner brings the vision, the judgment and the final say. Alone, you work like a full company; in a team, every member does.

## The team

A workspace runs a product with AI agents, each in a role, and one owner (you) who signs off. The kit's roles:

| Role | Owns | Decides | Brings to you |
|---|---|---|---|
| chief-of-staff | the brief, the sign-off queue, routing tasks, seats | how work is routed | every decision in one queue |
| product-manager | one spec per feature, the roadmap | nothing you have not decided | product decisions, framed with a recommendation |
| architect | contracts between repos, architecture decision records | reversible technical questions across repos | vendors, data handling, public API shapes |
| qa | independent verification | PASS or BLOCK | overrides of a block |
| security | security and privacy review of unpushed work | PASS or BLOCK | legal and disclosure questions |
| design-lead | UX and visual consistency inside the brand guide | layout and interaction choices | any brand change |
| finance | cost and pricing models | how to model | every price, plan and spend |
| brand-designer (optional) | brand files and the graphics made from them | choices inside the approved brand | any change to the brand, licenses |
| dba (optional) | database health; reviews migrations | PASS or BLOCK on data changes | anything run on a live database |
| code-reviewer (optional) | code review of each change | PASS or CHANGES | overrides of CHANGES |
| auditor (optional) | audits of what is in place | severity of findings | critical findings |
| backend, web, mobile, infrastructure | the product repos the team table assigns each (the builders) | how to build inside a repo, following its own conventions | changes to a repo's stack or tools; applying infrastructure |

Each role's file says what it owns, decides, escalates and may write. A project turns roles on or off (`CABINET_ROLES`; the optional ones are off until turned on), adds notes to one in `roles/<role>.md`, or adds a role of its own: `cabinet role add <role>` takes as little as a name, and an agent drafts the whole role for the project from what the owner said and what the project shows, listing its assumptions for the owner to confirm ([recipes](recipes.md#add-a-role)).

**Builders** are the roles that write the product's code. They are not in `CABINET_ROLES`: a builder is built when it owns a repo in the team table of `AGENTS.md`. When a repo whose owner is `TBD` first arrives on a machine, `bin/bootstrap.sh` gives it the builder it most looks like: `mobile` for an `ios/` or `android/` folder, a `pubspec.yaml`, an Xcode project, or React Native or Expo; `infrastructure` for Terraform, Pulumi, Helm or CDK files; `web` for React, Next, Vue, Svelte, Angular, Astro or Nuxt, or an `index.html`; otherwise `backend`. In a workspace with its own git, bootstrap commits that change (the team table, `ORG.md`, the built roles) unless those files held uncommitted edits of yours; then, and in a shared `cabinet/`, it leaves them for you to review and commit. Change the row to choose another builder, a project role, or `owner`, then `bin/role.sh build`. In a repo that already exists a builder learns how it is built (its `AGENTS.md`, scripts, CI, lint and style) and follows it; only a new, empty repo gets defaults (the kit's `core/rules/builders.md`, installed as `.cabinet/rules/builders.md`).

## Rules, guides and notes

What the agents follow, from the most general to the most specific:

1. `CABINET.md`: how every Cabinet workspace runs. From the kit; never edited in a workspace. It holds what every agent needs on every session; the detail only some roles or tasks need is in `.cabinet/rules/` (`builders.md`, `ready-to-build.md`, `reviews.md`, `seats.md`), which `CABINET.md` names with when to read each, and each role names the ones its job needs. Every session reads less, and nothing is lost.
2. `AGENTS.md` in the workspace: this project's team, contracts, house rules and product rules, and the "Guides" table.
3. `guides/`: standing documents, such as a brand guide, style guide, policy or business document. Agents read a guide before any work its row in `AGENTS.md` covers. A guide ranks with `AGENTS.md`.
4. `roles/<role>.md`: what this project adds for one role, built into that role's definition.
5. A repo's own `AGENTS.md`: rules for work in that repo.

On a conflict the more specific wins: a repo's `AGENTS.md` over the workspace's `AGENTS.md` and guides, over `CABINET.md`. Nothing can loosen "Never push, merge, publish or release" or "The builder never verifies". `notes/` is different: thinking and decisions on the record, read when relevant, not rules in force. How to add each: [recipes](recipes.md#add-your-own-rules-guidelines-and-business-documents).

## Repo ownership

Each repo has one owning agent, listed in the team table in `AGENTS.md`, and so does each workspace area (`specs/`, `specs/qa/`, ...). An area inside another belongs to its own row: the most specific row wins. No agent writes to a repo it does not own. When a change affects another repo, the agent files a handoff instead of editing it. The doctor flags an area with two owners (`team.single-owner`), notes a part of a repo given to another role than the repo's (`team.nested`) and a project role whose "What you may write" reaches another role's area (`roles.writes`), and `cabinet role add --owns` refuses an area that is already another role's.

## Critical areas

Some parts of a project cost more when they go wrong: payments, personal data, a public API, data imports, a store listing, a pricing page. The kit does not know which; you declare them under "Critical areas" in `AGENTS.md`, each with its paths, the reviewers it needs as well as the usual ones, the evidence they must see, and optionally a check, a script of your own in `tools/` that proves what a script can (a replay of saved inputs, an API comparison, a load test). Work touching an area, by its commits or by its spec's `areas`, is not ready to push until those reviewers pass, and a reviewer's PASS counts only when the check passes; its output is kept as evidence. Nothing changes for a project that declares none.

| Project | Area | Also reviewed by | Evidence | Check |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SaaS with payments | billing | security, finance | a test payment in the sandbox | a sandbox script |
| Data or analytics product | importers | architect | results compared | replay saved inputs |
| Mobile app | store listing, permissions | design-lead, security | real-device screenshots | none |
| Library | public API | architect | the API diff and version bump | an API diff tool |
| Client work | the deliverable | owner | a preview link | a link checker |
| Business with little code | pricing page | finance | old and new prices side by side | none |

`OPERATIONS.md`, the owner's manual, is also a page: `cabinet manual build` writes `OPERATIONS.html`, with contents, search and tick boxes for the daily and weekly lists, rebuilt after each brief.

`tools/` is the project's own scripts: updates never touch it, the manual names each one (the doctor checks), and jobs and checks call them.

## Ready to build

Nothing is built before it is defined. A small task (one repo, no contract change, no decision for you, easy to undo) goes straight to a handoff that says what done looks like, marked small (`cabinet handoff add --small`). The claim is checked against what was built: a PASS is refused when the commits span repos or change a file a contract lives in or a path listed as hard to undo in `AGENTS.md`, and the doctor flags one already passed (`handoffs.small`). Whether a decision should have been yours, no script can tell: qa blocks that. `cabinet config --hard-to-undo` sets the list, checking each path against the repos and suggesting what looks hard to undo in them. Anything bigger is built from a spec in `specs/`, which the product-manager writes, and a spec moves through statuses that `cabinet spec check` holds to what each needs:

- **draft** while it is written and its decisions wait on you.
- **ready** once it has testable acceptance criteria, nothing `TBD` in its rules, every decision answered, and the repos that build it, and qa has passed the criteria as testable (`cabinet spec record`). For anything people see, the design lead first designs it in the spec (the flows, screens and states) and passes that design. Only a ready spec is routed to builders (`cabinet handoff add --spec`).
- **building** once each builder has written its part of the plan (files, tests, order, risks) and, for work in more than one repo, the architect has passed the plan.
- **shipped** or **dropped** at the end.

Work that changes no repo (copy, research, a campaign) goes the same way with the checks that fit it: what done looks like, evidence of the result, and a verdict with no commits; the checks built on commits apply only to work that has them. A review counts only for what it reviewed: a change to the criteria or the plan after a PASS needs a new one. A builder given work that is not ready sends it back instead of guessing. The doctor flags a spec marked ready or building that lacks what its status needs (`specs.ready`).

## Handoffs

`HANDOFFS.md` is the one channel between agents. Each entry has an ID (`H-20261018-01`), who it is from and to, a status (`open`, `acknowledged`, `done`, `rejected`), what changed, what is needed, what it depends on, and its evidence: links to screenshots, recordings or output that show the work, which the brief carries to you. The addressee edits only the status line; everyone else adds a follow-up entry. Closed entries move to `handoffs/archive-YYYY-MM.md` daily. `bin/handoff.sh add` files an entry with the next free ID and commits it; `bin/handoff.sh list <name>` shows an agent its open entries.

## Decision tiers

Every decision belongs to exactly one tier:

1. **The agent:** reversible and inside its own files, following existing rules.
2. **The function's lead:** reversible, crosses repos or sets direction, costs nothing.
3. **You:** irreversible, public, or costs money. Pushes, deploys, publishing, prices, spend, brand, legal, and adding or changing an agent.

An agent unsure of the tier treats it as the higher one. When two roles disagree, or both think a decision is theirs, the function's lead settles it; across functions, or when whose call it is is unclear, it comes to you as one sign-off item with both views, and neither acts on it meanwhile. A reversible tier 3 item marked "default" may go ahead as local commits after 72 hours without an objection, but nothing is ever pushed, published or spent on silence.

## The brief and the sign-off queue

The chief-of-staff writes `BRIEF.md` on a schedule (`jobs/brief.job`). It verifies handoffs against git, checks the repos and the doctor, and puts every decision waiting on you at the top. Each decision has a plain question, lettered options with their consequences, each expert's recommendation, one overall recommendation, and whether it can be undone. You answer in one message; the agents apply your answers. Its parts sit under fixed headings (`## Sign-off queue`, `## Actions for the owner`, ...), so with several projects `cabinet digest` gathers every queue into one read. On a day when nothing changed (no commit, no new doctor problem, no answer, no work left uncommitted, no reversible item waiting for its 72 hours), the scheduled brief starts no agent and the last brief stands, for up to six days in a row ([quiet days](commands.md#jobsltjobgtjob)).



## Writing to the owner

How agents write to you is a house rule in `AGENTS.md`, asked at setup and by `cabinet config`, or set with `--writing` on `cabinet new`, `init` or `config`. `standard` is the sign-off format in plain words. `short` is for an owner with little time to read, or who reads best in small pieces (for example with ADHD): the same facts and decisions in fewer words.

- The answer, or what is needed from you, comes first, in one sentence.
- One point per line, with the word that matters in bold; three points at most, then "N more: ask".
- A decision in three lines: the question, the options on one line, the recommendation with whether it can be undone.
- No background unless you ask; plain words; how long an action takes, when known.
- The brief opens with what waits today ("Today: 2 decisions, 1 action, about 5 min."). The sign-off queue stays complete, and no warning about anything irreversible, money, security or data loss is ever cut.

The rules are in `CABINET.md`, "Writing to the owner", which every agent reads. Ask any agent for details on a point and it gives them.
## What agent runs cost

Every agent run costs money, as API spend or against a subscription's limits. Cabinet counts what its own runs cost (scheduled jobs and `cabinet role draft`), from what the agent tool reports, in `spend.tsv` in the workspace's log folder (time, job, runner, dollars, then uncached input, cached input and output tokens), on this machine only. Each built-in runner prints JSON for this; the reply still goes to the job's log, and output that is not that JSON (an error, a different version) goes there as it is.

| Runner | Reports | Seen on |
|---|---|---|
| `claude` | dollars | Claude Code's documented JSON |
| `grok` | dollars and tokens | Grok 1.0.62 |
| `opencode` | dollars and tokens; 0 dollars for a model it has no price for | opencode 2.0.32 |
| `codex` | tokens | Codex 0.163.0 |
| `cursor` | tokens | Cursor CLI 2026.10.16 |
| `qwen` | tokens | Qwen Code 0.25.3 (the shape of its result; no successful run yet) |
| `antigravity` | tokens | Antigravity CLI 1.4.2 |
| `custom` | nothing | |

Dollars a tool reports are what it says the run cost; on a subscription, that is what the run would cost through the API. For a runner that reports only tokens, set its price, in dollars per million tokens, as input, output and optionally cached input (cached input costs the input price when left out): `cabinet config --price "1.25 10 0.125"`, from the model's price list. Setup asks for it after the budget. With `opencode`, a price also counts runs of a model it reports at 0 dollars. Without a price, those runs are recorded in tokens only, and the doctor says so when a budget is set (`spend.unreported`). Sessions you or a teammate run in an agent tool are not counted, nor is a run stopped by its time limit.

- Each job's log ends a run with its cost and the week's.
- `cabinet job list` shows what each job cost this week, and the week's total.
- `cabinet digest` shows each project's week against its budget, and the total across every project on this machine.
- Setup asks for a weekly budget in US dollars, and a price for a runner that reports only tokens; `cabinet config --budget 20` sets or changes it. From 80% of it, the doctor reports `spend.budget`, so the brief lists it under "Actions for the owner"; past it, the doctor says so. Nothing is stopped: you decide whether to raise the budget, run jobs less often, or let the week end. The week starts on the day `AGENTS.md` names (Sunday by default).

Two settings keep the cost down: a brief that skips its agent on [quiet days](commands.md#jobsltjobgtjob), and fewer scheduled jobs.
## The builder never verifies

Work is ready for you to push only when qa and security have each recorded PASS on its handoff, and so has every other reviewer you enabled whose subject it touches (design-lead for anything people see, code-reviewer for code, dba for the database). A BLOCK, or a code-reviewer's CHANGES, holds the push until it is fixed or you override it. Whether work is ready is computed, not judged: `cabinet handoff list --ready` lists the work every reviewer it needs has passed at its latest commits, and the brief asks you to push only that. Turned on with `cabinet config --pipeline small|all --pipeline-limit <dollars>`, the same runs happen on a schedule while you are away, never past that much a run or your weekly budget, and the brief tells you what reached ready to push and what stopped. `cabinet spec run <spec>` does the same for a whole ready spec (routing, each builder's plan, the architect's review of it, then each piece of work in order), and `cabinet handoff run <ID>` moves one piece of work through those steps for you: the builder, each reviewer, the fixes after a BLOCK and the checks again, until it is ready to push or needs you, deciding nothing on its own. qa never passes work without evidence you can check without reading code (screenshots, a recording, a link to try it, or command output), and the brief links it. Each reviewer records its verdict with `cabinet handoff record`, as one line on the handoff, `- Verdict: qa PASS 2026-10-20 a1b2c3d specs/qa/2026-10-20-login.md` (role, PASS, BLOCK or CHANGES, date, commits, its note), and `cabinet doctor` flags a verdict in any other shape and a qa PASS with no evidence.

## Seats

A seat is a role filled by an agent or a person. The kit ships a small core of roles and none for each specialty: the team grows with the project. The chief-of-staff flags signs that a seat is needed, from the work (recurring work no seat owns, a function falling behind) and from the project itself (a website no one looks after for search, users with no one answering them, a goal you stated with no seat working on it), with evidence only, and every new seat is your decision, with its cost and the alternatives. A seat you decline is recorded in `notes/seats.md` and proposed again only with new evidence. A new seat is drafted for this project (`cabinet role add`).

## Titles and the org page

A role can carry a title and a display name ("Head of Product", "Product Agent"), set with `cabinet role add --title --name` or in its "## Team" section. Every decision brought to you names each expert by its title where it has one, so you read "Head of Engineering recommends B", not a file name. `ORG.md`, rebuilt with the roles whenever the team changes, shows each function with its lead and members, and for each role its title, what it does, what it owns, who it reports to and what it covers: a page for you, for someone joining, or the source for a public team page you approve. The kit ships no titles: a project that sets none gets the role names.

## Sub-teams

As a project grows, one role per function becomes a bottleneck. A lead can then grow a sub-team: roles that report to it and take on part of its work, such as `qa-mobile` reporting to qa and covering the mobile builder's work (`cabinet role add qa-mobile --reports-to qa --covers mobile`). It is proposed and approved like any seat, from the same evidence (the lead falling behind, a specialty it lacks, a new surface). Its lead onboards it, corrects it and settles its disagreements. On the work it covers, its review counts for its lead's, so the runner sends that work to it; for its first 30 days the lead must pass that work too, and after that the lead spot-checks, and either one's BLOCK holds the push. A builder's sub-team is a role owning a narrower repo or area, which the most specific row of the team table gives it. `cabinet role list` shows who reports to whom, and the doctor checks every lead is on the team and no role leads itself round a loop (`team.reports-to`). Each new seat goes through an onboarding checklist and a review after a month.

## Slugs and isolation

Every workspace has a slug. Everything it puts on the machine is named by it: schedules `ai.cabinet.<slug>.<job>`, its log folder `<slug>/` (below), the backup key `cabinet.<slug>.backup`, archives `<slug>-<YYYYMMDD>-<HHMMSS>.tar.gz.enc`. The log folder holds a `workspace` file naming its owner. Setup and `cabinet config` refuse a slug another workspace holds, bootstrap never replaces or removes a schedule that runs another workspace, and backup cleanup removes only the slug's own archives. Paths are compared with symlinks resolved, so a workspace reached through a link is still the same one.

## macOS and Linux

Cabinet works the same on both. Only where it keeps things on the machine differs, and one file, `bin/platform.sh`, decides it:

| | macOS | Linux |
|---|---|---|
| Schedules | launchd: `~/Library/LaunchAgents/ai.cabinet.<slug>.<job>.plist` | systemd user timers: `~/.config/systemd/user/ai.cabinet.<slug>.<job>.service` and `.timer`. On a machine that did not boot with systemd (many containers, older WSL): cron, as one block Cabinet writes into your crontab from `~/.config/cabinet/cron/`, keeping every line of your own. |
| Log folder | `~/Library/Logs/cabinet/<slug>/` | `~/.local/state/cabinet/<slug>/` (under `$XDG_STATE_HOME` when set) |
| Backup passphrase | the login keychain | the secret store, through `secret-tool` (`libsecret-tools` on Debian and Ubuntu); with cron, a file only you can read: `~/.config/cabinet/passphrases/cabinet.<slug>.backup` |
| Notifications | Notification Center | `notify-send` |

`CABINET_SCHEDULER` (`launchd`, `systemd`, `cron` or `none`) overrides the choice. On Linux:

- systemd runs a user's timers only while that user is logged in, unless lingering is on: `loginctl enable-linger "$USER"` once, on a server or a machine you leave logged out. A timer missed while the machine was off runs when it starts again, as launchd does after sleep.
- The secret store needs a desktop session. Without one, give scheduled backups the passphrase through systemd instead: `read -rs CABINET_BACKUP_PASSPHRASE; export CABINET_BACKUP_PASSPHRASE; systemctl --user import-environment CABINET_BACKUP_PASSPHRASE` (until the user's systemd stops; run it again after a restart). Cron jobs reach neither, so with cron the passphrase is kept in a file only you can read, `~/.config/cabinet/passphrases/cabinet.<slug>.backup` (under `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` when set; `bin/bootstrap.sh` prints the command that writes it). On any machine that file, when it exists, comes before the keychain or secret store, and one that other users can read is never used.
- Run `cabinet bootstrap` as yourself, not through `sudo`: schedules are per user.

## Agent tools and models

Cabinet works through agent tools, so it works with any model they offer. Everything is plain files: any tool that reads `AGENTS.md` can run the team, and acting as a role means reading `agents/<role>.md`. Scheduled jobs run with the tool in `CABINET_RUNNER`. Which tools have guardrails, and their limits: [guardrails](guardrails.md).

| Runner | Runs a job as |
|---|---|
| `claude` | `claude -p --agent <role> --permission-mode auto --output-format json` (tested with real scheduled jobs) |
| `codex` | `codex exec --json "<role instruction> <prompt>"` |
| `antigravity` | `agy -p "<role instruction> <prompt>" --output-format json --dangerously-skip-permissions` |
| `qwen` | `qwen --approval-mode auto -o json "<role instruction> <prompt>"` |
| `grok` | `grok -p "<role instruction> <prompt>" --permission-mode auto --output-format json` |
| `opencode` | `opencode run --format json "<role instruction> <prompt>"` |
| `cursor` | `cursor-agent -p --force --output-format json "<role instruction> <prompt>"` (run live) |
| `custom` | `CABINET_RUNNER_CMD`, with the prompt in `$CABINET_PROMPT` and the role in `$CABINET_AGENT` |

The role instruction is "Act as the <role> role: read agents/<role>.md and follow it as your instructions". Runners other than `claude` and `cursor` follow each tool's documented headless mode and are untested end to end as scheduled jobs (`grok`, `opencode`, `codex` and `antigravity` answered a one-line prompt in that mode; `qwen` needs an auth type set in its settings); Codex's default sandbox may not let a scheduled brief write its file. Headless Antigravity denies any tool it would ask about, and `--mode auto` is not open to every plan, so its runner skips the prompts: its deny rules are then the guardrail ([guardrails](guardrails.md)). Gemini CLI is no longer a runner: Google moved its users to Antigravity. A workspace still set to `gemini` is told to run `cabinet config --runner antigravity`; Gemini CLI keeps its guardrails for interactive use. Scheduled jobs get a PATH with the runner's and Node's folders.


========================================================================
File: docs/guardrails.md
========================================================================

# Guardrails

How Cabinet keeps every push, merge, release and publish with you, what each agent tool's rules can and cannot block, and how to undo them.

## The two layers

1. **The push gate.** A global git pre-push hook asks for `yes` at your terminal for every `git push`, from any tool. Agents run without a terminal, so their pushes are refused.
2. **Deny rules in each agent tool.** They block push, merge, release and publish commands, and the known ways around the push gate (git can be told to skip hooks).

Together they are a strong speed bump, not a boundary. For a hard boundary, protect your branches on the server (GitHub branch protection).

## What bootstrap installs

`bin/bootstrap.sh` installs the guardrails machine-wide, for every tool it finds. It is safe with several workspaces: rules are only ever added, never removed; a config file that is not plain JSON, whose shape is unexpected, or that holds a value a rewrite would change (a number written as `1.0` or `1e3`, one too large to keep exactly, or a key that is a whole number), is left exactly as it was, with a message; files are written in place, so their permissions and symlinks stay; and a backup copy `<file>.bak.<timestamp>` is made before any change. A file that already exists (the push gate, the Codex rules, the Gemini policy) is left as it is and checked, never replaced.

| Tool | Reads `AGENTS.md` | Guardrails | Checked by `bin/doctor.sh` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | through the `CLAUDE.md` link | `~/.claude/settings.json` `permissions.deny` / `ask` | yes |
| Grok | yes, in folders you trust | reads the Claude Code rules | yes, with `grok inspect` |
| Qwen Code | yes | `~/.qwen/settings.json`, the same rule list | yes |
| opencode | yes | `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` `permission.bash`, placed last because its last matching rule wins. A commented `opencode.jsonc` is never rewritten; opencode reads it after the `.json`, so a rule there can still override | on opencode 1.x; on 2.x it cannot (its debug commands need a background service), so check by hand |
| Gemini CLI | bootstrap sets `context.fileName` in `~/.gemini/settings.json` | `~/.gemini/policies/owner-control.toml` | yes |
| Codex | yes | `~/.codex/rules/default.rules`; also `approval_policy = "on-request"` in `~/.codex/config.toml`, so Codex asks before anything its sandbox does not allow | yes |
| Antigravity CLI | yes | its `settings.json` | yes |
| Cursor CLI (`cursor-agent` / `agent`) | yes | `~/.cursor/cli-config.json` `permissions.deny` | yes (the file) |
| Cursor editor | yes | none: its agent's command rules live in the editor's own settings, which the kit does not change. The push gate applies | noted |
| Any other tool | point it at `AGENTS.md` | the push gate only | named, as a note |

Two more machine-wide settings come with the push gate:

- **`git config --global core.hooksPath ~/.config/git/hooks`**, where the gate lives. A global hooks path makes git skip every repo's own `.git/hooks`, so bootstrap also places a pass-through stub there for the other client hooks (pre-commit, commit-msg, post-checkout and the rest; not push-to-checkout or fsmonitor-watchman, which change git's behavior just by existing). A repo's own hooks, such as a secret scanner, keep running. A repo that sets its own `core.hooksPath` (husky does) bypasses the gate; the doctor names it.
- **The workspace's secrets check,** a `pre-commit` hook in the workspace's own `.git/hooks` (bootstrap runs it through the pass-through stub). It runs `bin/secret.sh check --staged` and refuses a commit that adds a likely key, token or password, naming the file and line, never the value. A false alarm passes once its line has `not-a-secret` on it. An existing `pre-commit` hook is left as it is (the doctor notes it; your hook can call `bin/secret.sh check --staged` itself). A shared `cabinet/` inside a project gets none, since the project's own hooks run there; `bin/doctor.sh` still scans its files. It is a safety net, not a guarantee: it knows common key formats, not every secret.
- **Gemini CLI's `context.fileName`** is set to read `AGENTS.md` everywhere, so Gemini also loads `AGENTS.md` in folders that are not Cabinet workspaces.

## What each tool's rules block

The rule formats differ, so the coverage does too.

**Claude Code, Grok, Qwen Code, opencode** (one rule list, matched anywhere in a command, so also inside wrappers such as `env`, `bash -c` or `nohup`):

- push, `git send-pack` (which pushes without hooks), merge, release, `gh api` writes, publishing (npm, npx, bun, pnpm, yarn, also with options before `publish`);
- the ways around the gate: `-c core.hooksPath` in common spellings, `GIT_CONFIG_*` variables, `env -i` and `env -u`, a push behind a `HOME=` override (caught because `git push` is matched anywhere), `--no-verify` and its abbreviations, faking a terminal (`script`, `expect`, `unbuffer`, Python's `pty.spawn`);
- printing the GitHub token, and reading the keychain, the Linux secret store (`secret-tool lookup` and `search`) or the backup passphrase file (any command naming `cabinet/passphrases`).

Side effects: some harmless commands are refused too, such as an npm script named like `publish-docs`, or any command that mentions `git push` (for example in an `echo`).

**Gemini CLI** (regular expressions): the same list, with the hooks path matched in any letter case and `git push` matched anywhere in a command.

**Cursor CLI** (the command's first word plus an arguments pattern): push, `send-pack`, hook-path and `--no-verify` arguments to git, the terminal fakers, merges, releases, `gh api` writes, publishing, the GitHub token and the keychain. Probed live on Cursor CLI 2026.10.16 with harmless stand-ins:

- argument patterns match at the start and in the middle; first-word rules match;
- chained commands (`a && b`) are checked;
- a leading variable (`HOME=... git push`) is dropped before matching, so the git rules still catch it;
- wrappers are not looked through, so the kit denies `env`, `bash -c`, `sh -c`, `zsh -c`, `nohup`, `xargs`, `sudo`, `exec`, `command`, `nice` and `stdbuf` outright, and `timeout` or `time` with push, publish or `send-pack`. Any other wrapper is not caught.

**Codex and Antigravity** (rules match only how a command starts): push, `send-pack`, `env -i` and `env -u`, merge, release, publish and the terminal fakers are denied; `git -c ...` and `gh api` ask first. A bypass that does not start the command, such as `HOME=... git push` or `--no-verify` after other words, is not caught.

**Not caught by any tool's rules:** git config keys in unusual letter case (except in Gemini), an agent editing `.git/config` with its file tools (the doctor reports a repo's own `core.hooksPath` afterwards), and other ways of faking a terminal.

## Known limits

These are on the [roadmap](../ROADMAP.md):

- archives are encrypted with AES-256-CBC and no separate integrity check, so tampering shows only as an unreadable archive;
- any process of your user can read the backup passphrase from the keychain or secret store without a prompt (the deny rules stop agents in the tools above);
- the backup passphrase file, used where cron runs the schedules, is denied only to shell commands that name its folder, in Claude Code, Grok, Qwen Code, opencode and Gemini CLI: a tool's own file reader, a command that reaches it another way, and the other tools can still read it;
- opencode agent-level and project-level configs, and Qwen workspace settings, can loosen the global rules, and the doctor checks only the global result;
- on opencode 2.x the doctor cannot read the resolved rules.

## Undoing the guardrails

The guardrails are shared by every workspace on the machine, so removing a workspace leaves them. To remove them:

- **Rules in a tool's settings:** restore the `.bak.<timestamp>` copy bootstrap made next to the file, or delete the rules you no longer want (the kit's list is in each workspace's `.cabinet/guardrails/`).
- **The push gate and hook stubs:** `git config --global --unset core.hooksPath`, then delete `~/.config/git/hooks/`.
- **Codex:** remove `approval_policy` from `~/.codex/config.toml` and the kit's rules from `~/.codex/rules/default.rules`.
- **Gemini:** delete `~/.gemini/policies/owner-control.toml` and remove `context.fileName` from `~/.gemini/settings.json`.


========================================================================
File: docs/backups.md
========================================================================

# Backups

An encrypted daily archive of everything a lost machine would take with it, and a restore that never loses a file.

## What a backup holds

`cabinet backup create` (`bin/backup.sh create`, which the schedule runs) writes one archive with, for the workspace and every repo in `repos.tsv`:

- the full git history: every branch and unpushed commit;
- uncommitted changes, untracked files and stashes;
- `.env` files (git ignores them, so nothing else keeps them);
- the branch it was on, or that HEAD was detached.

It also includes Claude Code's memory for the workspace and `~/.claude/settings.json`. A repo with no commits yet (for example a workspace made without an owner identity) is kept as its files.

Archives are named `<slug>-<YYYYMMDD>-<HHMMSS>.tar.gz.enc`, encrypted with AES-256-CBC (PBKDF2, 200000 iterations), readable only by you (mode 600). The newest `CABINET_BACKUP_KEEP` (default 14) of this workspace's archives are kept; another workspace's archives in the same folder are never touched.

## Setting it up

1. Choose a folder **outside** the workspace and every repo it lists: a synced drive or an external disk. Setup, `cabinet config` and the backup itself refuse a folder inside them, because a backup there is lost with what it protects, copies itself into every later archive, and can be committed.
2. Set it with `cabinet config --backup-dir <folder>` (and `--backup-time "<time>"`, default 1:00 PM), then `bin/bootstrap.sh` to schedule it.
3. Put the passphrase in the keychain (macOS), the secret store (Linux) or, where cron runs the schedules, a file only you can read, and keep the same one in your password manager: without it no archive opens. `bin/bootstrap.sh` prints the command for your system; on Linux without a desktop session see [macOS and Linux](concepts.md#macos-and-linux).

```sh
security add-generic-password -a "$USER" -s cabinet.<slug>.backup -w
```

Or set `CABINET_BACKUP_PASSPHRASE` in the environment. Never put it in `cabinet.env`, which git tracks.

## Restoring

```sh
bin/backup.sh restore <archive> [folder]     # folder: where the workspace goes (default: this workspace)
bin/bootstrap.sh                      # then guardrails, links and schedules
bin/doctor.sh
```

On a new machine, put the passphrase in the keychain or secret store first, then run `backup.sh restore` from a copy of the kit (or a clone of the workspace's repo). Restore never loses a file:

- **A repo that already exists** gets the archive's branches under `refs/remotes/backup/*`, to compare and merge by hand. Its patches are copied to `recovered/`.
- **A missing repo, or an empty folder,** is restored with its uncommitted work, on the branch it was on (or detached, as it was).
- **The workspace folder itself, or a project folder holding nothing but the workspace being restored** (the inside layout), is checked out in place. Any file the archive would replace with different content, tracked or untracked, is first copied to `recovered/<archive>/`.
- **Any other folder that already holds files of its own** is left alone, and the repo is restored into `recovered/<archive>/<name>/repo` instead. A folder such as your home folder is never turned into a repo.
- `.env` files are restored only where missing. Stashes are kept as patches in `recovered/`.
- Claude Code memory and settings are restored only where missing.

Inside a project with the private layout, the pointer files (`CLAUDE.local.md` and the others) are ignored by the project's git and so not in the archive: `bin/role.sh build`, run by bootstrap, rebuilds them.

## Checking it

`bin/doctor.sh` reports the newest scheduled backup's age (from `backup.log` in the log folder, never by listing the backup folder, which can trigger a macOS access prompt), whether the passphrase is in the keychain or secret store (or in `CABINET_BACKUP_PASSPHRASE`), and a backup folder in the wrong place. Once a quarter, check that the newest archive really restores:

```sh
cabinet backup verify      # or bin/backup.sh verify [folder]
```

It restores the newest archive of this workspace into a temporary folder, as `backup.sh restore` would, and deletes that copy when it is done (it holds your secrets). For the workspace and each repo it prints one line: restores exactly as it is now, restores with so many files or commits changed since the backup (work done after it), or a problem. A problem is an archive that does not open (a wrong passphrase, or a damaged file), a history that does not rebuild, uncommitted changes that do not apply, files that do not unpack, or a repo that is not in the archive. Any problem makes it exit 1: back up again, then verify that archive. It never touches the workspace, its repos or your settings, and does not check Claude Code's memory or settings. A good result is recorded in `~/Library/Logs/cabinet/<slug>/backup-verified`, and `bin/doctor.sh` notes when none is recorded or the last is older than 92 days.
