File: docs/troubleshooting.md
========================================================================

# Troubleshooting

Every message `bin/doctor.sh` can print, what it means and how to fix it. `FIX` lines make the doctor exit 1; `note` lines are information. `<...>` stands for a name, path or number the doctor fills in. Run the doctor again after a fix. The ID names the check: `cabinet doctor --json` gives it with each result, and it stays the same when a message is reworded, so scripts and agents match on the ID, never on the text.

## Tools

| Message | ID | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ok the tools cabinet needs are here (<...>)` | `deps.required` | git, node and npm are all found. | Nothing. |
| `ok Node.js is 18 or newer` | `deps.node` | The Node.js found can run the scripts' JavaScript. | Nothing. |
| `FIX cabinet needs Node.js 18 or newer; this is <...> (<...>)` | `deps.node` | The Node.js found is too old for the scripts' JavaScript, so most commands stop with the same message. Ubuntu 22.04 and Debian 11 install an older one. | `brew upgrade node` on macOS; on Linux, a current Node.js from [nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org). `cabinet new`, `init` and `bootstrap` stop with this message before changing anything. |
| `FIX cabinet needs <...>, not found (<...>; cabinet doctor --fix runs it, asking first)` | `deps.required` | A tool Cabinet needs is missing. The message names the install command for this machine (`brew`, `apt-get`, `dnf` or `pacman`), or where to get a package manager. | `cabinet doctor --fix` in a terminal, or run the command yourself. |
| `FIX backups need <...>, not found (<...>; cabinet doctor --fix runs it, asking first)` | `deps.backups` | Backups are on, and openssl (or, on Linux, `secret-tool`, unless `CABINET_BACKUP_PASSPHRASE` is set) is missing. | The same. |

## Product repos

| Message | ID | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `FIX <...>: no repo at <...> (run bin/bootstrap.sh)` | `repos.present` | A repo in `repos.tsv` is not where its row says. | `bin/bootstrap.sh` clones it (it needs a clone URL in the row), or fix the path column. |
| `FIX <...>/<...> missing` | `repos.local-file` | A local-only file listed in `repos.tsv` is not in the repo. | `bin/bootstrap.sh` restores it from `local/<repo>/`. |
| `FIX <...>/<...> not in snapshot (run bin/repo.sh snapshot)` | `repos.snapshot` | A local-only file has no copy in `local/<repo>/`. | `bin/repo.sh snapshot`, then commit the workspace. |
| `note <...>/<...> changed since last snapshot` | `repos.snapshot` | A local-only file differs from its copy. | `bin/repo.sh snapshot` when the change is finished, then commit. |
| `FIX <...>/<...> is tracked in the product repo but listed as local-only` | `repos.local-file-tracked` | The file is committed in the product repo, but `repos.tsv` says it lives outside git there. | Remove it from that repo's git (`git rm --cached`), or from the row's local-only list. |
| `FIX <...>/CLAUDE.md is not a link to AGENTS.md` | `repos.claude-link` | A repo whose row says `yes` to the link has no `CLAUDE.md` link. | `bin/bootstrap.sh` creates it (when the repo has an `AGENTS.md` and no `CLAUDE.md`). |
| `FIX <...>: instruction files show as untracked (missing exclude entry)` | `repos.instructions-excluded` | A repo's local `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md` shows in its `git status`. | Add them to that repo's `.git/info/exclude` (keep the entries in `local/<repo>/git-info-exclude`). |
| `repos.tsv: skipped the row named "<...>" (not a plain folder name)` | - | A row's name has spaces or other characters. | Rename it to letters, digits, `.`, `_` or `-`. |

## Kit and roles

| Message | ID | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `FIX kit files edited here (an update will refuse them; move the change to a project file or into the kit): <...>` | `kit.unedited` | A file the kit owns (`CABINET.md`, `bin/`, `.cabinet/`) was changed in the workspace. | Move your change to a project file (`AGENTS.md`, `roles/`, `jobs/`), then `git checkout -- <file>`. |
| `FIX workspace CLAUDE.md link missing (run bin/bootstrap.sh)` | `kit.claude-link` | The workspace's `CLAUDE.md` link to `AGENTS.md` is gone. | `bin/bootstrap.sh`. |
| `FIX HANDOFFS.md missing` | `kit.handoffs-file` | The handoff log was deleted. | Restore it from git. |
| `note the <...> role is not drafted yet (cabinet role draft <...>, or ask your agent to draft the <...> role)` | `roles.drafted` | `cabinet role add` made the role from your brief, and no agent has drafted it yet. Until then it does only what the brief asks. | `cabinet role draft <role>`, or ask your agent to draft it ([recipes](recipes.md#add-a-role)). |
| `note project roles behind the workflow: <...> (redraft each: cabinet role draft <role>, which keeps what you confirmed)` | `roles.workflow` | A drafted role of the project's own misses part of the workflow its job touches, usually because it was drafted before the kit added it: it never sends the agent to `CABINET.md`; it talks of PASS, BLOCK or CHANGES without `bin/handoff.sh record`; it says nothing of how a disagreement with a neighbouring role is settled; or it owns a repo and says nothing of its plan or its evidence. Each role is named with what it misses. These are text checks for known gaps, not a judgment of the role. | `cabinet role draft <role>` redrafts it under the current rules, keeping your brief and what you confirmed; or add the missing part to `roles/<role>.md` yourself. |
| `note project roles that may write another role's area: <...> (narrow the role's "What you may write", or change the team table)` | `roles.writes` | A role of the project's own lists, under "What you may write", a path the team table gives another role (the most specific row decides). `HANDOFFS.md` and `specs/evidence/` are shared and never count. | Narrow the role's "What you may write" to its own areas (redraft it, or edit `roles/<role>.md`), or give it the area in the team table if that is what you want. |
| `note roles/<...>.md is a whole role and the kit also has a <...> role: yours is used, not the kit's (rename yours, or remove its frontmatter to add notes to the kit's role)` | `roles.shadows` | A role file of yours with frontmatter has a kit role's name, for example one a later kit added. Yours is built as it is; the two are never mixed. | Keep it if that is what you want. To use the kit's role, rename yours (and its name in `CABINET_ROLES`), or turn yours into notes by removing its frontmatter. |
| `FIX <...> (run bin/role.sh build)` | `kit.roles` | A built role is missing or out of date (for example after editing `roles/` or `CABINET_ROLES`). | `bin/role.sh build`. |

## Push guardrails

| Message | ID | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `FIX git push gate not installed (run bin/bootstrap.sh)` | `guardrails.push-gate` | No pre-push hook in the global hooks path. | `bin/bootstrap.sh`. |
| `note repos' own git hooks (pre-commit and others) do not run under the global hooks path: run bin/bootstrap.sh` | `guardrails.hook-passthrough` | The pass-through stubs are missing. | `bin/bootstrap.sh`. |
| `FIX <...> sets its own core.hooksPath (<...>), which bypasses the push gate` | `guardrails.repo-hookspath` | A repo sets its own hooks path (husky does), so the global gate is skipped there. | Remove it (`git config --unset core.hooksPath`), or add the gate to that repo's hooks folder yourself. |
| `FIX Claude Code is missing <...> deny rule(s) (run bin/bootstrap.sh)` | `guardrails.claude` | `~/.claude/settings.json` lacks some of the kit's rules. | `bin/bootstrap.sh`. If it says the file is not plain JSON, fix the file first. |
| `FIX Codex push rule missing (run bin/bootstrap.sh)` | `guardrails.codex` | Codex does not forbid `git push`. | `bin/bootstrap.sh`; if `~/.codex/rules/default.rules` already exists, add the kit's rules (`.cabinet/guardrails/codex-default.rules`) to it. |
| `FIX agy push deny rule missing (run bin/bootstrap.sh)` | `guardrails.agy` | Antigravity's settings lack the push rule. | `bin/bootstrap.sh`. |
| `FIX Gemini CLI policy missing (run bin/bootstrap.sh)` | `guardrails.gemini` | No `~/.gemini/policies/owner-control.toml`. | `bin/bootstrap.sh`. |
| `FIX Qwen Code is missing <...> deny rule(s) (run bin/bootstrap.sh)` | `guardrails.qwen` | `~/.qwen/settings.json` lacks some of the kit's rules. | `bin/bootstrap.sh`. |
| `FIX Cursor CLI is missing <...> deny rule(s) in ~/.cursor/cli-config.json (run bin/bootstrap.sh)` | `guardrails.cursor` | The Cursor CLI's config lacks some of the kit's rules. | `bin/bootstrap.sh`. |
| `note the Cursor editor keeps its agent's command rules in its own settings, which the kit does not set: only the git push gate applies there` | `guardrails.cursor-editor` | Information: the kit cannot set the editor's rules. | Set its command denylist in the Cursor editor's settings if you want more than the push gate. |
| `FIX Grok does not load the rules in ~/.claude/settings.json (check: grok inspect)` | `guardrails.grok` | Grok is not reading the Claude Code rules (its Claude compatibility may be off). | Turn it on in Grok, or add the rules to `~/.grok/config.toml` by hand. |
| `FIX opencode does not deny: <...> (run bin/bootstrap.sh; a rule in opencode.jsonc comes last and wins)` | `guardrails.opencode` | On opencode 1.x, the resolved rules do not end with the kit's denies. | `bin/bootstrap.sh`; if it still fails, remove the overriding rule from `opencode.jsonc`. |
| `note <...> of opencode cannot be checked from here: confirm its permission settings by hand (the kit's rules are in ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json)` | `guardrails.opencode` | opencode 2.x has no command to print its resolved rules. | Check in opencode that it refuses `git push`. |
| `note <...> is installed and cabinet has no guardrails for it: only the git push gate above applies` | `guardrails.unguarded-tool` | An agent tool the kit does not cover. | Use it for reading and local edits, or add its own deny rules by hand. |
| `FIX scheduled jobs cannot find the runner '<...>' (install it, or fix CABINET_RUNNER / CABINET_RUNNER_CMD, then run bin/bootstrap.sh)` | `runner.found` | The runner is not on the PATH scheduled jobs get. | Install it, or fix the setting; then `bin/bootstrap.sh` from a shell where it is on your PATH, so the schedule gets its folder. |
| `FIX scheduled jobs find <...> but not node, which it needs (run bin/bootstrap.sh after installing node)` | `runner.node` | The runner is a Node script and Node is not on the scheduled PATH. | Install Node, then `bin/bootstrap.sh`. |
| `ok scheduled jobs find node` | `schedules.node` | Node is on the PATH scheduled jobs get, so the workspace scripts' JavaScript (`bin/lib.js`) runs in them. | Nothing. |
| `FIX scheduled jobs cannot find node, which the workspace scripts need (install Node.js, then run bin/bootstrap.sh)` | `schedules.node` | Node is not on the PATH scheduled jobs get (the PATH found when `bin/bootstrap.sh` last ran), so the brief, handoff and spec steps of a job would fail. | Install Node.js where your shell finds it, then `bin/bootstrap.sh` saves the new PATH into the schedules. |
| `note the custom runner '<...>' has no cabinet guardrails: only the git push gate covers its scheduled runs` | `runner.custom-unguarded` | A custom runner the kit does not know. | Add its own deny rules by hand. |

## Skills and plugins

| Message | ID | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `note skill '<...>' not installed` | `skills.skill` | A skill in `CABINET_SKILLS` is not in `~/.claude/skills/`. | Install it, or remove it from `CABINET_SKILLS`. |
| `note plugin '<...>' not installed` | `skills.plugin` | A plugin in `CABINET_PLUGINS` is not installed in Claude Code. | Install it, or remove it from `CABINET_PLUGINS`. |

## Guides

| Message | ID | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `FIX guides/<...> has no row in the Guides table of AGENTS.md, so agents never read it` | `guides.listed` | A file was added to `guides/` without a row in the "Guides" table. | Add a row: `` `guides/<file>` ``, what it covers, who follows it. See [recipes](recipes.md#add-your-own-rules-guidelines-and-business-documents). |
| `FIX AGENTS.md lists <...>, which does not exist` | `guides.exists` | A row in the "Guides" table names a file that is not in `guides/`. | Restore the file, fix the path, or delete the row. |

## Manual and handoffs

| Message | ID | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `note OPERATIONS.html is older than OPERATIONS.md, or missing (cabinet manual build; the brief rebuilds it each morning)` | `manual.page` | `OPERATIONS.md` changed since the page was built (agents update the manual whenever they change a script, job or role), or the page was never built. | `cabinet manual build`, or wait for the next brief. |
| `FIX OPERATIONS.md does not mention: <...>` | `manual.complete` | The manual has fallen behind a script (the kit's in `bin/`, or the project's own in `tools/`), a job or a role. | Add it to `OPERATIONS.md` (`cabinet config --roles` adds role rows for you). |
| `FIX these handoff IDs are used more than once: <...>(file the next free number)` | `handoffs.unique-ids` | Two entries share an ID. | Give the later one the next free number, or mark it with a `- Note: duplicate ID` line. |
| `FIX verdicts not in the format, or naming a note that does not exist: <...> (rewrite each as - Verdict: <role> <verdict> <YYYY-MM-DD> <commits> <note under specs/>, and commit its note)` | `handoffs.verdicts` | An open entry has a `- Verdict:` line in another shape (the verdict is `PASS`, `BLOCK` or `CHANGES`), or its note is not in the workspace. Each entry is named by its ID. | Have the reviewer commit the note and record the verdict again with `cabinet handoff record`, which writes the [verdict format](concepts.md#the-builder-never-verifies). |
| `note PASS, BLOCK or CHANGES written outside a Verdict line, so not counted: <...> (the reviewer records it with bin/handoff.sh record)` | `handoffs.unread-verdicts` | An open entry has a verdict written in prose, usually on its status line ("qa PASS"), which readiness never reads, so that work does not show as ready. Each entry is named by its ID. | Have the reviewer record it with `cabinet handoff record`, and set the status line back to a status. |
| `FIX handoffs marked small that were not: <...> (route the work again from a spec)` | `handoffs.small` | A handoff filed with `--small` has a PASS, but its commits span more than one repo, are in no repo on this machine, or change a path `AGENTS.md` guards (a contract's files, "Hard to undo"). Each is named with the reason. | Route the work again from a spec ([ready to build](concepts.md#ready-to-build)); the reviewer records BLOCK meanwhile. A commit in no repo here: clone or fetch that repo. |
| `FIX qa PASS on handoffs with no evidence: <...> (the builder adds an Evidence line, or qa changes its verdict to BLOCK)` | `handoffs.evidence` | qa passed work whose entry has no `- Evidence:` line, so you would approve it without seeing it. | The builder adds evidence with `cabinet handoff attach <ID> <file or URL> --from <builder>`, or qa records BLOCK. |

## Critical areas

| Message | ID | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `FIX critical areas in AGENTS.md that cannot hold: <...> (fix its row)` | `areas.declared` | A row under "Critical areas" names no paths, a path in a repo not in `repos.tsv` or that does not exist there, no reviewer or one not on the team, or a check that is not a command in `tools/` that can run. Work in that area waits on a reviewer who cannot come, or a check that cannot run. Each problem is named. | Fix the row in `AGENTS.md`: the paths, the reviewers (or turn the role on), or the check (put it in `tools/`, `chmod +x`). |

## Specs

| Message | ID | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|

| `FIX specs not ready for their status: <...> (fix each, or set it back to draft; cabinet spec check)` | `specs.ready` | A spec marked `ready` or `building` lacks what that status needs: testable criteria with a qa PASS, no `TBD` in "Rules", every decision answered, its repos, and for `building` a plan (with an architect PASS for more than one repo). A PASS no longer counts when the part it reviewed changed. Each spec is named with its problems. | Fix what is named and ask for the review again, or set the spec's `status` back to `draft` (or `ready`) until it is. See [ready to build](concepts.md#ready-to-build). |

A false alarm: add `not-a-secret` to its line. |
| `note commits are not checked for secrets: the workspace has no pre-commit hook running bin/secret.sh (run bin/bootstrap.sh; a hook of your own can call bin/secret.sh check --staged)` | `secrets.hook` | Bootstrap has not run, or the workspace has its own `pre-commit` hook. | `bin/bootstrap.sh`, or call `bin/secret.sh check --staged` from your hook. |

## Team

| Message | ID | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `note parts of a repo owned by another role than the repo's: <...> (the most specific row wins; if that is not meant, change the team table)` | `team.nested` | The team table gives a path inside a product repo (`api/docs/`) to a different role than the repo's own row. That is allowed, since the most specific row wins, but it splits a repo, so it is your call. | Keep it if it is meant. Otherwise remove the inner row, or give it to the repo's owner. |
| `FIX sub-team roles that do not fit the team: <...> (fix the Team section of each in roles/<role>.md)` | `team.reports-to` | A role's "## Team" section names a lead who is not on the team, leads back to itself through others, or covers something that is no builder or repo. Each is named. | Fix `- Reports to:` or `- Covers:` in `roles/<role>.md`, or turn the lead on (`cabinet config --roles`). |
| `FIX more than one owner in the team table of AGENTS.md: <...> (give each one owner)` | `team.single-owner` | The same repo or area has rows with different owning agents, so two roles would act on it. Each is named with its owners. | Keep one row per repo or area. Work the other role does there goes to the owner as handoffs. |
| `note open handoffs addressed to no role or repo on the team: <...> (readdress or close them)` | `handoffs.addressee` | An open entry's `To:` names something that is not a role on the team, a repo in `repos.tsv`, or the owner: a role turned off, a repo removed, or a typo. Each is named with its ID. | Readdress it to whoever owns the work now (a follow-up entry), or close it with a reason. |

| `note <...> has <...> uncommitted file(s): work in progress, or finished and not committed?` | `work.uncommitted` | A repo has uncommitted changes. | Commit finished work; leave work in progress. |

## Schedules

| Message | ID | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `FIX jobs/<...>.job has a WHEN bootstrap cannot schedule ('<...>'): use a time like 7 AM for every day, or days and a time like fri 4 PM or sun,mon,tue,wed,thu 8 AM` | `schedules.when` | A mistyped time or day. Bootstrap keeps the working schedule meanwhile. The forms are in [commands](commands.md#schedule-times). | Fix `WHEN`, then `bin/bootstrap.sh`. |
| `FIX <...>.<...> not scheduled (run bin/bootstrap.sh)` | `schedules.job` | A job has a time but no schedule. | `bin/bootstrap.sh`. |
| `note jobs are not scheduled on this machine (CABINET_SCHEDULES=off in cabinet.local.env): another machine runs them; cabinet bootstrap --schedules turns them on` | `schedules.off` | This machine was set up with `cabinet bootstrap --no-schedules`, so the job checks are skipped here. | Nothing, when another machine runs the jobs. To run them here: `cabinet bootstrap --schedules`. |
| `FIX <...>.<...> runs another workspace: give this one its own slug (cabinet config --slug)` | `schedules.job-owner` | Two workspaces share a slug. | `cabinet config --slug <new>` in one of them. |
| `FIX <...>.<...> is written but not loaded by <...> (run bin/bootstrap.sh)` | `schedules.job-loaded` | The schedule file exists, but the scheduler (launchd, systemd or cron) has not loaded it. | `bin/bootstrap.sh`. |
| `FIX <...> still runs this workspace under an old name (<...>)` | `schedules.old-slug` | A schedule left over from an earlier slug. | Run what it names: on macOS `launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/<label>`, with systemd `systemctl --user disable --now <label>.timer`; then delete the file it names. |
| `FIX no scheduler on this machine (a running systemd user session, or cron), so no job runs on its own: install cron, then run bin/bootstrap.sh` | `schedules.scheduler` | Linux without a systemd user session or `crontab`, as in many containers. Jobs only run by hand. | Install cron (or run under systemd), then `bin/bootstrap.sh`. |

## Spend

| Message | ID | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `FIX the scheduled runner is on with no cost limit, so it runs nothing (cabinet config --pipeline-limit <dollars>)` | `pipeline.ready` | `CABINET_PIPELINE` is `small` or `all`, and `CABINET_PIPELINE_LIMIT` is empty. The same ID reports a value other than off, small or all, a runner whose cost cannot be counted, or a missing `jobs/pipeline.job`. | `cabinet config --pipeline-limit <dollars>`, `--price` for a token runner, or `--pipeline off`. |
| `FIX CABINET_PIPELINE is '<...>', not off, small or all (cabinet config --pipeline small, all or off)` | `pipeline.ready` | `cabinet.env` was edited by hand to a value the runner does not know, so it runs nothing. | `cabinet config --pipeline small`, `all` or `off`. |
| `FIX the scheduled runner is on, but <...>'s cost cannot be counted, so it runs nothing (cabinet config --price, or another runner)` | `pipeline.ready` | The runner reports no dollars (a token runner with no price, or `custom`), so a cost limit could not hold. | `cabinet config --price "<input> <output> [<cached input>]"`, or `--runner` claude, grok or opencode. |
| `FIX the scheduled runner is on, but jobs/pipeline.job is missing (cabinet config --pipeline <...> adds it)` | `pipeline.ready` | The job file was deleted, so nothing runs it on a schedule. | `cabinet config --pipeline small` (or `all`) makes it again; then `cabinet bootstrap`. |
| `FIX agent runs cost $<...> this week, <...>% of the $<...> budget: cabinet job list shows what each job cost; raise it with cabinet config --budget <dollars>` | `spend.budget` | The agent runs Cabinet started this week cost 80% or more of `CABINET_BUDGET`, as the agent tool reported it. See [what agent runs cost](concepts.md#what-agent-runs-cost). | `cabinet job list` shows which job cost what. Raise the budget (`cabinet config --budget <dollars>`), run jobs less often (`WHEN`, `QUIET_DAYS`), or let the week end. |
| `FIX agent runs cost $<...> this week, over the $<...> budget: cabinet job list shows what each job cost; raise it with cabinet config --budget <dollars>` | `spend.budget` | The week's runs passed the budget. Nothing is stopped. | The same. |
| `note <...> reports tokens, not dollars, so the $<...> budget is not tracked: set its price with cabinet config --price "<input> <output> [<cached input>]" (dollars per million tokens)` | `spend.unreported` | A budget is set, and the runner (codex, cursor, qwen or antigravity) reports only tokens. | `cabinet config --price "<input> <output> [<cached input>]"`, from the model's price list. See [what agent runs cost](concepts.md#what-agent-runs-cost). |
| `note <...> does not report what a run costs, so the $<...> budget is not tracked (the built-in runners report it)` | `spend.unreported` | A budget is set, and the runner is `custom`. | Use a built-in runner to track it, or remove the budget: `cabinet config --budget off`. |

## Backups

| Message | ID | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `note backups are off on this machine (cabinet.local.env; cabinet config --this-machine --backup-dir <folder> turns them on)` | `backups.enabled` | This machine turned backups off for itself (`cabinet config --this-machine --backup-dir off`). | Nothing, when another machine backs up. To back up here: `cabinet config --this-machine --backup-dir <folder> --apply`. |
| `note backups are off (set CABINET_BACKUP_DIR in cabinet.env, then run bin/bootstrap.sh)` | `backups.enabled` | No backup folder set. | `cabinet config --backup-dir <folder>`, then `bin/bootstrap.sh`. See [backups](backups.md). |
| `FIX CABINET_BACKUP_DIR must be an absolute path` | `backups.dir-absolute` | A relative backup folder. | `cabinet config --backup-dir <absolute folder>`. |
| `FIX the backup folder is inside <...>: a backup there is lost with it and can be committed (choose a folder outside, then cabinet config)` | `backups.dir-outside` | The backup folder is inside the workspace or one of its repos. | Choose a folder outside them with `cabinet config --backup-dir`. |
| `FIX no scheduled backup in <...>/backup.log yet (<...>)` | `backups.recent` | No scheduled backup has run yet. | Run what it names (`launchctl kickstart` on macOS, `systemctl --user start` with systemd, `cabinet backup create` with cron), or wait for the time set. |
| `FIX newest backup is <...>h old (<...>): <...>` | `backups.recent` | No scheduled backup in the last 36 hours (the machine was asleep or the job failed). | Read `backup.log` in the log folder (`~/Library/Logs/cabinet/<slug>/` on macOS, `~/.local/state/cabinet/<slug>/` on Linux). |
| `note no restore of a backup has been verified on this machine yet (cabinet backup verify)` | `backups.verified` | `cabinet backup verify` has not passed on this machine. | `cabinet backup verify` ([backups](backups.md#checking-it)). |
| `note the last verified restore was <...> days ago (<...>): verify again (cabinet backup verify)` | `backups.verified` | The last good verify is more than 92 days old. | `cabinet backup verify`. |
| `FIX backup passphrase missing from the <...> (<...>: <...>)` | `backups.passphrase` | No item `cabinet.<slug>.backup` in the keychain (macOS) or the secret store (Linux), or with cron no passphrase file (a cron run cannot reach the secret store), and `CABINET_BACKUP_PASSPHRASE` is not set. | Run the command it names, with the same passphrase as in your password manager: `security add-generic-password -a "$USER" -s cabinet.<slug>.backup -w` on macOS, `secret-tool store --label=cabinet.<slug>.backup service cabinet.<slug>.backup account "$USER"` on Linux, and with cron a command that writes `~/.config/cabinet/passphrases/cabinet.<slug>.backup` readable by you only ([macOS and Linux](concepts.md#macos-and-linux)). |
| `FIX the passphrase file <...> can be read by other users, so it is not used: chmod 600 <...>` | `backups.passphrase` | The passphrase file exists, but its permissions let others read it, so backups ignore it. | `chmod 600` on the file, as the message says. |

## Other commands

- **`cabinet: not inside a cabinet workspace, or a project with cabinet/ in it`:** a workspace command (`doctor`, `bootstrap`, `brief`, ...) ran outside any workspace. `cd` into the workspace or its project, or start one with `cabinet new` or `cabinet init`.
- **`cabinet: unknown command '<...>'`:** exit 2, with the list of commands.
- **`Not safe to delete: <...>`:** from `cabinet remove`, when the workspace has uncommitted changes or commits on no remote. Commit and push (or copy) that work first; `--force` deletes it anyway.
- **`--fix asks before each step: run it in a terminal, or add --yes`:** `cabinet doctor --fix` had no terminal to ask in.
- **`cabinet: the slug '<...>' is already used by the workspace at <...>`:** choose another with `--slug`. When it says that workspace no longer exists, it lists the steps to free the slug.
- **`cabinet: <...> already has a cabinet workspace: use cabinet update`:** `init` runs once per folder.
- **`cabinet: <...> is inside the repo <...>: run cabinet init at its top folder`:** run it there.
- **`cabinet: these files already exist at paths the kit uses: <...>`:** rename or move those files, then run `cabinet init` again.
- **`<...>: the merge did not produce a valid file (its shape is not what the kit expects), left as is`:** from bootstrap. The file is unchanged; add the kit's rules by hand, or fix the file's shape.
- **An update stops with "edited here, left as is"** or **"already here and not the kit's":** move your change to a project file, restore the kit's file, then `cabinet update` again.


========================================================================
File: core/CABINET.md
========================================================================

# CABINET.md - how this workspace runs

This file comes from the Cabinet kit and is replaced on every kit update. Do not edit it here: project rules go in `AGENTS.md`, standing documents (brand, style, policies, business documents) in `guides/` with a row in the "Guides" table of `AGENTS.md`, and project notes for a role in `roles/<role>.md`. A change that should reach every project goes into the kit itself.

Every agent reads this file first, then `AGENTS.md`, then the `AGENTS.md` of the repo it works in, and before any work a guide in `AGENTS.md` covers, that guide. On a conflict the more specific file wins: repo `AGENTS.md` over workspace `AGENTS.md` and its guides over this file. Nothing in a project file or guide may loosen "Never push, merge, publish or release" or "The builder never verifies".

You work for the owner and multiply what they can do; you never stand in for them. The owner brings the vision, the judgment and the final say: carry their vision into your work, recommend, and bring every decision that is theirs to the sign-off queue.

## The workspace

One folder holds the files that tie the project's repos together, and usually the repos themselves; a repo can also live elsewhere (the path column of `repos.tsv`), such as a project the workspace sits beside or inside. The workspace is its own private git repo (except a shared `cabinet/` inside a project, which is part of the project's); each product repo has its own `.git` and is ignored here.

| Path | What it is | Owned by |
|---|---|---|
| `CABINET.md` | This file: how any Cabinet workspace runs | the kit |
| `AGENTS.md` (`CLAUDE.md` links to it) | This project: the team, the contracts, the house and product rules | the project |
| `cabinet.env` | Project settings: name, slug, roles, agent tool, backups, layout (the owner and week start are in `AGENTS.md`, the brief time in `jobs/brief.job`) | the project; `cabinet config` changes it |
| `HANDOFFS.md`, `handoffs/` | The one channel between agents, and its closed entries | every agent, by the rules below |
| `BRIEF.md` | The daily brief and the owner's sign-off queue (untracked) | chief-of-staff |
| `OPERATIONS.md` | The owner's manual | the owner, kept current by every agent that changes `bin/`, `jobs/` or the team |
| `agents/`, `.claude/agents/` | The role definitions, generated by `bin/role.sh build` from the kit's roles and `roles/` | generated |
| `roles/<role>.md` | This project's notes for a role, appended to the kit's definition | the project |
| `jobs/<job>.job` | Scheduled agent runs | the project |
| `guides/` | Standing documents every agent follows when its work touches their subject; listed in the "Guides" table of `AGENTS.md` | the owner; agents edit one only when asked |
| `specs/`, `notes/` | Specs, ADRs, verdicts; the owner's notes and decisions | as each role says |
| `repos.tsv` | Every product repo: clone URL, local-only files, `CLAUDE.md` link, and where it lives when not in the workspace | the project |
| `bin/`, `.cabinet/` | Kit scripts, roles, rules read when a task needs them (`.cabinet/rules/`), guardrails and schedule templates | the kit |

A workspace can also be a `cabinet/` folder inside a project (`cabinet init --inside`). Then the project's `AGENTS.md` points here, and every path in this file and in the roles is relative to `cabinet/`: run `cabinet/bin/handoff.sh list` from the project's top folder, or work from inside `cabinet/`. The project's repo is the `..` row of `repos.tsv`. When `cabinet.env` says `CABINET_LAYOUT="inside"` and `CABINET_VISIBILITY="private"`, nothing in `cabinet/` ever goes into the project's history; never move its contents into a tracked file of the project.

## Start of every session

1. Read this file, then `AGENTS.md` (its "Guides" table included), then your repo's `AGENTS.md`. Before any work a guide covers, read that guide and follow it.
2. Run `bin/handoff.sh list <your repo or role>`: it prints, in full, every open entry addressed to you. Pick up each one (see "Handoffs").
3. Before changing anything that crosses a repo line, check the contracts table in `AGENTS.md`.
4. If `BRIEF.md` exists, read its line for you.
5. Before a task one of these covers, read it; your role names the ones its job needs:

   | File | Read before |
   |---|---|
   | `.cabinet/rules/builders.md` | any work in a product repo you own (every builder session) |
   | `.cabinet/rules/ready-to-build.md` | writing, reviewing, routing or building from a spec, or filing work for a builder or taking it on |
   | `.cabinet/rules/reviews.md` | handing work on with something to show, or recording a verdict |
   | `.cabinet/rules/seats.md` | proposing, onboarding, reviewing or drafting a role |

6. `notes/` holds the owner's decisions and research. Read a note when the owner points to it or your task touches its `topic` or `repos`, and follow its `status` (`draft`, `decided`, `superseded`). Edit notes only when asked.

## Ownership

Each agent owns its repos end to end, documentation included, as the team table in `AGENTS.md` assigns them, one owner for each repo or area. An area inside another (`specs/qa/` inside `specs/`) belongs to its own row's owner: the most specific row wins. A part of a product repo given to a role other than the repo's owner is the owner's call, and `bin/doctor.sh` notes it (`team.nested`). No agent writes to a repo it does not own; reading any repo is always fine. A repo with no owning agent is changed only when the owner asks. When your change affects another repo, you file a handoff; you never edit that repo.

## Builders

Product repos are built by builder roles: `backend`, `web`, `mobile`, `infrastructure`, or any role that owns a product repo in the team table. A builder learns each repo before changing it and follows how it is built, works only from work that is ready to build, changes with a test, runs the repo's own checks, commits locally, hands finished work on with evidence, never verifies its own work, and keeps to its repos. The whole method is `.cabinet/rules/builders.md`.

## Ready to build

Nothing is built before it is defined, and nothing bigger than a small task before it is planned. A small task (one repo, no contract change, no decision for the owner, easy to undo) goes straight to a handoff filed with `--small`; anything else is built from a spec that `bin/spec.sh check` finds ready, routed with `--spec`; work that changes no repo takes the checks that fit it. Unsure whether a task is small? It is not. A builder given work that is not ready sends it back instead of guessing. The steps and what each status needs: `.cabinet/rules/ready-to-build.md`.

## Handoffs

`HANDOFFS.md` is the one channel between agents. It is durable, so work is never lost when a session ends, and it gives the owner one place to see everything in flight.

- **When your change affects another repo,** file an entry with `bin/handoff.sh add --from <you> --to <them> --changed "..." --needed "..." [--depends-on "..."] "<title>"`, which picks the next free ID and commits it; never by hand, since a hand-numbered entry can take an ID another agent is filing. It records who it is for, exactly what changed (endpoint, field, limit, status code, default, version, file), what they need to do, and the commit or branch it depends on. Name the entry ID in your summary.
- **Evidence is a link the owner can click:** what shows the work, filed with `--evidence <file or URL>`, or later with `bin/handoff.sh attach` (`.cabinet/rules/reviews.md`).
- **When an entry is addressed to you,** verify it against the code before acting: a handoff describes a change, the code is the truth. Set it to `acknowledged` when you start and `done` when your side lands, with the date and your commit. If it is wrong or not needed, set it to `rejected` with the reason.
- **Commit every edit to `HANDOFFS.md` at once,** as its own commit (`handoffs: ...`). If the file holds someone else's uncommitted lines, stage only yours and name the leftovers in your summary; chief-of-staff commits leftovers in its daily run.
- **Only edit entries addressed to you, and only their status lines.** Add a follow-up entry instead of rewriting another. Two more lines are written on an entry by others: the sender's `Evidence:` line, and each reviewer's `Verdict:` line. One exception beyond those: chief-of-staff may set any entry to `done` when the code shows it landed, and applies the owner's sign-off answers to the entries they name.
- **Dates in an entry's ID and status line are ISO (`2026-10-18`):** a machine format `bin/handoff.sh list` reads to age entries. Prose in an entry uses the house date format.
- **Status lines hold the current state only:** status, date, commit, one sentence. Replace the old state; git keeps the history.
- **A verdict is one line, written only with `bin/handoff.sh record`,** never by hand: `- Verdict: <role> <PASS|BLOCK|CHANGES> <date> <commits> <note>`. Its rules, and what `record` refuses: `.cabinet/rules/reviews.md`.
- **Entries addressed to `owner`** (`founder` means the same person) are decisions or actions only the owner can take.
- **Closed entries leave the file.** chief-of-staff runs `bin/handoff.sh archive` daily: it moves every committed `done` or `rejected` entry to `handoffs/archive-YYYY-MM.md` and commits the move. Archive files are read only. An ID stays unique across all of them (`bin/doctor.sh` checks).

## Decision rights and sign-off

The aim: an organization that runs itself and brings the owner only what needs the owner.

**Functions and leads.** Operations: chief-of-staff. Product: product-manager, with design-lead. Engineering: architect, with the repo agents. Quality and trust: qa, with security. Business: finance. A project enables the roles it needs in `cabinet.env`; a function whose lead is not enabled falls to the owner. A lead can grow a sub-team: roles that report to it and cover part of its work (`.cabinet/rules/seats.md`, "Sub-teams").

**Three tiers. Every decision belongs to exactly one.**

| Tier | Who decides | What | Logged in |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The agent | Reversible, inside its own repo or files, follows existing rules | Commit message or handoff status line |
| 2 | The function lead | Reversible, crosses repos or sets direction for the function, costs nothing | Spec Decisions table (product), ADR (engineering), `specs/design/` (design), qa and security verdicts |
| 3 | Owner sign-off | Irreversible, public, or costs money: push, merge, deploy, publish, release; prices, quotas, plans, coupons, any spend or paid service; the brand guide, logo, positioning, public copy; legal, privacy policy, data retention; adding, changing or removing an agent or its authority | The owner's sign-off queue |

A lead may move a tier 2 question up to the owner when unsure. Nobody moves a tier 3 question down. An agent unsure of the tier treats it as the higher one.

**When roles disagree,** or two roles each think a decision is theirs: within one function, its lead decides, as a tier 2 decision logged where that tier logs. Across functions, or when it is unclear whose call it is, it goes to the owner as one sign-off queue item with each role's view and recommendation. Neither role acts on the disputed point until it is settled.

**The sign-off queue.** One place: the top of `BRIEF.md`, kept by chief-of-staff. The owner answers in batches; chief-of-staff applies the answers into the right specs, ADRs and handoffs. Every decision put to the owner, by any agent, has:

- a plain-language question that stands on its own: what it is and why it matters now, with no unexplained item numbers, file names or jargon;
- lettered options, each with its consequence in one line;
- the recommendation of each relevant expert role, each with a one-line reason, the role named by its title where it has one (`bin/role.sh list`);
- one overall recommendation;
- whether the decision can be undone;
- for work to approve, its evidence links, copied from the handoff as they are.

Keep each item short. In a session, give each evidence link as its full path instead, which a terminal opens on a click.

**Silence.** A reversible tier 3 item marked "default" in the queue may go ahead after 72 hours without an objection, but only as far as local commits. Nothing is ever pushed, merged, deployed, published, spent or sent on silence.

**The builder never verifies.** Work is ready for the owner to push only when qa and security have each recorded PASS on its handoff, and so has every other reviewer the project enabled whose subject the change touches: design-lead for anything people see, code-reviewer for code, dba for a schema, migration or heavy query, and every reviewer a critical area it touches names (`AGENTS.md`, "Critical areas"; `.cabinet/rules/reviews.md`). A BLOCK (or a code-reviewer's CHANGES) holds the push until fixed; only the owner can override it. `bin/handoff.sh list --ready` computes it from the verdicts. qa never records PASS on a handoff without evidence (`.cabinet/rules/reviews.md`), so whatever reaches the owner to push shows what was built. A project without qa or security enabled sends that verification to the owner.

## Writing to the owner

Everything an agent writes for the owner (the brief, sign-off items, answers in a session, a handoff addressed to `owner`) follows "Writing to the owner" in `AGENTS.md`, "House rules".

**standard**: the sign-off format above, in plain words, each item short.

**short**: for an owner with little time to read, or who reads best in small pieces. Same facts and the same decisions, fewer words:

1. **Answer first.** The first line is the answer, or what you need from the owner, in one sentence.
2. **Lines, not paragraphs.** One point per line, about 15 words at most. Bold the word that matters in each line.
3. **Three points at most** per part or answer; then "N more: ask". Never cut a sign-off item, or a warning about anything irreversible, money, security or data loss.
4. **A sign-off item in three lines:** the question; the options on one line (`A: ... B: ...`, a few words each); `**Recommended: B**`, a reason in a few words, and `Undo: yes` or `Undo: no`. Name the experts only where one disagrees.
5. **No background** (history, reasoning, what was checked) unless the owner asks. End with one "Ask for details" line, not one per item.
6. **Plain words.** No file names, IDs or jargon unless the owner must act on them; then give the exact command or name. Evidence links stay, with a plain name as the link text ("the login page").
7. **Time to act**, when known: "2 min".

The brief, short: its first line says what waits today ("Today: 2 decisions, 1 action, about 5 min."), then the same `## ` headings (the digest reads them), each part at most three lines except the sign-off queue, which is always complete.

## Seats

A seat is an agent or a person, with the same rules for both. The kit keeps a small core of roles: any other seat is proposed from evidence in the work and in the project, as one sign-off item, and drafted for this project. Every seat is the owner's decision. How seats are spotted, proposed, onboarded, reviewed and drafted: `.cabinet/rules/seats.md`.

## The owner's manual

`OPERATIONS.md` is how the owner runs everything. Any change to `bin/`, `jobs/`, the roles or the owner's routine updates it in the same commit. `bin/doctor.sh` fails when the manual stops naming a script, job or role.

## Schedule

Agents also run on a local schedule (`bin/job.sh run`, one `jobs/<job>.job` each), starting with the daily chief-of-staff brief. Jobs are added as the owner trusts them. The scheduled runner (`jobs/pipeline.job`) moves ready work through build and review unattended, only when the owner turns it on, within a cost limit per run, and writes what it did to `PIPELINE.md`. `cabinet.env` names the agent tool that runs them (`CABINET_RUNNER`).

## Rules for every repo

- **Never push, merge, publish or release.** Only the owner does. It is enforced in every agent tool Cabinet knows (`bin/bootstrap.sh` installs the guardrails; the kit's `docs/guardrails.md` lists each tool and its limits): they deny `git push`, `gh pr merge`, `gh release`, write calls through `gh api`, package publishing, reading the GitHub token or the keychain, and the known ways of skipping git hooks as far as each tool's rule format allows; and a global git pre-push hook refuses any push not confirmed at the owner's terminal. Do not try to work around either: a way around them is a reason to stop and ask the owner, never a way to proceed.
- **Local commits are the only git write.** No push, merge, rebase, amend, reset or other history rewrite. A commit that fails review is reverted, or fixed in a follow-up commit; never amended.
- **Commit finished work at once.** Every agent commits its own finished, tested changes locally, each one separately with a clear message in the repo's style, authored and signed as `AGENTS.md` says. Uncommitted changes mean work in progress, and only that; an agent ending a session with uncommitted work says so and why. Commit only your own changes, by pathspec (`git commit -- <paths>`), never someone else's uncommitted work.
- **No fabrication.** Never invent names, limits, prices, dates, library choices or other specifics the owner has not stated or the code does not show. Write TBD, describe the capability, or read the canonical source. When corrected on a fabrication, audit recent work for the same mistake.
- **Missing tools are the owner's to install.** When `bin/doctor.sh` reports a tool Cabinet needs (`deps.required`) or one a feature needs (`deps.backups`), or `cabinet next --json` has the step `deps`, tell the owner in plain words what is missing, what stops working without it, and the exact install command it gives (`cabinet doctor --fix` runs it, asking first). Never install system packages yourself: they change the owner's machine and can need the owner's password.
- **No secrets in files.** Keys, tokens, passwords and `.env` values never go into a repo, a note, a handoff or a log. The workspace's pre-commit hook (`bin/secret.sh check`) refuses a commit that adds one; never mark a real secret `not-a-secret` to get past it.

## Working in a tool other than Claude Code

Everything here is plain files, so any agent tool, with any model it offers, can run the team. `AGENTS.md` is read by Codex, Antigravity, Qwen Code, Grok, opencode and Cursor, bootstrap sets Gemini CLI to read it, and `CLAUDE.md` links to it for Claude Code. To act as a role, read `agents/<role>.md` and follow it as your instructions. Claude Code also loads the same definitions from `.claude/agents/`.

A tool `bin/doctor.sh` names as having no guardrails is covered only by the git push gate: it could still merge, release or publish. Use it for reading and local edits, or ask the owner before giving it a task that touches GitHub or a package registry.


========================================================================
File: ROADMAP.md
========================================================================

# Roadmap

What Cabinet does next, in order. Each item says what is missing today, what it takes, and when it counts as done. Items move to `CHANGELOG.md` when they ship. Command names below follow `AGENTS.md`, "Command conventions", and are settled when an item is built (a new verb joins the verb list then).

**One rule for every item:** Cabinet is shaped by the people who use it, not built around one kind of project. It has to fit any product (a web app, a mobile app, a library, a service, client work, a business with little code), any team (one person to a small company, people and agents in any mix) and any experience (new to everything, or expert in some areas). So every item below is optional, turned on and tuned per project in its own settings, and has a sensible default for a project that does not care; nothing assumes a number of repos, a stack, a market, an outside service or a way of working. Where an item needs project-specific detail (what is critical, which contracts exist, what a release is), the project declares it, and the kit supplies the mechanism, not the content. The same holds for roles: the kit ships a small core, and every other seat is proposed from what the project has and needs and drafted for it, never added to the kit for one kind of project.

## 1. Windows support, through WSL

Windows runs Cabinet through WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux), which gives it Cabinet's Linux support (systemd timers when WSL runs systemd, else cron). Native Windows (PowerShell, or Git Bash, which lacks tools the scripts use) is not a goal.

- A README section: installing WSL, where the workspace should live (the WSL file system, not a mounted Windows drive, for git speed and file permissions), and running the agent tools inside WSL.
- The guardrails for agent tools installed inside WSL; a note on tools installed on the Windows side, which those guardrails do not cover.
- The test suite run under WSL once.

Done when: the full test suite passes under WSL, and the README walks a Windows user from nothing to a working workspace.

## Toward a single download

The goal: a person installs one thing, and Cabinet needs nothing else but git and an agent tool. Today it needs git, Node.js and npm (openssl for backups). New logic is JavaScript run with Node, using only Node's own modules, so it can be compiled later (`AGENTS.md`, rule 3). What is left:

- **One file, no runtime.** Waits until it is needed (people without Node). Until then the bash moves to JavaScript one command at a time, when a command is slow or being reworked, never as a rewrite on its own. When the shell scripts are thin wrappers, Cabinet is compiled with Bun into one file per platform (macOS on Apple and Intel chips, Linux on x64 and ARM), with Bun's built-in encryption in place of openssl. It is installed with a one-line installer, Homebrew or a GitHub release; npm stays as a wrapper that fetches the right file. The workspace scripts (`bin/*.sh`) become one-line wrappers that call it, so agents and schedules work as before. This also opens native Windows, not only WSL. Done when: a machine with only git and an agent tool installs Cabinet with one download and the full test suite passes against the compiled file.

## For founders without every skill

The goal: Cabinet is equally useful to a founder with no technical or business background and to one who is expert in one area (engineering, design, sales) and lacks the rest, and equally useful for a project that is only an idea and for an established one with code, users, a team and its own ways of working. The team fills what the founder lacks, explains what the founder must decide in the founder's terms, and stays out of the way where the founder is the expert. Today the kit is strong at governance (who decides, independent review, guardrails, the daily sign-off) but assumes the founder knows how to build and run a product. Items marked **pick first** come before the rest. Every item works for both kinds of project: for an established one it learns what is there and follows it, and it never replaces the project's stack, conventions or rules with defaults.

- **The founder's profile.** Ties the items below together. At setup (and with `cabinet config`), the founder says what they know well and what they do not, area by area: engineering, design, product, marketing, finance, legal and admin. Every role reads it: where the founder is expert, agents bring fewer and more technical decisions and skip the explanations; where the founder is new, they explain more, bring the choices pre-made with a recommendation, and say when a professional is needed. Done when: the same decision reaches an expert founder as a short technical choice and a new founder as a plain question with the trade-offs explained, from one profile setting.
- **From an idea to a plan** (pick first). Today the kit starts once a product exists, with `TBD` lines in `AGENTS.md` to fill. A kickoff, run once at setup or any time after, in one of two modes. For a new idea, the product-manager interviews the founder (the problem, who has it, what is in and out of the first version, how success is measured). For an established project, the team first learns what exists (the code, the docs, the git history, the open issues, how it is built, tested and deployed) and asks the founder only what none of that tells. Either way it writes `AGENTS.md`, the specs and a roadmap (for an established project, the current state and what is next), each marked for the founder to confirm, and proposes the seats the project needs from what it found (`CABINET.md`, "Seats"), each as a sign-off item, so the team starts shaped to the project. Done when: a founder with only an idea, or with a running product, ends the kickoff with no `TBD` in "What the project is" and "Product rules", and a ranked roadmap that starts from where the project really is.
- **Guard the founder's time and money** (pick first). Today Cabinet counts what its own runs cost when the runner is `claude`, with a weekly budget the doctor warns about from 80% (`cabinet config --budget`). Every built-in runner is counted (token-only runners at a price the owner sets). Still missing: a successful live run with `qwen`, and one with cache reads on `antigravity`, to confirm their success output, the cost of sessions people run in an agent tool, and a daily cap on the sign-off queue (for example five decisions, ranked; the rest wait, and the brief says how many), since for a solo founder the queue is the bottleneck, and every role a project adds sends it more. Done when: the week's spend counts sessions too, and no brief asks more decisions than the cap.
- **Setup without terminal skills.** Today `cabinet new`, `init`, `bootstrap` and `doctor --fix` check the tools Cabinet needs and offer to install the missing ones, but Node.js and npm must be there first (npm installs Cabinet), and setup still uses quoted options and terms like launchd. One install command, run before Node.js exists, that installs it and Cabinet; messages in plain language, with the technical detail one step away; and `cabinet next` steps that say why each matters. Done when: a founder who has never used a terminal reaches a working workspace by following the screen.
- **Decisions that do not assume expertise.** Today a founder can be asked to pick a database, a host or a payments provider without knowing the trade-offs. Starter stacks, for new projects only: one recommended, well-supported stack for each kind of product, so the first technical choices are made and can be changed later (an established project keeps its stack). And in every technical decision, new or established, what each option costs and what changing it later would take. Done when: a new project's first technical choices arrive made, an established project's stack is never replaced by a starter, and each technical decision shows cost and the cost of changing course.
- **After launch: running, customers and growth.** Today no seat covers production, customers or growth, and the kit will not ship a role for each: the kit keeps a small core, and other seats come from the project. When the product goes live, or at setup for one already live, the team proposes the seats it needs from what the project has (its hosting, monitoring, support inbox, analytics, audience and channels) and drafts each for this project (`cabinet role add`), with its checklist: incidents and rollback for running it, support replies turned into specs, launch and growth work drafted for the owner to approve. Done when: a live product gets a proposed owner for incidents, customers and growth, each drafted from the project, with no kit role added for them.
- **Business basics.** Today nothing tracks the business side a founder without advisors misses: forming a company, a privacy policy and terms, taxes and invoicing, app store rules. A checklist role that tracks these, reminds at the right moment and says when to get a professional; its definition forbids legal or tax advice of its own. Done when: a workspace shows which basics are done, open or need a professional, and the role never gives a legal or tax answer itself.
- **People and agents side by side.** Today every repo or area has an owning agent. An established team has people who own parts of it. Each repo or area is owned by an agent, by a person, or shared: where a person owns it, agents read and propose (a branch, a patch or a handoff with the change) and the person reviews and decides; the team table and the brief say which is which. Done when: no agent changes a person-owned area except by a proposal that person accepts.
- **Work the team's way.** Today agents commit locally and the owner pushes. A team may work through branches, pull requests, required reviews and CI. Agents follow the project's own workflow (branch names, commit style, opening a pull request for review where the team does) while push, merge and release stay with people, as the guardrails already make sure. Done when: in a project that works by pull requests, every agent change arrives as one, and nothing merges without a person.
- **The existing backlog** (needs the owner's decision first: it reads an outside service). An established project's open issues and roadmap live in its tracker. A one-time import, then a regular read, turns them into specs and handoffs with links back, without changing the tracker. Done when: the team's open work appears in the workspace, each item linked to its source, and nothing is written to the tracker.
- **Learn by example.** Today the templates show the format, full of `TBD`. A filled example workspace for a made-up product (a finished `AGENTS.md`, real-looking handoffs, a brief with its sign-off queue, a spec, a guide), shipped in the docs and kept in step with the templates by the tests. Done when: every template file has a filled counterpart in the example, and the tests fail when they drift apart.

## Running the work

Patterns proven in daily use of an agent team, made general. Each is optional and declared by the project; items marked **pick first** come before the rest.

- **An inventory of what exists** (pick first). Today nothing records what the project actually holds and what state each piece is in: specs say what was planned and handoffs what changed, never the whole. A living list of every piece of work, its state, where it lives, what it depends on, and the source it is checked against, re-checked against those files by an agent and verified by qa. What a row is and which states it has are proposed for the project at setup and confirmed by the owner, as seats are: for an app, a capability (planned, built, behind a flag, live), read from the code; for an album, a track (demo, recorded, mixed, mastered, released), from the project files; for a design system, a component or screen (draft, in review, approved, in use), from the design files and exports; for any other work, whatever it delivers. It is the base for the roadmap, pricing and plans, the first thing the kickoff writes for an established project, and part of making work that is not code as complete as code (below). Done when: every piece of work in the project's files is in the list, and a re-check reports any that were added, changed or removed, for a code project and for at least one other kind, such as a design or content project.
- **Push deploys, said plainly** (pick first). Today nothing marks a repo where pushing goes live. A column in `repos.tsv` says what a push does (nothing, deploys a preview, deploys to production, publishes a release), and the brief, the digest and the sign-off queue say so beside every push the owner is asked for: "pushing this goes live". Done when: every push request for a repo marked as deploying says it is a live deploy.
- **Checks on contracts between repos.** Today the contracts table names each contract and its source of truth, and nothing verifies them. A contract can name its check (a script, a schema comparison, a test), run by the doctor and by qa before a push; a change on one side that breaks the other is caught then, not by users. Done when: a declared contract with a check fails the review of a change that breaks it.
- **One Cabinet per person, one rulebook.** Today teammates share one workspace: one team table, one handoff log, one sign-off queue. The way Cabinet was first used by a team was different: each person ran their own Cabinet, with their own agents and their own sign-off, all following one shared set of guides, design system, workflow and process toward the same goal. First check what the shared layout already gives (the guides, roles and rules travel with the workspace; `BRIEF.md` is per machine), then close the gaps: personal workspaces that follow a team's shared guides and rules, updated from one place, with handoffs between people's Cabinets where work crosses. Done when: two people each run their own Cabinet on one project, both follow the same guides without copying them, and a change to the shared guides reaches both.
- **Work that is not code, as complete as code.** Today Cabinet's defaults assume code: builders own repos, the pipeline ends at "ready to push", and the guardrails guard push and publish. Other work (design, writing, marketing, music, finance) already runs through roles drafted for it and specs on workspace areas, but nothing is shaped for it. Each kind of output gets what code has: an owner that makes it, an independent review before it counts as done, a "ready" state, and a guardrail on the step that makes it public or spends money (publishing a post, releasing a track, sending a payment). Done when: a project with no code runs from spec to reviewed, ready output, and nothing goes public or costs money without the owner.
- **One writer for shared outputs.** Today two agents can work in the same repo copy and collide. A project can name a repo or area with a single writer (a docs site, a website, a release): the others write their part in their own repos and hand it off, and only the writer commits there. Done when: in a single-writer area, every commit comes from its writer, and the others' content arrives through handoffs.
- **A market watch job.** Today nothing keeps an eye on the market. An optional weekly job tracks what the project names: other products, prices, launches, reviews, rules in its industry, and reports what changed since last week, for the team only. Done when: a project that turns it on gets a weekly report of changes, and nothing from it reaches anything published.

## Ideas to pick from

Not ranked yet; each is picked and ordered when its implementation starts.

### The daily loop

- **Answer from the digest.** Today `cabinet digest` gathers every sign-off queue, but each answer still means going into that workspace. `cabinet -C <workspace> answer "1: approve; 2: no"` delivers the answers to that workspace, where its chief-of-staff applies them on its next run, as if given there. Done when: answers given from anywhere reach the right workspace once, are applied there, and the next digest no longer lists them.
- **A decisions log.** Today the owner's answers are applied into specs and handoffs, so "what did I decide about X, and when" means searching several files. Each answer is recorded with its date, the question and the outcome in one file per workspace, and `cabinet decision list [word]` searches it. Done when: every applied answer has its entry, and a search by word finds it.
- **A weekly review job.** Today the daily brief looks at today. An optional job, on the day the week starts, sums up the week: what shipped, which handoffs closed, which decisions were made, what is stuck and for how long, and how that compares with the week before. Done when: a workspace can turn it on in setup or config, and it runs on the week's first day.
- **Run history and failure alerts.** Today a failed scheduled run shows only as a late brief the next day. `cabinet job list` shows each job's recent runs (when, how long, success or failure, from the job logs), and a failed scheduled run, or one stopped by its time limit, can send a notification and is named in the next brief. Done when: a failing job is reported the same morning, and `cabinet job list` shows its last runs.

### Cost

- **The brief's facts from a script.** Today chief-of-staff gathers most of the brief by hand on every run: open handoffs and their ages, commits named in handoffs and whether they are pushed or on the main branch, each repo's branches and uncommitted files, the doctor's problems, commits against the house rules (`roles/chief-of-staff.md`, "The brief", steps 1 to 9). These are facts, not judgment, and every run pays for an agent to collect them. `bin/brief.sh facts` (with `--json`) gathers them in shell, the brief job passes them in, and the agent writes only what needs judgment: ranking the queue, what is stale or wrong, what to pick up next. Done when: the same workspace gives the same brief with the facts gathered by the script, the facts are right in cases the tests set up (a pushed and an unpushed commit, a side branch, a stale entry), and a run reads fewer files.

### Control

- **Write limits per role, enforced.** Today each role's "What you may write" is an instruction the agent follows; only push, merge and publish are enforced, by the guardrails. The doctor compares a project role's write list with the team table (`roles.writes`) and `cabinet role add --owns` refuses an area another role owns, but nothing stops a write, and every agent commits as the same person, so nothing tells which role made a change or recorded a verdict (`--role` on `record` is what the agent types). The more roles a project has, the more places one can step outside its lane unnoticed until a reviewer sees it. Where a tool supports rules per agent (Claude Code agents' tools and permissions, for example), build each role with deny rules for the paths and repos it does not own, from the team table; elsewhere, a check after each run (or a pre-commit hook in the workspace) that names the files a role changed outside its own. Each tool's per-agent rule shape is confirmed live before the kit relies on it. A run that knows its role (a scheduled job, `cabinet role start`) passes it on, so `record` takes the role from the run instead of from what is typed. Done when: in each tool that can enforce it, a role cannot write outside what the team table gives it, in the others the change is reported the same day, and a verdict recorded in a role's run carries that role.
- **Pause and resume.** Today stopping the schedules for a holiday, a trip or a project on hold means turning them off one by one and setting them up again. `cabinet pause [until <date>]` stops every schedule of one workspace, or of all of them with `--all`, and `cabinet resume` (or the date passing) brings them back exactly as they were; `cabinet list`, the digest and the doctor show a paused workspace as paused, not broken. Done when: pause and resume leave every schedule as it was, and a pause with a date ends on its own.
- **Guardrails status and removal.** Today the guardrails are checked per workspace by the doctor, and removed by hand from each tool's settings. `cabinet guardrail list` shows, for every agent tool on the machine, which of the kit's rules are in place, and `cabinet guardrail remove` takes out exactly what Cabinet added (from the backups bootstrap made, or rule by rule), leaving the owner's own rules. Done when: after `remove`, each tool's settings match what they were before the first bootstrap, apart from the owner's later changes.

### Starting and working

- **Choose the model, and check it exists.** Today Cabinet chooses only the agent tool (`CABINET_RUNNER`); every scheduled job runs with that tool's default model, and the only way to name a model is a custom runner command, which nothing checks and which loses what the built-in runners pass (such as the named role). A `--model` setting for the workspace (`CABINET_MODEL`) and an optional `MODEL=` per job file (one model for the brief, another for heavier jobs), passed through each tool's own model option. The check: where a tool can list its models without a paid call, setup, config and `cabinet doctor` confirm the model is there; where it cannot, an explicit opt-in check makes one short real call, since that costs a little. Each tool's model option and listing command is confirmed live before the kit relies on it, as the Cursor rules were. Done when: a mistyped model is caught before the first scheduled run in every tool that can tell, and the docs say for each tool which kind of check it gets.

- **`cabinet role start <role>`.** Today a session as a role is set up by hand in the agent tool. `cabinet role start qa` opens the configured agent tool in the workspace with that role's definition and its open handoffs loaded, for every tool Cabinet supports. Done when: one command starts a working session as any enabled role, in each supported tool.
- **Adopt an existing agent setup.** Today a workspace built by hand (its own `AGENTS.md`, handoff log, role definitions, notes) can only be rebuilt from scratch. `cabinet adopt` maps what it finds onto Cabinet's files, keeping the content and history, and lists what it could not map. Done when: a hand-built workspace becomes a Cabinet workspace without losing a file, and `cabinet doctor` passes on it.

### Teams

- **A shared library of roles and guides.** Today a role or guide written for one project is copied by hand into the next. `cabinet role add <git url | workspace>` (and `cabinet guide add`) installs it, records where it came from, and updates it the way the kit updates, never over a local edit. Done when: a team keeps one copy of a role or guide and every project that uses it can take its updates.
- **Handoff IDs across copies of a workspace.** Today one workspace folder never gives two handoffs the same ID (filing takes a lock, and only `cabinet handoff add` files), but two copies, such as a teammate's clone, each number on their own, and the doctor finds a clash only after they are merged (`handoffs.unique-ids`). Each copy gets a short tag of its own in `cabinet.local.env`, added to the IDs it files (`H-20261020-03-k7`), read everywhere an ID is read today (`list`, `attach`, `record`, the archives, the doctor). Wait until a team shares a workspace. Done when: two copies filing on the same day never make the same ID, and IDs from before the change still work.
- **`cabinet update --dry-run`.** Today an update applies at once and stops only on an edited kit file. The dry run lists every kit file the update would change, with the diff, and the changelog it would show, and writes nothing. Done when: the dry run predicts exactly what the update then does.

### Needing the owner's decision first

These send data out of the machine or depend on outside services, so each starts as a decision for the owner.

- **Digest notifications by email, Slack or Telegram**, for owners away from the machine.
- **A CI check for shared workspaces**, verifying the handoff log, the built roles and the guides table on every pull request.

## Later, when a project needs it

- **Hardening found in review:** archives use AES-256-CBC without a MAC (tampering shows only as a tar or gzip error); the keychain item can be read without a prompt by any process of the user (deny rules stop agents in the guarded tools; creating the item to always ask would need a decision for scheduled backups); the passphrase file used with cron is denied to agents only in shell commands that name its folder (a file reader, Cursor, Codex and Antigravity can still read it); opencode agent-level and project-level configs, and Qwen workspace settings, can loosen the global rules (`bin/doctor.sh` checks only the global result); folder names without Latin letters or digits need `--slug`; on opencode 2.x, `bin/doctor.sh` cannot read the resolved permission rules (its debug commands need opencode's background service), so its guardrails are unverified there.

- **Linux beyond Debian:** the kit is tested on Debian only. Done when: the suite passes on Fedora and Arch too.

- **More than one owner:** today the kit assumes one person signs off. Two founders, or a lead per area, each sign off their own decisions: owners named in `AGENTS.md` with what each decides, every sign-off item addressed to one of them, the brief's queue grouped by owner, and the digest showing each person only their own. The push gate and guardrails stay per person. Wait until a team needs it: it is the largest change here. Done when: an item addressed to one owner reaches only that owner, and an owner's answer applies only to their items.
- **One machine runs the jobs, without asking teammates:** in a shared workspace, a teammate must remember `cabinet bootstrap --no-schedules`, or their machine schedules the brief too and the team gets two. A choice to study: record in the shared `cabinet.env` which machine runs the jobs (filled at setup with the owner's machine), so bootstrap on any other machine skips schedules on its own and names the machine that runs them, while `--schedules` still lets a machine take over. Open questions: how to tell machines apart (the computer name changes when a machine is renamed, which would stop its schedules until re-recorded), what the doctor reports on each side, and how a handover works when the owner's machine is gone. Done when: a teammate who clones a shared workspace and runs a plain `cabinet bootstrap` schedules nothing, and the owner's machine keeps its schedules.
- **Projects in other languages:** `cabinet init` reads `pyproject.toml`, `Cargo.toml`, `go.mod` and `composer.json` for the name, description and test commands, as it reads `package.json` today.
- **Install without Node.js:** `git clone` and one symlink, with the version pin kept as a git tag in `cabinet/.cabinet/` and read by `cabinet update`. The npm package stays the main route.
- **Search by meaning across the workspace's history:** today agents find past decisions and handoffs by reading the files and searching them by word, which works while the archives are small. When a project's handoff archives (and the decisions log, once it exists) outgrow that, so agents miss an earlier decision or a search returns more than they can read, an optional index answers questions by meaning ("what did we decide about pricing?"). The Markdown stays the only source of truth: the index is built from it, rebuilt when it changes, never committed or backed up, never written by an agent, and can be deleted at any time; every agent tool keeps working without it. Wait until a real workspace needs it. Done when: with the index on, an agent finds a past decision that a word search misses, and deleting the index loses nothing.


========================================================================
File: CHANGELOG.md
========================================================================

# Changelog

Each version says what changed and anything a workspace must do by hand after `npx cabinet update`, which prints these entries.

## 0.1.2 - Unreleased

### Commands

- `cabinet update` commits the update itself (`cabinet: update to <version>`, with the pin from `npm update`; an edit of the owner's own elsewhere in `package.json` keeps it and its lockfile out of the commit, and the commit it prints for them names `package-lock.json` only when there is one) in a workspace with its own git, unless the files it rewrites held uncommitted edits of the owner's; then it ends with the commit to run, as before. Its last line is now one short sentence instead of a long command. Where there is nothing to commit (a workspace with no git of its own, or a private `cabinet/` the project ignores) it ends with `Updated to <version>.`, and says "Nothing changed" only when the workspace was already on that version.
- `cabinet config` commits its change (`cabinet config: <the settings changed>`, only the files that run wrote, so a handoff or another file someone else writes while it runs stays theirs) in a workspace with its own git that had no uncommitted changes before; otherwise it says to review and commit, as before. `cabinet repo add`, which goes through `config`, commits the same way (`cabinet config: add repo`). With `role add`, `role remove`, `update` and `bootstrap`, these commands now commit their own change; the rest, such as `repo snapshot`, still leave it to review and commit.
- `cabinet version`, in a terminal, shows the approved tagline beside the mark ("One person, a whole team. Build anything with AI agents, and stay in charge."), as does the brand guide's sample of it; it showed an older one.
- `cabinet next` no longer asks to fill the TBDs of a finished `AGENTS.md`: it counted the template's own instructions, which quote `TBD` as code ("write `none` in place of `TBD`"). Only a TBD left to fill counts.
- `cabinet help` shows each group of commands once, with all its commands under it; "Daily" and "Team" appeared twice.
- A mistyped command gets a short answer instead of the whole help: `cabinet: unknown command 'docter'`, `Did you mean: cabinet doctor` when one is near, and `Every command: cabinet help`. It still exits 2.
- A critical area whose name has spaces (`| setup and untrusted values | ...` in `AGENTS.md`) can now be named in a spec's `areas`. `cabinet spec check` split the names into words and refused it as no critical area, and `cabinet handoff list` and the brief did the same with the spec's list, so work routed from that spec missed the area's reviewers. Area names are kept whole, split only on the commas of `areas: [...]`; one-word names work as before.
- `cabinet config --backup-dir <folder>` works in a workspace whose `cabinet.local.env` has no backup folder of its own (any new workspace). It ended with exit 2 and no output, writing nothing; now it lists `backups: off -> <folder>`, writes it and commits it.

### Releases

- The release workflow checks out the full history with its tags, so the check on changes after a release runs on GitHub too; without the tags it passed unseen.
- The tests fail when the test file itself does not parse. Before, a syntax error in it ended the run with success, so a release could have published with no tests run.

### Schedules

- A scheduled run that finishes on its own is no longer reported as stopped by its time limit when the machine slept during it. The limit counts only time awake, but the report compared the clock on the wall, so a morning brief that ran across a sleep and finished was logged as stopped, with exit 124. Now only a run the time limit actually stopped is reported as stopped.

### Docs

- The docs no longer show 0.1.0 as the current version: the README's status line points to the changelog instead of naming a version, and the tutorial and the brand guide show the current one. The tests fail when a doc shows a Cabinet version other than the one in `package.json`, so a release cannot leave the docs behind.
- The README says Cabinet is built and maintained with Cabinet.
- The kit's `AGENTS.md` says several sessions may work in the repo at once, and how each commits only its own changes, leaving the rest as they are (rule 12).

## 0.1.1 - 23 Oct 2026
